#5613. Autonomous site reliability engineering startup Traversal bags $120M in funding at a $1B valuation

Traversal Inc., a startup that’s trying to automate site reliability engineering tasks with artificial intelligence agents, seems to be closing in on that goal after raising $120 million in fresh funding, bringing its valuation to $1 billion.

The newly minted unicorn’s round was led by Kleiner Perkins, Redpoint Ventures and Khosla Ventures, three of Silicon Valley’s highest-profile venture capital firms, whose names should give it the credibility it needs to accelerate its growth plans. Sequoia Capital – another big VC name – also participated in the round, alongside Battery Ventures and Amex Ventures.

AI might have made the job of software developers much easier than it used to be, but for the site reliability engineers tasked with maintaining the infrastructure to run that code, it has only made life much more difficult. The influx of AI-generated code has put infrastructure engineers under intense pressure, and they’re struggling to keep up.

According to a report earlier this year by Splunk Inc. and Oxford Economics, enterprise downtime costs have risen more than 50% in the last two years, draining up to $600 billion annually from businesses worldwide. That’s because software developers have increased their code output by around 180% over the same timeframe, which means those poor infrastructure engineers are forced to work harder than ever to match their growing output.

Enter Traversal, which is coming to the rescue with a highly promising autonomous site reliability engineer that’s designed to assist human specialists by diagnosing, remediating and preventing information technology infrastructure problems. Instead of just keeping watch and firing off alerts to human engineers when an outage occurs, Traversal actively investigates any issues that pop up and does its best to fix them so as to ease their ungodly workload.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Anish Agarwal said there’s an urgent need for a specialized AI site reliability engineer, because not even the best general-purpose large language models have been able to show they’re up to the task. He points to the ORCA-bench benchmark that his company co-developed alongside researchers from Cornell Tech and Columbia University. It reveals that even the most advanced frontier models barely achieve 25% accuracy on medium-difficulty SRE tasks, with their hallucination rates often exceeding 40%.

“Site reliability engineering is one of the hardest problems in applied AI because every company’s software environment is different, and with downtime costing companies as much as $600 billion a year, the stakes are clearly enormous,” Agarwal said.

Traversal’s AI far surpasses what the best frontier models can do. It’s designed to be deployed in enterprises’ IT environments, where it sits and analyzes massive volumes of operational telemetry, including logs, metrics and traces, so as to establish a baseline for normal behavior. When problems occur, it uses causal machine learning to identify the root cause of the issue, and then works out a solution so all the human engineer has to do is accept its recommendation to restore normal service.

Agarwal’s background in causal machine learning is the key to Traversal’s AI SRE’s much higher accuracy. It’s an AI discipline that combines causal inference with machine learning to identify cause-and-effect relationships, rather than relying on statistical correlations. In essence, it enables Traversal’s models to simulate the effects of various actions, interventions and policy changes have on IT infrastructure, so it can quickly work out what the likely cause of a problem is.

Agarwal said the company is striving to build a “superintelligent AI SRE” that can finally help enterprises to keep pace with the rapid velocity of their AI-enabled developer teams. And he believes it’s well on the way to achieving that goal. “After two years refining our technology, we’re seeing customers expand how they use Traversal across increasingly complex production environments,” he said.

In the last year, Traversal has grown its revenue more than nine-fold and its number of monthly active users has multiplied by 20. Some of its best-known customers include Pepsi Co., DigitalOcean Holdings Inc., Nubank and Harvey AI Corp.

Traversal’s momentum is impressive, but Agarwal said the company is only just getting started. With $120 million in the bank, it’s going to accelerate hiring within its engineering, go-to-market and research and development teams so it can get closer to its goal of building a superintelligent AI SRE.

Kleiner Perkins’ Aditya Naganath said Traversal is the first company he has seen that brings “real intelligence” into complex production environments, and he’s confident there’s going to be enormous demand for it. “As AI dramatically accelerates the pace at which software is written and shipped, the complexity of managing production will only grow,” he predicted. “Traversal gives engineering teams the intelligence they need to understand their systems, resolve incidents faster and operate with confidence at scales that simply weren’t possible before.”

#5612. To Sell or Rent? How To Choose the Best Path for Your House.

Selling your house is a big step, and you want it to go smoothly. And with houses taking a little longer to sell these days, renting it out might start to sound like a nice backup plan.

But the reality is, while renting can work well for some people, it’s also a big commitment. So before you decide, it helps to see the whole picture first.

Lately, some sellers are choosing to hang on to their houses and rent them out instead. According to Parcl, around 9% of homes for rent right now were previously up for sale.

Some homeowners put their houses on the market expecting a faster process than they got or a certain price buyers didn’t respond to. And when things didn’t go exactly as planned, they decided to rent instead. As Kara Ng, Senior Economist at Zillow, explains:

“Bargaining power is tilting toward buyers and homes are taking longer to sell, making renting out a property one way to buy time rather than compete aggressively on price.”

But here’s the important distinction. Just because some sellers are choosing to rent doesn’t mean selling isn’t working. In many cases, the difference comes down to how well a house is priced, prepared, and marketed for today’s buyers.

Parcl data shows where these “accidental landlords” – owners who planned to sell but decided to rent instead – are most common (see graph below):

They make up around 17% of homes for rent in places like Sherman and Houston, TX, but less than 4% in markets like Des Moines, IA and Bloomington, IN.

That’s a pretty big difference. And it shows why you have to know what’s happening in your neighborhood. Your market, your asking price, and your strategy all play a role in how your sale goes.

A local agent can show you how houses like yours are selling, what strategies work best, and help you weigh your options – not to push you to sell, but so you at least have the full picture based on today’s market. And part of making an informed decision is understanding what renting your house would actually take.

While renting might sound like easy passive income on paper, in practice, it’s a hands-on job with rules to follow. As Invest West Management puts it:

“Even if you never intended to become a landlord, the law still sees you as one — and you must meet all legal obligations that come with that role. This often includes registering the tenancy, providing tenants with certain disclosures, and ensuring the property meets safety standards.”

You’d also be the one chasing missed rent payments, fixing damage between tenants, and covering unexpected repairs. Not to mention fielding weekend calls about leaky dishwashers or broken AC units.

There are expenses beyond regular maintenance and repairs, too. According to Bankrate, these are a few of the biggest:

Insurance premiums (landlord insurance typically costs about 25% more than a standard homeowners policy)

Management fees (if you hire a property manager, they usually charge around 10% of the rent)

Gaps between tenants, when you pay the mortgage without rental income

If you want to be a landlord and you’re prepared for the responsibility, renting may be a great fit. But if you’d really rather sell, don’t let today’s market convince you that you can’t.

A great agent can make it happen. The key is having an open conversation up front with your agent about pricing and how to market your house. Nailing those details from day 1 helps your house make a great first impression, so renting doesn’t have to be your fallback.

Renting can be a good fit for the right person with the right house, but it isn’t the only option. A smart sales strategy can help your house stand out to buyers from day one.So, if you’re on the fence, a local real estate agent can help you compare what selling and renting would each look like for you.

#5611. Sentra raises $150M to control what AI agents can reach in corporate data

Data security startup Sentra Inc. today revealed it has raised $150 million in new funding to expand its platform for controlling what artificial intelligence agents can reach inside corporate data stores.

Sentra, which provides data security software, says its business grew more than 300% over the past year. The platform works on data at rest, wherever an enterprise happens to keep it.

Each customer gets classification tuned to its own business. Alongside that sits an identity map of which people, service accounts and AI agents can reach a given dataset, inherited permissions included.

Every AI agent a company switches on is another identity reading its data, often around the clock, with no central control plane overseeing it. Sentra expects agent counts at large enterprises to climb steeply over the next few years. Only a small minority of organizations have governance in place to control what those agents touch, according to the company.

Sentra co-founder and Chief Executive Yoav Regev called agents “the busiest consumers of enterprise data.” In Regev’s view, many of them inherit access to data that has never been fully classified or governed, and traditional perimeter controls were not built for agents moving at machine speed. “What organizations can do is make sure the data those agents reach is already secured,” he said.

To get there, Sentra removes stale and high-risk data that no agent has any reason to see, and service accounts and agents get only the minimum access their work calls for. An agent that later reaches for sensitive data it does not normally touch gets flagged. The platform can then strip the permissions or sharing involved on its own, and the worst cases are passed to whoever owns the data.

After an incident, legal and compliance teams get a record from Sentra of everything the agent could have reached, including business context on each dataset.

The analysis behind all of this happens inside the customer’s own environment, so sensitive data never leaves it. Sentra contends that tools that copy customer data into a vendor’s environment leave buyers with a second data estate to protect, adding retention and residency risk in regulated industries.

Product spending from the round will focus on visibility into the agents, copilots and models touching sensitive data. Faster containment is another priority, for cases where an agent behaves unexpectedly. Commercially, Sentra plans to scale its field and channel programs and push into new geographies.

Capital One Financial Corp.’s venture arm, Capital One Ventures, led the Series C round and will place a representative on Sentra’s board of directors. The firm joins existing investors Bessemer Venture Partners LP, Zeev Ventures, Standard Investments Inc., Munich Re Ventures and Key1 Capital. Key1 led a $50 million Series B round for the company in April 2025. Sentra did not disclose a valuation.

Regev started Sentra in 2021 with Asaf Kochan, Ron Reiter and Yair Cohen. Kochan is a former commander of the Israeli military’s Unit 8200, where Regev once headed the cyber department. Including the new round, investors have put more than $260 million into the company since its launch.

#5610. Why More Buyers Are Turning To Adjustable-Rate Mortgages Today

When mortgage rates climb, buying a home can start to feel like trying to hit a moving target. Every jump in rates makes monthly payments bigger, and that pushes a lot of buyers to look for another way in.

More and more of them are finding it in the adjustable-rate mortgage, or ARM.

Here’s how an ARM differs from a more traditional mortgage. With a regular fixed-rate mortgage, your rate stays the same for your whole loan. But with an ARM, your rate is locked for the first few years, then it can move up or down based on market conditions.

Some people don’t like that level of uncertainty – and that’s okay. But others are drawn to this option specifically because there’s usually a lower rate to start when you opt for an ARM. And in an affordability-strapped market, that’s going to gain popularity.

Bankrate recently found that, in September, rates for ARM products were over a full percentage point lower than a regular fixed-rate loan. Depending on the ARM product, that can make a difference of $150-300 in the monthly payment on a median-priced home.

And for some buyers, that’s enough to turn “not right now” into “let’s do this.” You can see it in the numbers. Data from the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) shows that, in October, roughly 1 in 10 people applying for a mortgage chose an ARM (see graph below):

If you think you may want to consider this yourself, here’s what you need to know about how it works.

An ARM is like a phone or cable plan that has an introductory deal for new customers. You start out at a lower price, and then it adjusts after a specified amount of time. A popular loan is the 5/1 ARM.

The “5” means your introductory rate is locked for the first five years, and the “1” means that the rate can change every year after that. The rate change is called the “reset.” And here’s the really important part.

When your rate resets, your mortgage payment could go up or down. The good news is that most ARMs have caps, which are limits on how much your rate can rise each year and over the life of the loan. But either way, you have to be ready.

To see if this type of loan may be right for you, here are some things to think about and discuss with your loan officer:

Before you decide, ask your lender to work up the numbers and walk you through the different potential scenarios you could run into with an ARM. That way, you go in with your eyes open.

And, if you do go with an adjustable-rate mortgage, just know that you’ll have choices when the reset time arrives. You could:

Do nothing and keep your loan in place if the new payment still fits your budget.

Refinance into a fixed-rate loan with a payment that never changes.

Refinance into another ARM with a new lower rate locked for a specified timeframe.

Talk to the loan servicer about assistance or modification.

Remember, a refinance is a brand-new loan that you’ll have to qualify for – even if it’s on a home you already own. So, keep tabs on your credit and debt levels and ask your loan officer how major financial moves like job changes and major purchases will affect your mortgage readiness. It’s important to keep your credit and finances in “mortgage shape.”

One more quick note. ARMs got a bad name after the financial crisis of 2008. Back then, there were some risky loans with small starting payments that later shot way up. Others let people borrow without proving how much money they earned.

But now, there are new laws to protect both borrowers and lenders. The biggest change is the Ability-to-Repay Rule, which says that before a lender makes a home loan, it has to check real paperwork (like pay stubs, W-2 forms, and tax returns) to make sure you can afford it. The lender also has to look at what your payment could be after the reset, not just the low starting payment.

So, you don’t have to worry that today’s ARMs are the same as the ones we saw back during the crash.

Today's market has more options than many people realize. Finding the right one could be as simple as getting more information about tools like ARMs. A trusted lender can run the numbers with you, walk you through the what-ifs, and help you explore the possibilities.Is an ARM a good option for you? Talk to a loan officer to find out.

#5609. Xavier Becerra Wins California’s Gubernatorial Election in a Landslide After Pledging To Tackle Housing Shortage

Democratic candidate Xavier Becerra has won the California gubernatorial contest, trouncing Donald Trump-endorsed Republican hopeful Steve Hilton in a landslide win.

The Associated Press called the race immediately after polls closed, reflecting Becerra's undeniable lead over his GOP opponent. The victory was part of Tuesday night's "blue wave," in which Democrats reclaimed control of both the House and the Senate.

"What a great night to be a Californian," Becerra said at a victory party in West Sacramento, CA. "What a great night to be an American."

In his concession speech, Hilton, 57, congratulated Becerra on his win, but also predicted that a Republican will become governor in 2030.

"Enjoy it while it lasts," he told his opponent.

Becerra, 68, who served as secretary of Health and Human Services under President Joe Biden, entered the midterm elections on Tuesday holding a commanding lead of 27 percentage points over Hilton, a Fox News contributor, according to the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times.

The decisive victory marks a historic milestone as Becerra becomes the first Latino elected as governor of California, and the first Latino to hold the office since Romualdo Pacheco, who was elevated to the post from lieutenant governor in 1875 following the resignation of Gov. Newton Booth.

Becerra will be sworn in on Jan. 4, 2027, replacing the term-limited Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who campaigned for his successor on Sunday alongside former Vice President Kamala Harris. Both Newsom and Harris are expected to consider presidential runs in 2028.

Becerra becomes California's third consecutive Democratic governor, cementing the party's dominance in the deep-blue state.

California's 41st governor inherits a tangle of economic challenges anchored by the state’s acute housing affordability crisis.

In the run-up to the election, Becerra, a former congressman, made housing one of the main pillars of his campaign, promising to declare a housing-shortage state of emergency on his very first day in office and appoint senior officials across state agencies who will be tasked with removing obstacles to construction projects.

Becerra’s ambitious platform includes proposals to enforce 90-day "shot clocks" for building permits to accelerate construction, slash impact fees, streamline reviews for modular homes, and overhaul financing for affordable housing.

"The Becerra win signals that California intends to keep pushing for more housing, with an approach aimed at making building simpler," says Realtor.com® economist Jiayi Xu. "Taken together, it points to California doubling down on a pro-supply approach."

For the nation's most populous state, these changes could not come soon enough: on this year's Realtor.com® State-by-State Housing Report Card, part of the Let America Build campaign, California earned an F grade thanks to its to ultra-low housing affordability score.

Additionally, a Realtor.com analysis of the latest available housing and the Census Bureau's American Community Survey data found that the typical household in California earns 49% less than the income needed to buy a median-priced home—a shortfall of $98,292—making it the second-most unaffordable state behind Montana.

In a bid to unlock housing supply, Becerra plans to pursue zoning reforms, expand by-right approvals near job and transit hubs, and introduce more duplexes and small condos to put homeownership within reach of renters.

As part of his plan to tackle California’s entrenched homelessness epidemic through prevention, Becerra has proposed offering rental assistance to vulnerable families and bolstering tenant protections, which he views as more economical than spending thousands of dollars down the line on shelter beds.

Looking ahead, Xu expects Becerra to face significant hurdles, beginning with potential legal challenges and pushbacks on the housing front.

"For example, his plan targets lower impact fees, but some cities rely heavily on those fees to pay for infrastructure, and his campaign has not detailed how that lost revenue would be replaced," notes the economist. "A clearer plan for cities will be needed to win their cooperation."

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5608. Why Builders May Be More Motivated To Sell Than Homeowners

Here’s something most homebuyers don’t think about. When the housing market slows down, homeowners and builders don’t always respond the same way.

Think about it. If you’re selling your house and aren’t getting the offers you want, you could make the choice to take it off the market and stay put, and wait for things to improve.

But builders? They may be more motivated to stay the course.

They’ve already invested money in building those houses. And every completed home that sits unsold means money tied up in a property, plus ongoing costs that can add up.

That’s why some builders may be more motivated to negotiate right now. And that could work in your favor.

You’ve probably seen the headlines. According to the latest report from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), pending home sales – homes that have gone under contract but haven’t closed yet – fell 7.3% in September and 11.3% compared to last year.

Why? Higher mortgage rates are making it harder for buyers to make the numbers work. Now, that report tracks existing homes, not new construction. But we’re seeing signs of the same slowdown on the builder side, too.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), builder confidence dropped to 29 in October, its lowest level since June 2012. Traffic from prospective buyers also dropped to its lowest level in more than a decade, excluding the start of the pandemic.

As Robert Dietz, Chief Economist at NAHB, explains:

“Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines.”

A homeowner may be able to wait for the right offer. But a builder with several finished houses sitting unsold may have more reason to get those homes sold sooner rather than later.

And that means they may be more willing to work with you than you think.

If you’ve always assumed builders don’t negotiate, take a look at what they’re actually doing. According to the latest survey from NAHB, in October:

65% of builders are offering sales incentives.

43% are cutting prices, the highest share recorded between 2020 and 2026.

And 6% is what they’re typically taking off the price.

So, yes. Builders absolutely do negotiate. And with demand slowing, there’s good reason to explore just how flexible they may be right now.

That could mean asking for a lower price. But it could also mean asking for a mortgage-rate buydown, help with closing costs, or upgrades that would otherwise cost you extra.

And here’s a tip that could make a real difference.

Don’t just look at the newest communities or the prettiest model homes. Look for builders with completed houses that haven’t sold yet.

Those are sometimes called quick move-in homes or spec homes. And the longer one of those move-in ready homes sits unsold, the more reason a builder may have to consider an offer that helps get it off their books.

Don’t assume the advertised price or incentive package is the best they’ll do.

This is where having your own agent can really pay off. An agent who knows the local market can help you compare what builders are offering, identify communities with more available homes, and understand where there’s room to negotiate.

Of course, not every builder will offer the same incentives. And some may be more flexible on closing costs or mortgage rates than on the price itself.

The trick is knowing where to look, what to ask for, and how much room there may be to negotiate. And that’s where having your own agent is key.

A homeowner who isn't ready to accept a lower offer may be able to wait. But a builder with finished houses to sell has a different set of priorities. #5607. Exclusive: BlueFlag Security expands AI agent governance to cover unapproved coding agents

Software development security startup BlueFlag Security Inc. today expanded the artificial intelligence agent governance tools in its developer risk platform to cover unapproved coding agents, including those running on engineers’ laptops outside the code repository.

The update also brings automated fixes for some of the risks the platform turns up.

BlueFlag is going after a problem that has grown fast as coding assistants have evolved into agents that plan their own work and spin up the environments they need. Many sign in with a developer’s credentials. An agent working that way inherits every permission the developer holds.

Raj Mallempati, BlueFlag’s co-founder and chief executive, described the AI agent as “the most powerful and least governed identity in the development environment.” The company plans to start interrupting attack paths as they form early next year, he said. For now, the platform reports them.

In the current release, the work starts with finding the agents, which BlueFlag does from activity in the code. It picks up each agent through the commits and pull requests it produces, then classifies it by what it does with the code and whose identity it uses. Security teams can trace any agent back to the developers who work with it and the repositories it operates in, with unapproved agents marked as such.

AI tools running locally on a developer’s machine are harder to spot. To catch those, BlueFlag reads data from endpoint detection and response products such as those from CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. and SentinelOne Inc., so nothing new has to be installed on the device.

Human review gets its own checks. BlueFlag now flags pull requests approved by an AI agent, along with commits an agent wrote from start to finish and pipeline runs that went out with no person signing off. Organizations can also require a human review before anything merges or deploys. For any software release, customers can document where a person was in the decision and where one was not.

A separate inventory looks at AI inside the applications a company builds. It records the model providers and agent frameworks each application relies on and scores them against the Open Worldwide Application Security Project’s Top 10 for Agentic Applications.

AI spending is measured as well. BlueFlag ties the tokens and dollars each developer burns through to the commits and accepted code that came out of them, and it points to places where spending keeps climbing with no new commits behind it. Paid seats that sit idle show up in the same report.

Remediation runs through two new tools. AccessGuard targets identity problems such as overpermissioned accounts and stale credentials.

Misconfigured repositories and pipelines are handled by DriftGuard, which corrects settings such as missing branch protections that drift over time. Fixes can be applied by hand from written instructions or run automatically with one click, and automated changes can be rolled back.

Auto parts supplier Marelli Holdings Co. Ltd. is a customer. Kristie Pfosi, its global chief information security officer, said agentic AI made the unknowns inside her company’s own development environment bigger “overnight.”

“Within the first week BlueFlag showed us which AI agents were working in our repositories, which developers they worked with, and where the gaps were in how they were approved, scoped and reviewed,” Pfosi said. “Those are findings we can act on the same day.”

The launch comes a day after BlueFlag published its first research report, “The State of Developer Risk 2026.” Its figures come from metadata the platform collected on tens of thousands of identities and access tokens at a subset of BlueFlag’s enterprise customers, in a snapshot taken in September.

Unapproved coding agents turned up in 83% of the organizations measured, and more than two-thirds of the identities agents operate under carry administrator rights. In 22% of organizations an autonomous agent had already merged code with no human involved.

Older problems have not gone away. Nonhuman identities that can reach code repositories outnumber human developers eight to one, and 99% of access tokens are set never to expire.

The new features are generally available now. BlueFlag says the platform connects through application programming interfaces that are read-only by default and can be running in under five minutes, with automated fixes applied only when a customer opts in.

The company launched in March 2024 with $11.5 million in seed funding. Maverick Ventures and Ten Eleven Ventures led that round and came back to lead a Series A this past March that took total funding to $28 million.

#5606. Louisiana Passes New Property Tax Relief Amendments for Seniors

On Tuesday, Louisiana voters passed four ballot measures on property tax exemptions, aimed at providing tax relief for seniors, surviving spouses of disabled veterans, and entrepreneurs who rehab dilapidated homes.

Voters passed Amendment 1 with 76% support. Amendment 1 allows the surviving spouse of a disabled veteran transfer the homestead property tax exemption to a new home.

Currently, disabled veterans receive a homestead property tax exemption that is commensurate with the degree of disability they experience. Spouses are able to maintain the exemption in the event of their veteran spouse passing away. However, this amendment allows a one-time opportunity to the surviving spouse to transfer the exemption to a new property as well.

The Louisiana Department of Veterans Affairs as well as Leaders for a Better Louisiana and Louisiana Realtors® all expressed support for the measure.

Meanwhile, the Power Coalition for Equity and Justice opposed the measure, saying: "We support veterans and their families, but we do not need another special tax exception written into the state constitution."

Amendment 6 passed with 65% support. It proposes a property tax exemption of up to $30,000 for homeowners over age 65 who already qualify for an income assessment-based freeze.

Introduced by state Rep. Les Farnum, the amendment received support from both Democrats and Republicans.

The nonpartisan Leaders for a Better Louisiana, Power Coalition, and the nonprofit Pelican Institute for Public Policy all opposed the amendment.

In its explanation for its opposition to the amendment, Leaders for a Better Louisiana wrote: "While we like the idea of shielding senior citizens from taxes they have no control over...we wish it provided more flexibility for local governments to tailor tax breaks in a way that might be more suited to their individual goals and situations. As we have stated elsewhere, the better approach would be to untie the hands of local governments with regard to property taxes, rather than putting more rules in the constitution.The Louisiana Realtors expressed support for the amendment: "No community is forced to do anything. Each one decides for itself whether helping its seniors age in place is worth it. That is how local control should work."

Meanwhile, 59% of voters supported Amendment 9, which raises the income level for seniors to qualify for a property tax freeze from $100,000 to $150,000, allowing more people to qualify for the freeze.

The amendment aims to offer increased financial relief to seniors, many of whom live on fixed incomes. Proponents argued that the amendment could attract more seniors to the state. Critics said it would further reduce the tax dollars local governments require for social services.

Currently, around 230,000 people qualify for the freeze in the state.

The last time voters approved an increase in the income limit for the special property tax assessment was in 2020, when voters approved an increase in income limit from $50,000 to $100,000.

Louisiana Realtors expressed support for the amendment, saying that "the income limit to qualify has not kept pace with the cost of living."

Amendment 10, which allows communities to create optional property tax exemptions for blighted and derelict property that has been rehabilitated, also narrowly passed with 53% support.

Under the initiative, up to 75% of a rehabilitated property's assessed value would be exempt from property taxes for up to 20 years. Meanwhile, cleared lots would receive a 25% exemption on assessed value for up to 10 years as long as they weren't next to residential or commercial buildings.

Proponents argued this would incentivize the rehabilitation of derelict properties and positively impact the safety and well-being in a community. Communities could choose to opt in or out of the initiative depending on local needs.

In the U.S., property tax rates are determined at the local level and vary widely. The average effective property tax rate on owner-occupied housing in Louisiana is 0.55%, which is relatively low compared with states like New Jersey and Illinois, where the effective tax rate is 1.88%, according to the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan tax policy nonprofit.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. #5605. Who’s Buying Homes with Cash Right Now?

Ryan Serhant, CEO of SERHANT, says there isn’t just 1 housing market right now. There are really 4: cash buyers, buyers who need a mortgage, homeowners with low mortgage rates, and builders.

Today, let’s zoom in on the 1st group – cash buyers.

According to the National Association of Realtors (NAR), 27% of homes sold in September were bought with all cash. That’s more than 1 in 4 buyers. And that’s a pretty big number, especially when so many people are struggling with affordability.

So where is all that cash coming from? When you hear a number like that, it’s easy to picture wealthy investors buying up houses left and right. But that’s not necessarily the case. Some of those cash buyers are actually homeowners who’ve built up enough equity to buy their next home outright.

Here’s what you should know about who’s paying cash and what that really means for the market.

Cash buyers tend to fall into a few groups, according to NAR:

Homeowners who sold a house and are using that money to buy their next one

So, it’s not all those big investors social media talks about. That 1st group may include people a lot more like you. Here’s how. According to Cotality, the average homeowner with a mortgage has about $310,000 in equity.

That’s a big deal right now. Many homeowners feel stuck because they don’t want to give up the low mortgage rate they have today. But once they learn they may have enough equity to move and pay cash for their next home, today’s rates don’t matter nearly as much. Because buying in all cash means…

No need to borrow at today’s mortgage rates

No loan approval process, so you may be able to close faster

And even if the equity won’t cover the whole purchase, putting more of it toward the next home means borrowing less. That can mean a smaller monthly payment, too.

But cash buyers like this are more common in some places than others. And how big of a segment of your local market this is, is going to depend on where you live.

For example, Realtor.com data shows cash buyers made up almost 47% of sales in Mississippi and 46% in Montana earlier this year (see map below).

According to Realtor.com, the states with the most cash buyers reflect “a mix of affordability, wealth and buyer demographics.” Think places with lower home prices, or lots of retirees and 2nd-home buyers.

So, depending on where you live, you may see a lot more (or a lot fewer) cash buyers than the national number suggests. An agent who knows your area can tell you who’s actually buying near you.

And if all of this has you thinking everyone’s paying cash, they’re not. If you’re planning to buy and need a mortgage, you’re actually in the majority.

Based on NAR’s numbers, nearly 3 out of 4 home purchases still involve financing. And for homes priced between $200,000 and $750,000, only about 1 in 5 sold for cash, according to Realtor.com (see graph below):

That means most people buying in that price range are financing their purchase, too. So, there’s no need to assume you’re at a disadvantage just because you’re using a loan.

So, what does all this mean for you? Maybe more than you think.

If you already own a house, you may have enough equity to make your next move more affordable than you realize. And if you’re buying with a mortgage, remember, you’re in good company. Most buyers are financing their purchases, too.

The takeaway? Don’t make assumptions about what’s possible based on how other people are buying homes. What really matters is your equity, your budget, and what’s happening in your local market.

Cash buyers are a meaningful part of today’s market, but they aren’t the whole market.Whether you’re hoping to put your equity to work or you’re buying with a mortgage, a local real estate agent can help you see how much equity you have, who’s buying in your area, and what that means for your next move.

Cash buyers are a meaningful part of today’s market, but they aren’t the whole market.

Whether you’re hoping to put your equity to work or you’re buying with a mortgage, a local real estate agent can help you see how much equity you have, who’s buying in your area, and what that means for your next move.

#5604. Google fine-tunes its Agentic Data Cloud to support highly scalable autonomous AI workers

Artificial intelligence is no longer just about conversational assistants that tell people what to do. These days, it’s all about work automation, and Google Cloud is making sure it’s right at the forefront of that trend with its revamped Agentic Data Cloud platform, which received a host of new updates today.

The Agentic Data Cloud was launched earlier this year at Google Cloud Next. It’s meant to be the architectural “system of action” for AI agents, replacing the brittle extract, transform and load-based data pipelines, or ETL, that feed legacy software applications. The key advantage of Agentic Data Cloud is that it meets customers where their data is, so rather than forcing them to squeeze all of their information in a large, centralized data warehouse, it enables AI agents to access it wherever it lives.

In a blog post, Sirish Chandrasekaran, Google’s vice president of product management for data analytics, outlined the company’s belief that autonomous agents rather than humans will soon become the primary consumers of data. As such, it makes sense to build a purpose-built infrastructure stack specifically for them, prioritizing low latency, zero data movement and automated governance. “That is why we built the Agentic Data Cloud — a system of action designed to activate all your data by breaking down walled gardens, deliver high accuracy and trust, and operate proactively at low cost,” Chandrasekaran said.

The flagship new feature in Agentic Data Cloud is borderless Lakehouse, a special version of Google’s “cross-border Lakehouse” product that also debuted at Cloud Next. Chandrasekaran said borderless Lakehouse is built upon the open-source Apache Iceberg table format and designed to eliminate multicloud friction with new caching capabilities for Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure. This allows companies to query remote data held in those cloud platforms over a secure private link, without having to pay egress fees.

Chandrasekaran detailed how it works, saying that it automatically caches retrieved data blocks within Google Cloud to accelerate subsequent queries. There’s also a new AlloyDB integration that allows users to query external Iceberg tables with standard PostgreSQL queries without having to copy data. In this way, it bridges real-time transactional data with historical lakehouse records.

One of the big problems with autonomous agents is that they can be prone to hallucinations without proper guardrails in place, which is why Google has overhauled another capability within Agentic Data Cloud. The Knowledge Catalog, which is a kind of map of business meaning that’s meant to inform AI agents of the peculiarities of the organization they work for, is getting a new self-learning enrichment capability in preview.

According to Chandrasekaran, it works by continuously scanning unstructured data in Google Workspace, Jira, SharePoint and GitHub to translate operational knowledge into Open Knowledge Format context sets. These can be used to ground AI agents in organizational knowledge, and the results from early adopters shows that it can help make the average agent four-times more accurate, while reducing token consumption by up to 75%.

Knowledge Catalog is seen as so important to Google’s agentic future that it’s also being enabled by default in the Gemini application starting today. Because it’s so tightly integrated, it can resolve issues around business metric definitions and access controls before it translates user’s prompts into Structured Query Language queries. Companies can also choose to ground agents in semantic models for specific data platforms, including Google BigQuery, Snowflake, SAP, Looker and dbt.

“Agents are only as accurate as the business context they’re grounded in,” Chandrasekaran said. “Whether an agent is calculating net revenue for finance or customer churn for operations, it applies the exact same governed formulas your business teams rely on.”

Gemini is also getting new autonomous machine learning capabilities that can help to streamline everyday work for both technical teams and business workers. For instance, data engineers can now tell Gemini a specific business outcome they want to achieve in natural language, and Gemini will generate the PySpark code, run the notebooks and fix any data pipeline errors as it works toward that goal. Meanwhile, business users will be able to generate reliable, real-time operational reports in Gemini simply by asking for them.

“Gemini uses operational reporting skills integrated with BigQuery and the Knowledge Catalog to construct and save the query,” Chandrasekaran explained. “Once saved, teams can run reports on demand without incurring token costs, guaranteeing consistent and verified answers every time.”

Google also has a few gifts for software developers, starting with the new Data Agent Kit, which is generally available from today, bringing Model Context Protocol tooling into integrated development environments such as VS Code, Claude Code and Antigravity. This means that developers can now just define their business intent in natural language and have agents automatically create, fine-tune and test the associated data pipelines.

Developers can also take advantage of infrastructure updates that are designed to facilitate “high-concurrency agent interactions,” so that thousands of AI agents can query the same database simultaneously without swamping it and causing problems. These include the broader preview of AlloyDB Express, a highly scalable database that supports sub-two-second provisioning for rapid agent prototyping. There’s also PostgreSQL for agents in AlloyDB, which provides an isolated workload environment that can handle three million queries per second.

Finally, Google said BigQuery Graph is now generally available, bringing petabyte-scale graph analytics into relational database tables with zero ETL. It’s joined by previews of the TimesFM 3.0 forecasting model and TabFM predictive analytics model.

#5603. Gina Hinojosa Ousts Greg Abbott in Texas Governor’s Race—What Her Win Means for Housing

Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa made history Tuesday night, becoming the first Latina elected as governor of Texas and the first Democrat to win the office in 36 years.

Her victory was a major upset that denied Republican Greg Abbott a record-setting fourth term—and could signal a change in direction for the state's housing policies.

Hinojosa campaigned on making homeownership more attainable by restricting corporate investors, cutting residential property taxes, and cracking down on predatory rental practices.

The proposals put her on a different path from Abbott, who emphasized removing barriers to home construction and expanding the state's existing property tax relief. The Lone Star state is already the nation's largest homebuilder, accounting for 14.6% of all building permits issued, and received an A- on its Affordability Report Card from Realtor.com® in June.

Speaking to supporters in Austin, Hinojosa framed her victory as a rebuke of wealthy corporate interests and their influence over state government.

“Tonight, Texas, we answered—and we didn’t whisper," she said. "We answered loud enough for every billionaire, every lobbyist, and every corrupt politician in Austin to hear: Texas belongs to us."

One of Hinojosa's central housing promises is to curb corporate investors' purchases of single-family homes, which she argues have made it harder for ordinary Texans to compete for homeownership.

It's an issue she's been advocating for since her time in the state House. In 2025, Hinojosa introduced House Bill 2910, which would have prohibited covered corporate owners from holding more than 10 single-family rental properties in Texas.

Another proposal, House Bill 2334, would have prevented investment firms from entering contracts to purchase newly listed single-family homes during their first 30 days on the market.

Neither bill became law, but the state could be particularly fertile ground for the proposals.

"Texas is where this type of policy would bite hardest, though I'd still expect a modest effect on affordability," says Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com.

Megainvestors accounted for 1.9% of all home purchases in Texas during the first half of 2026, the highest share of any state and roughly three times the national rate of 0.6%, according to Jones' research.

And in some markets, corporate buyers are even more concentrated. Investors accounted for 15.9% of home purchases in San Antonio, 15.6% in Dallas-Fort Worth, 13.5% in Houston, and 12.4% in Austin, according to research from Realtor.com.

In three of those four markets, investors purchased homes at prices substantially below the overall median, suggesting that competition remains concentrated in the more affordable segments of the housing market.

A federal law enacted in July will prohibit institutional investors controlling 350 or more single-family homes from purchasing additional properties beginning in January 2027, subject to certain exceptions—but "Hinojosa’s cap goes further than the federal law," according to Jones.

Still, she cautions that limiting corporate purchases would address only a fraction of the forces keeping homeownership out of reach.

"The effect on homeownership is limited because the policy only touches that segment, which is a small slice of total purchases," she explains, noting that housing supply, mortgage rates, insurance, and property taxes remain bigger drivers of affordability.

"Build-to-rent is the key question," Jones says, referring to developments constructed specifically as rental housing. The federal law exempts qualifying build-to-rent projects, but Hinojosa's proposal did not explicitly offer the same protection.

"Limiting investor [single-family rental] supply would more likely push rents up than down, which works against the affordability goal."

Hinojosa has also promised to address rental practices, including landlords' use of algorithmic pricing software and rent increases imposed during the application process.

Texas has been one of the nation's most welcoming markets for data centers, attracting tech giants with cheap land, abundant energy and generous tax incentives. The state accounts for an estimated quarter of U.S. data center capacity planned by 2030, according to Reuters.

But growing opposition over electricity costs, water consumption, and other neighborhood impacts has begun changing that equation. About 61% of National Association of Realtor members said their clients were concerned that data centers would raise energy costs, and 56% reported concerns about water usage, according to survey data released in September.

It was enough to make Abbott—once an enthusiastic supporter of the industry—halt new data center permits in September, pending an environmental and energy audit.

Now, Hinojosa has promised to go further, calling for a legislatively backed moratorium, greater local control over development, and protections against data center-driven utility increases.

Her victory heightened concerns that Texas could become a more difficult place to build. Shares of Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX fell Wednesday as investors weighed the prospect of tighter restrictions.

Hinojosa and Abbott both campaigned on cutting homeowners' property taxes, but differed over how to pay for that relief.

In 2025, Texas raised its school district homestead exemption from $100,000 to $140,000, saving homeowners hundreds of dollars annually—a measure that Hinojosa voted in favor of.

Now, she wants to go further by eliminating corporate subsidies and using the savings to reduce residential property taxes, with the eventual goal of eliminating them altogether.

Abbott, meanwhile, proposed eliminating school district property taxes on owner-occupied homes, using state surpluses to replace the lost revenue.

The proposals also reflect differences over public education. Abbott championed a $1 billion private-school voucher program in 2025, while also signing an $8.5 billion public school funding package. Hinojosa opposed the vouchers and has pledged to repeal the program while increasing support for public schools and teachers.

But her tax plan faces a substantial funding question: Replacing homeowners' school maintenance-and-operations property taxes alone would cost an estimated $8.6 billion annually. Hinojosa has yet to detail how eliminating corporate subsidies would cover that cost without reducing school funding.

Hinojosa will take office in January 2027, but many of her proposed housing reforms would require the approval of state lawmakers.

And while Tuesday's elections changed the political landscape in Austin, it didn't guarantee Hinojosa a friendly Legislature. Democrat Vikki Goodwin unseated Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, giving Democrats leadership of the state Senate. Republicans, however, are expected to retain their majority in that chamber.

Meanwhile, control of the Texas House remained undecided Wednesday morning. Democrats needed to flip 14 seats to take control for the first time since 2003, and were gaining ground in several Republican-held districts.

But even if Democrats capture the House, Hinojosa would still need Republican support in the Senate to advance her housing agenda.

The newly elected governor seemed undaunted Tuesday night, closing her victory speech by invoking her grandmother's advice: "No te dejes," she said, which loosely translates to "don't let yourself get pushed around."

Hinojosa's campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Realtor.com.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5602. Don't Let the Fear of a Buyer Backing Out Scare You Away from Selling

There’s nothing quite like the excitement of getting an offer on your house. You’re one step closer to moving on to what’s next. But what happens if that buyer backs out or ghosts you before closing?

If you’ve been seeing headlines about more home sales falling through lately, that possibility may be keeping you up at night. And it’s true. According to Redfin and Cotality, canceled contracts have been on the rise.

But here’s what those headlines don’t always tell you…

Most sales still go through. Only 10-15% hit this snag. And even so, there are things you can do to help keep your sale from becoming one of them.

The key is knowing what tends to scare buyers away and getting ahead of those issues before they have a chance to derail your move.

Today’s buyers are being more cautious. Mortgage rates are stretching budgets, and with more homes to choose from, buyers have more freedom to walk away if something doesn’t feel right. As Redfin explains:

“That gives house hunters more options and makes them more likely to walk away if an inspection uncovers problems, an appraisal comes in low or the seller doesn’t agree to concessions.”

That’s why an accepted offer isn’t always a guaranteed sale. But it doesn’t mean you should be afraid to put your house on the market, either.

It just means getting ahead of potential problems matters more than ever.

A Redfin survey asked real estate agents why some buyers are backing out. And their answers give you a short of cheatsheet into what could go sideways and how you can get ahead of those headaches (see graph below):

This is the big one. And the good news? It’s also one of the areas where you can be the most proactive.

One simple way to head this off is by getting a pre-listing inspection before your house goes on the market. That way, if something needs attention, you can decide whether to fix it upfront (before you sell), adjust your price, or disclose it and come in already prepared for what’s likely to pop up in negotiations. It’s a lot better to find the skeletons in the closet before a buyer does.

Even buyers who are pre-approved can run into financing issues before closing. And with mortgage rates putting extra pressure on affordability, some buyers are finding it harder to make the numbers work.

While you can’t control whether a buyer’s loan goes through, you can work with your agent to look closely at their financing before accepting an offer. And if affordability is the concern, your agent can help you explore whether incentives like closing cost credits or a mortgage-rate buydown could make a difference.

Sometimes, your buyer needs to sell their house before they can buy yours. And if their sale falls through, yours could be affected too.

That’s why it’s important to understand any home-sale contingencies before accepting an offer. Your agent can help you look at where the buyer is in their own selling process and what protections you may want in place.

The goal isn’t to eliminate every possible risk. It’s to avoid being caught off guard by the ones you can plan for.

Just remember when you read headlines about canceled deals, they don’t give you the full picture. Most home sales still make it to closing.

And if a sale does fall through, that doesn’t automatically mean your house won’t sell. Sometimes a buyer’s circumstances change. Sometimes an issue comes up that can be addressed before the next offer.

What matters is having an agent who knows how to spot potential problems early, help you navigate negotiations, and keep your sale moving forward.

Because while you can’t control every twist and turn, you can control how prepared you are.

There's no need to let the fear of a buyer backing out hold you back. While no sale comes with guarantees, a little preparation upfront can go a long way toward making the whole process smoother.If you're ready to make a move, talk to a local agent about whether a pre-listing inspection makes sense for you.

#5601. Oumi’s Frontier AI Engineer now builds AI agents and retrains the models behind them

Enterprise artificial intelligence platform company Oumi PBC today extended its Frontier AI Engineer agent so it can build AI agents for customers and retrain the models those agents run on.

The release goes after a problem that tends to surface once agents leave the demo stage. A failing agent might have a bad prompt, a broken tool or a weak underlying model.

Oumi says enterprises have traditionally tried to fix it with prompt and harness engineering because retraining a model’s weights has required skills normally found at frontier AI labs. That approach often stalls before the agent is reliable enough to put to work.

Oumi’s Frontier AI Engineer already sets objectives, designs evaluations and runs training experiments for custom models on its platform. With today’s update, a team can describe in plain language what it wants an agent to accomplish, and FAiE helps define the tools and environments that agent needs before moving on to evaluation and training. Whatever goes wrong once the agent is in production is turned into evaluation sets and training data for the next round.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Manos Koukoumidis said better prompts and bigger generic models will only take agents so far. The ones that succeed will improve “by training the weights of the models powering them, learning from their own work,” he said, pointing to failed tasks and user preferences as the signals that count.

Companies that already run agents elsewhere can keep them there. Under a feature Oumi calls Bring Your Own Harness, the customer’s orchestration, tools and memory stay put and connect to Oumi for evaluation and model training. Models end up tuned in the same environment the agent works in every day.

Oumi is also adding direct preference optimization to the supervised fine-tuning it already supported, so a model can be trained on examples of the behavior users preferred. Reinforcement learning arrives through group relative policy optimization, which grades a model on task outcomes. Several methods can be chained together in a single multistage training run, and FAiE helps choose the strategy, set up rewards and diagnose problems along the way.

The training work feeds Oumi’s broader argument about model ownership. Most enterprise agents run on general-purpose models from frontier AI providers that aren’t optimized for a particular customer’s work. The company’s pitch since launching a commercial platform for custom models in March has been that a specialized model the customer owns outright can do better work at lower cost.

Group relative policy optimization is launching in private preview, and the Seattle company is taking requests for access. Oumi is a venture capital-backed startup that raised a $10 million seed round led by Venrock Management and Obvious Management Services in January 2025. The founding team includes former engineering leaders from Google LLC’s Gemini group.

A sleek Nichols Canyon estate in Los Angeles, perched above the treetops, has recently hit the market for $4,994,000.

Built in 1978, the four-bedroom home has been entirely reimagined by an acclaimed design studio and now offers a timeless 2,798-square-foot floor plan.

“Ome Dezin acquired the property in 2025 with a clear vision to reimagine and resell it, completing the renovation in October 2026,” says listing agent Claire O’Connor of Compass. “What made this home compelling was its inherent architectural character.

"Rather than strip away its identity, they saw an opportunity to build upon it, creating something that feels distinctly contemporary while remaining rooted in its 1970s origins.”

Set on nearly half an acre, the hillside retreat has wood ceilings, exposed beams, marble, wood, and terrazzo floors, built-ins, and three fireplaces.

“Entertaining feels intrinsic to the architecture rather than an afterthought,” O’Connor said. “The interiors unfold naturally toward the outdoor spaces, culminating in a dramatic infinity pool suspended above the canyon. There’s an intimacy to the scale that makes it equally suited to a quiet evening or a gathering of friends. It’s a home that encourages connection without feeling performative.”

An expansive deck overlooks the infinity-edge pool, which is cantilevered over the hillside to create the illusion of floating above the canyon.

“I see this appealing to a buyer who values provenance and individuality over square footage,” she noted. “There’s a growing sophistication among luxury buyers in Los Angeles, with an increasing appreciation for homes that feel curated rather than manufactured. This is someone who recognizes that true luxury isn’t necessarily about having more, but about finding something that can’t easily be replicated.”

O’Connor notes that the home’s location in Nichols Canyon is “a particularly interesting position in Los Angeles."

"It offers an almost pastoral sense of seclusion within minutes of Hollywood and the Sunset Strip," she says.

"The winding roads, mature landscape, and dramatic topography create a sense of discovery that’s increasingly rare in the city. It’s that tension between urban proximity and natural isolation that makes it so desirable."

#5599. Credit Scoring Is Changing: 3 Things Homebuyers Should Know

Quick, what credit score do you need to buy a home? If a number pops into your head, there’s a pretty good chance it’s wrong. And the right answer is getting harder to pin down, because the way credit scores are determined and delivered is changing – for the better.

Here’s what you need to know in today’s changing credit climate.

Fannie Mae has been tracking consumer perceptions about mortgage requirements since 2015 and found that consumers consistently overestimated the minimum credit score lenders required to qualify for a mortgage. As recently as 2023, the average guess was 652.

In reality, the long-standing benchmark for loans backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac is lower, at 620, and today even that isn’t a hard rule for every mortgage they back.

Like the Fannie Mae research, a recent survey from Veterans United found consumers continue to overestimate what it takes to qualify for a home loan:

The takeaway? Guessing wrong can cost you.

A renter who assumes their score is too low and they can’t qualify for a mortgage may never take steps to find out for sure.

For decades, the mortgage industry relied on one set of scores – Classic FICO. Thanks to a push to promote competition, make credit scoring more inclusive, and help more Americans become homeowners, the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the use of new credit score models such as FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0.

A different model can mean a different number for the same person. VantageScore says its model can score about 33 million adults that the Classic FICO’s model can’t. So the score you saw on an app last month may not be the one your lender pulls.

Remember: the models may be new, but the basics haven’t changed.

Your credit score is important – no matter how it’s measured. Following the same basic rules will benefit your profile in the old and new score models:

Because while credit models may change, the general advice for you to improve your score doesn’t. Financial awareness and consistency mixed with a little willpower can go a long way.

Don't make credit or homebuying decisions from a chart, an app, or a friend's advice. #5598. DC Mayor-Elect Janeese Lewis George Promises 72,000 New Housing Units

Democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George has been elected the first new mayor of Washington, DC, in 12 years after breezing past a crowded field to cap off a campaign focused on affordability.

The Associated Press called the election for Lewis George before 7 p.m. Tuesday, reflecting her commanding lead over Rhonda Hamilton, a community advocate running as an independent; Robert L. Gross, representing the DC Statehood Green Party, and 11 write-in candidates. That race did not include a Republican contender.

The win potentially places Lewis George, a 38-year-old D.C. Council member, on a collision course with President Donald Trump, who previously labeled her a "communist" and suggested that she was a threat to the safety and prosperity of the nation's capital.

"The people of D.C. elect the mayor of D.C., and I am willing to work with this administration to the benefit of D.C. residents," Lewis George told FOX 5 DC after her victory. "And I'm also willing to stand up to this administration when it comes to doing just that."

Lewis George will replace outgoing Democratic Mayor Muriel Bowser, who decided last year not to seek reelection for a fourth term.

"Congratulations to Mayor-Elect Janeese Lewis George," Bowser wrote on X Wednesday morning. "I’ll run through the tape and support a seamless transition. I love you, DC."

When she is sworn in on Jan. 2, Lewis George will become DC's first democratic socialist mayor, joining the ranks of New York City's Zohran Mamdani, Seattle's Katie Wilson, and Mayor-elect David Morales, of Providence, RI.

The cornerstone of Lewis George’s platform is her "Homes for All" plan, which includes provisions for rent stabilization, a coordinated affordable housing development system, stricter code enforcement, and expanded down-payment assistance.

Her long-term goal is to add 72,000 new housing units throughout DC within five years.

Additional housing-related planks in the mayor-elect's platform include amending the city’s zoning restrictions to add more homes and mixed-income housing, especially closer to transit lines.

"Increasing supply, paired with policies to protect residents, really is critical to stopping further displacement and making housing more affordable for all," she wrote in an op-ed.

The latest American Community Survey numbers from the U.S. Census Bureau reflect the urgent need for change. Buyers in DC have to contend with a 25% gap between earned income and the minimum required income to afford a home.

On the broader affordability front, Lewis-George campaigned on lowering utility bills for the district's 700,000 residents and pushing through universal affordable child care.

Lewis George easily won the Democratic primary in June, but President Trump does not count himself among her supporters.

Trump said after her victory that he "wouldn’t like" having Lewis George as mayor and threatened to carry out a federal takeover of DC if she won.

"Maybe we’ll take back Washington, run it on a federal basis," he said. "We won’t put up with it. We’re not going to lose our businesses."

Lewis George responded at the time that threatening the revocation of the city's home rule "because you do not like how residents vote is an attack on democracy itself."

However, now that the Democrats reclaimed control of the House and Senate, DC is expected to be shielded from Trump's potential efforts to encourch on its autonomy, since it is the Congress, not the president, that has legislative power over the district, according to the Associated Press.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5597. Descope launches Envoy to let consumer apps accept personal AI agents as users

Customer and agentic identity platform company Descope Inc. today launched Envoy, a service that lets consumer websites and apps accept personal artificial intelligence agents acting for their customers without rebuilding how people sign in.

Agents arriving through Envoy get an identity of their own, separate from the customer’s. The launch goes after a choice consumer businesses have been stuck with since agents such as Meta Platforms Inc.’s Muse started shopping and paying for things on people’s behalf.

Amazon.com Inc. blocked Muse from its store in September, saying the agent did not identify itself as one when placing orders, and JPMorgan Chase & Co. moved a month later to keep outside agents away from customer bank accounts. Descope expects blocking will get harder to maintain as more customers do their shopping through an agent.

The alternative, in Descope’s telling, is an agent that signs in as the customer with the person’s own password and one-time code. Nothing in that session shows software was involved, so when a fraud rule fires the logs point at the person. The business ends up absorbing the cost in disputed orders and returns.

Envoy is built around a proposed standard that offers a third option. Meta and Sierra Technologies Inc. published a 0.1 draft of the Personal Agent Protocol in October to set rules for how an agent signs in for someone without posing as them. Under Poppy, as the draft is known, a business publishes the endpoints agents should use and verifies which agent is calling. The business then issues a session bound cryptographically to that agent until the interaction ends.

Developers who adopt Envoy do not have to implement Poppy themselves or keep pace with revisions to it. Descope runs discovery and agent identification, and agents need no advance registration because each one presents a published client metadata document. Session tokens are tied to a key the agent holds through the Demonstrating Proof of Possession standard. Envoy supports all three of the draft’s sign-in types.

Inside Envoy, businesses spell out what an agent is allowed to do on a customer’s account through the Rich Authorization Requests extension to OAuth. In the example Descope gives, a retailer could let a shopping agent place orders for a customer and still keep it away from the payment methods on file. How long any elevated access lasts is left to the retailer as well.

Sensitive actions can go back to the customer for approval on a separate channel, using Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication. Another example from Descope has an agent booking travel hold a fare it found overnight and send the details to the customer’s phone for approval the next morning.

Every token and log entry records the customer and the agent as separate parties, so a company can revoke an agent’s access without signing the customer out. Envoy runs alongside whatever customer identity system a business already has.

Descope co-founder and Chief Executive Slavik Markovich said every login page on the internet was built for a person on the other side, and “that assumption no longer holds true.” In his view, the Personal Agent Protocol is doing for consumer agents what the Model Context Protocol did for enterprise tools.

GoFundMe Inc. and GoodRx Holdings Inc. are among the launch and design partners working with Descope on Envoy over the coming months. Each donation on GoFundMe is “an act of trust,” according to Arnie Katz, the fundraising platform’s chief product and technology officer. He said Envoy will keep the donor and the agent distinct in every session and ask users to approve donations from their phones.

At GoodRx, Chief Technology Officer Nitin Shingate expects people to send agents out to compare pharmacies and find the lowest price on a prescription before they reach the counter. Agents there will get limited permissions covering pricing information.

Agent builders get a tool of their own. A Poppy software development kit, released alongside Envoy, lets any agent work with the protocol, with Descope handling discovery and session management behind it. The kit is written in TypeScript and has no external dependencies.

Envoy sits on top of Descope’s Agentic Identity Hub, which the company updated last month with controls aimed at agents employees build or adopt inside their own organizations. The hub now handles authentication and access control for more than 1,000 MCP servers and millions of agent transactions each month, according to Descope.

Descope is a venture capital-backed startup whose investors include Lightspeed Venture Partners, Notable Capital and Dell Technologies Capital. The company has raised $88 million to date, including a $35 million seed extension in September 2025.

#5596. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5595. Tencent releases Hy4, a powerful frontier AI model introducing visual understanding and computer use

Tencent Holdings Ltd. today introduced Hy4, a new large language model that adds computer-use capabilities for the first time, using advanced visual understanding, reasoning and tool-calling to deliver long-horizon agentic performance.

The company said the model marks a significant leap in performance over its Hy4 Preview, which arrived Aug. 28, weighing in at 770 billion parameters with 49 billion active parameters. Both provide a 1 million-token context window, putting it in the same range as current open-weights frontier models from European and Chinese developers, including Mistral AI SAS, Beijing Moonshot Technology Co. Ltd. and Z.AI Co. Ltd.

The company said it substantially scaled up both pre-training and post-training, reporting gains over the preview version in instruction following, long-context understanding, agentic long-horizon tasks and deep research. Tencent also identified excessive reasoning and over-verification during the previous version’s “thinking” processes.

The new model focuses heavily on real-world productivity for workplace collaboration, human experience and professional work. The company said it optimized long-context learning capabilities to understand complex information, including web development, document summarization, visual creative tasks, document presentation, and more.

The company added that it also enhanced its capability for front-end and game development, high-complexity tasks that include intricate business logic, state management and orchestration. Some models struggle with producing stateful, elegant and beautiful user interfaces that are visually polished and also fully functional.

It is not uncommon for professional game developers, industry engineers and amateur vibe coders to use AI models as part of their work. However, a recent spate has had coders begin to reproduce, reverse-engineer and clone older and semi-recent video games. That prompted Anthropic PBC to block Claude Code and its underlying Opus 5.5 model from assisting in these tasks.

The company said it integrated deeply with major engines such as Unreal Engine, Unity and Godot, giving it the capability to support complex game logic and multiplayer implementations. Compared wit the preview, Tencent said, Hy4 improved by 19.1 percent in the GameDev bench and 9.8 percent in GameLogic benchmarks, although the actual baseline numbers remain internal and weren’t released.

To advance scientific reasoning, Tencent advanced the next stage of Recursive Self-Improvement to enhance research and development capabilities. Using the Hyra 2.0 harness, an autonomous AI research agent system, the model optimized the pre-training infrastructure for smaller models sharing the same architecture.

The model is currently available on Tencent Cloud TokenHub, WorkBuddy, CodeBuddy, Yuanbao, WeCom’s AI Assistant, Ima and more. It can also be accessed via third-party sources such as OpenRouter, Hermes and OpenCode. The company added that, despite its significant enhancements over Hy4 Preview, it kept costs low, maintaining the same pricing at around 90 cents per million input tokens, $2.70 per million output tokens and 4.5 cents per million cached input tokens.

The Flash version of the model is scheduled for release soon to deliver greater cost efficiency for users. The company also said it intends to release the model weights and system cards in coming days.
