#5594. Inside Joe Rogan’s Incredible $14.4 Million Austin Mansion—and Home to His Very Controversial Podcast

Podcaster Joe Rogan has once again found himself at the center of controversy after he was confronted about his past political views.

Rogan, 59, was on the receiving end of scrutiny when comedian Sam Tallent called Rogan out for voting for President Donald Trump in the 2024 election.

"Dude it's weird, cuz like, I talk to people a lot who I don't share like, the exact ideals with, like, I don't like that you f—n' endorsed Trump, but like, I have a lot of friends who voted for Trump," Tallent said.

Tallent added, "No, it's fine. Listen, it used to be that people used to be able to differ in their opinions and have conversations. But today we have become so divided, and I think a big factor is social media, echo chambers, propaganda, bots, gaslighting. And it seems like there's so much riding on everything constantly, because you're looking at your phone all the time.

"And everything on the phone is, 'This is the end. This is the end, this is the beginning of the end, this is a signal of the end, the only hope is to stop this,' and on both sides. People are addicted to their phones, so like, the information you're getting almost all day long is very bleak and very dire."

Rogan's podcast has long been known as a hotspot for the internet personality to share his outspoken opinions on everything from from celebrity gossip to political policy.

"The Joe Rogan Experience," which he records largely at his $14.4 million home in Austin, TX, is widely regarded as one of the most successful podcasts in the world, but it seems listeners on Apple have a different opinion.

Rogan, who drew a gargantuan audience with his three-hour-long interview with Trump during his campaign for president, has seen his podcast tumble down the Apple rankings of most popular shows—falling to third place, behind the New York Times' "The Daily" and a true-crime hit called "Crime Junkie."

The news came shortly before Ukrainian boxer Wladimir Klitschko accused the podcaster of "pushing Russian propaganda on his podcast," amid the war in Ukraine. Klitschko slammed Rogan's comments about President Joe Biden's decision to provide U.S.-made missiles to Ukrainian forces.

In a previous episode with music producer Scott Storch, the two discussed their relief that Trump had won the election, and then criticized the Biden administration for providing Ukraine with long-range missiles for use in its war with Russia.

“I feel safer knowing that Trump is in office,” Storch told Rogan.

“What I don’t feel safer about is that now they’re launching missiles into Russia,” Rogan replied. “How are you allowed to do that when you’re on the way out? [There] should be, like, some sort of, like, a pause for, like, significant actions that could potentially start World War III.

“Yeah, [Vladimir] Putin should not have invaded Ukraine, yes, 100%, but don’t start World War III,” Rogan added.

In a video response, Klitschko addressed Rogan directly: “You talk about these American weapons being sent to Ukraine, which you believe will lead to the third World War.

“So, let me tell you that you’re repeating Russian propaganda. Putin’s Russia is in trouble, so they want to scare you and people like you.”

He added, “Putin’s Russia wants to destroy Ukraine quietly, they want America to stay quiet. Not great, but quiet. A great America is not an America that abandons countries that defend freedom with their lives.”

Klitschko offered to come on Rogan's podcast so they could further discuss the topic as "free men."

Rogan is no stranger to provoking outrage and controversy with his comments, and his show retains the top spot in Spotify's rankings. However, his lackluster showing in the Apple charts will no doubt come as something of a surprise to the podcaster.

Indeed, Rogan's show has proven so popular that even Vice President Kamala Harris reportedly considered an appearance on "The Joe Rogan Experience." She ultimately opted for the more female-focused "Call Her Daddy" with host Alexandra Cooper.

Still, the podcaster has managed to lure dozens of A-list celebrities to his new $14.4 million home on Lake Austin in Texas, where he moved to from California in 2020, and where he has built a custom studio to record his show.

Rogan, a former comedian, previously provided UFC color commentary before launching his podcast in 2009. By 2015, he was one of the most popular podcasters.

Rogan interviewed everyone from Edward Snowden to Neil deGrasse Tyson, J.D. Vance, and Bernie Sanders. (After Sanders appeared on his show in 2020, Rogan endorsed the Democratic Party candidate in the 2020 presidential race.)

In 2020, Rogan moved from Southern California to Austin after reportedly agreeing to an estimated $100 million deal to broadcast exclusively with Spotify.

In February 2024, Rogan reportedly signed a new $250 million agreement with Spotify that allowed him to broadcast on other platforms, including YouTube and Apple.

That same year, Rogan opened up about his decision to relocate to Texas, explaining that California's strict COVID-19 restrictions were partly to blame.

"Everything’s shut down, everything’s staying shut down," he recalled of the pandemic in California. "All my friends that were in the restaurant industry were struggling.

"I started looking out here in May [of that year], and I went to a restaurant with my kids, and they were like, 'We don’t have to wear a mask? We could eat at a restaurant?' Then we went to the lake, and people are playing music and jumping in the water, and [my children] were like, 'We want to live here!

"That was it. Two months later I lived here."

In 2022, he explained that he believed he would find "more freedom" in Texas than he was able to enjoy on the West Coast.

Since his Texas move, he seems to be recording shows in a studio built inside his sleek mansion, which sits right on Lake Austin.

Rogan's 4-acre property comes with 300 feet of Lake Austin frontage, according to the original listing. The 11,000-square-foot mansion was built in 2008 and offers eight bedrooms and 10 baths.

The parklike surroundings include “views of the lake and the undeveloped preserve land on the opposite side.” There are three docks, a pool, and terraces.

The mansion features a formal dining room with built-ins, a dual-island kitchen with a casual eating area, a living area with floor-to-ceiling windows, and an office. A gym can also be found on the grounds.

Rogan's Instagram account reveals several upgrades he made in addition to his studio, including a cold plunge tub and a sauna.

The locale, not far from downtown Austin but seemingly a world away, was a draw for Hollywood A-lister Sandra Bullock, who reportedly owns a home in the area.

#5593. Earnings Roundup: Higher Rates Test Green Brick, Meritage, and Dream Finders

The challenging housing environment remained front and center as Green Brick Partners, Meritage Homes, and Dream Finders Homes reported third-quarter results.

Rising mortgage rates and affordability constraints continued to pressure consumer sentiment and margins. Green Brick Partners grew orders and deliveries despite the difficult backdrop, while Meritage Homes prioritized margins over a higher sales pace. Dream Finders Homes achieved record third-quarter closings while absorbing costs associated with its acquisition of Beazer Homes.

“Despite continued affordability pressures, broader economic uncertainty, and an increasing rate environment, demand across our markets remained resilient as buyers responded to our incentive strategy and attractive product offerings, particularly within Trophy Signature Homes. We continue to respond to deteriorating market conditions to maintain sales pace.”— Jim Brickman, co-CEO and co-founder, Green Brick Partners

“In the third quarter of 2026, we navigated an increasingly challenging home buying environment marked by rising mortgage interest rates and persistent geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty. Constrained affordability weighed on consumer sentiment, which was reflected in our 15% year-over-year decline in third quarter orders despite achieving an average absorption pace of 3.0 net sales per month per store.”— Steven J. Hilton, executive chairman, Meritage Homes

“Buyers faced a challenging summer, as rising mortgage rates further strained affordability and weighed on consumer confidence. I’m proud of how our team navigated these market conditions. We closed 1,967 homes in the quarter, a third-quarter record, and 6,127 homes year-to-date, also a record, while net sales increased 6% compared with the prior year.”— Patrick Zalupski, founder, co-chairman and CEO, Dream Finders Homes

Since quarter-end, Dream Finders Homes completed its approximately $2.2 billion acquisition of Beazer Homes. #5592. Inside Legacy Hills’ Strategy for Reaching a Broad Range of Buyers

Developed by Centurion American, the Legacy Hills master-planned community (MPC) spans over 3,000 acres in Celina, Texas, and is planned for up to 7,000 homes at full buildout. The community opened in April 2024 and includes a diverse mix of builders, lot sizes, and floor plans. Pricing generally ranges from the $300,000s into the mid-$500,000s.

Importantly, Legacy Hills is not relying on a single buyer profile. Its product strategy creates multiple entry points into the community, with housing choices that can appeal to buyers at different price points and stages of life.

That product diversity is paired with a layered amenity program. Plans call for seven amenity centers throughout Legacy Hills, along with a 27-acre sports park and a 3-mile walking and biking trail. The planned 1876 Country Club adds a destination component with an 18-hole championship golf course, clubhouse, driving range, putting green, and short game facilities.

For families moving to Legacy Hills, children in the broader community attend Celina ISD, while future school sites are planned within the development. The community also broadens its reach further through Del Webb’s dedicated 55+ neighborhood, which adds to Legacy Hills’ family-oriented offerings with age-targeted homes and amenities.

The strategy is unfolding against a strong demographic backdrop. Celina’s population and household base are projected to more than double between 2020 and 2029, expanding the potential pool of buyers around the community.

At the same time, the broader housing environment remains competitive. The Zonda Market Ranking for MPCs characterized Dallas as slightly underperforming per August data, yet Legacy Hills stood out. In the Q2 2026 Master Plan Outlook report, the MPC recorded the largest year-over-year percentage increase in last 12-month sales among qualifying MPCs with at least 200 sales in the previous 12 months.

Legacy Hills illustrates the value of creating several paths into a large-scale community rather than building around a narrow customer profile. Differentiated housing, offerings for multiple life stages, and amenities ranging from everyday recreation to destination experiences give the development multiple ways to appeal to buyers.

#5591. VMware gets simpler AI deployment and low-cost version for basic private clouds

Broadcom Inc. is expanding its VMware portfolio with new capabilities that simplify artificial intelligence workload deployment, strengthen infrastructure security and simplify disaster recovery.

The company is also introducing a lower-cost virtualization platform aimed at smaller customers that don’t need a full private cloud platform.

Today’s updates span VMware Cloud Foundation, the company’s flagship private cloud platform, and a collection of optional advanced services. Several capabilities are already available in VCF 9.1.1, which was released in September, while others are scheduled for the first quarter of Broadcom’s 2027 fiscal year, which began on Monday.

The changes are part of a broader Broadcom effort to position VCF as a common infrastructure platform for traditional virtual machines, containers and increasingly demanding AI workloads.

More than 2,600 customers had deployed VCF 9 as of September, representing more than 24 million allocated cores, according to Prashanth Shenoy (pictured), Broadcom’s chief marketing officer and vice president of marketing for cloud platform, infrastructure and solutions.

Broadcom is introducing AI Infrastructure Quickstart, an automated deployment capability designed to simplify the initial configuration of private AI environments.

It combines vCenter cluster deployment, vSphere Supervisor activation and VMware Kubernetes Service cluster provisioning into a single workflow, replacing multiple manual configuration processes. “We have consolidated all of that, made a quick start workflow and streamlined the workflow completely so they can get it up and running day zero in a matter of minutes,” Shenoy said.

Broadcom is also adding native S3-compatible object storage through VMware vSAN. The feature, expected to become generally available in the upcoming VCF release, supports AI applications that depend heavily on unstructured data and lets developers provision storage through self-service interfaces.

On the security front, Broadcom is incorporating additional capabilities directly into VCF rather than requiring customers to purchase them separately. These include confidential computing support for Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Intel Corp. processors, which was already available in VCF 9.1.1, as well as planned policy-based virtual private cloud connectivity and automated infrastructure configuration compliance.

Broadcom said the compliance features will continuously monitor infrastructure settings against industry benchmarks, identify configuration drift and provide remediation guidance.

The virtualization maker is also moving disaster recovery functionality into the core VCF and VMware vSphere Foundation platforms. The capability will provide orchestrated recovery across thousands of workloads, including recovery from outages, equipment failures and natural disasters.

Additional protection will be available through VMware HyperArmor, a previously announced service that provides hypervisor-level defenses including virtual patching, continuous monitoring and multifactor authentication.

Two other advanced services, VMware Live Recovery and VMware Compliance and Configuration Management, address cyber recovery and continuous compliance enforcement for virtual machines and containers.

The company is also broadening its portfolio at the lower end with VMware vSphere Express, a new offering for environments containing up to 128 processor cores. Based on vSphere 9, Express includes live virtual machine migration, high availability, distributed networking, security and simplified patching.

Shenoy said the product is intended for customers that need basic virtualization without purchasing the more comprehensive and costly VMware vSphere Foundation or VCF platforms. “They don’t need a whole cloud in their two-server environment,” he said.

Customers can upgrade to the larger platforms as their requirements grow. Broadcom didn’t disclose pricing, although Shenoy indicated Express would be substantially less expensive than its higher-end offerings.

#5590. 8 Resilience Moves Builders Can Make Before Extreme Weather Hits

When extreme weather hits, small construction details can make a big difference in how well a home performs.

According to Fred Malik of the Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS), research continually points to roofs, openings, and structural connections as potential failure points. Damage in these areas can allow wind and water into a home and trigger larger, cascading losses.

For builders, stronger construction can also help reduce disruption for homeowners, limit warranty-related costs, and protect a company’s reputation for delivering durable homes.

“Resilient, durable buildings are usually the result of making several intentional decisions,” Malik says.

Here are eight steps builders can take to improve resilience ahead of severe weather:

Rather than approaching roofing as a collection of individual products, Malik recommends treating the entire roof as one interconnected system. The goal is to keep the roof intact and prevent an initial failure from creating a pathway for additional wind or water damage.

A sealed roof deck creates an additional layer of protection beneath the primary roof covering. If shingles or other roofing materials are damaged or blown off during severe weather, this secondary layer can help limit water intrusion into the home.

Small details can have an outsized impact on performance. Builders should carefully install and inspect flashing at roof edges, roof-to-wall transitions, vents, chimneys, and other penetrations. These areas can become pathways for water if they aren’t properly protected.

Windows, entry doors, and other openings need to withstand both wind pressure and wind-driven rain. Following manufacturer installation instructions and properly installing flashing are critical to maintaining the home’s building envelope.

Garage doors represent a large opening in the building envelope and need to withstand pressures generated by high winds. Malik notes that this is important even in inland markets, where tornadoes can cause significant structural damage.

In areas exposed to more severe winds, builders should consider a professionally designed continuous load path connecting the roof to the walls and ultimately the foundation. Strong connections throughout the structure help transfer wind forces safely through the building instead of allowing individual components to fail.

In flood-prone areas, elevate or otherwise protect mechanical, electrical, and utility equipment. Keeping critical systems above anticipated flood levels can reduce damage and make it easier for homeowners to return to their homes after an event.

Programs such as IBHS’ FORTIFIED standards provide builders with a framework for putting resilience measures into practice. FORTIFIED goes beyond minimum code requirements with an emphasis on keeping the roof on, keeping water out, and tying the structure together.

The program also requires third-party documentation of critical resilience measures, including construction details that may no longer be visible once finishes and other materials are installed.

Overall, resilience isn’t dependent on a single product or construction technique. It’s the cumulative result of getting multiple details right, Malik says.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5587. Former Landsea Homes President and COO Mike Forsum to Lead New Land Finance Platform

Home building industry veteran Mike Forsum has been tapped to lead a new land finance platform aimed at providing public and private home builders and developers with more flexible capital options.

Wafra, a New York-based global alternative investment manager, and Hunt Cos., a privately held real estate and investment company, have launched Strata Land Partners, with Forsum serving as CEO.

The platform has launched with projects comprising approximately 1,300 single-family lots and is designed to serve as a long-term capital partner for builders navigating land investment and development in an uncertain housing market.

Forsum brings more than 40 years of home building industry experience to the venture. Most recently, he served as president and chief operating officer of Landsea Homes. His experience navigating builders’ operational challenges and investment decisions will help shape Strata’s approach.

“Strata was built by builders, for builders,” Forsum said. “Having spent my career in home building, it is apparent that there is significant demand for a strategic capital partner that understands the industry’s operational nuances and thoughtfully supports builders in achieving their goals.”

He added that the platform’s goal is to “bridge that gap and play our part in building the new homes this country needs.”

Strata enters the market as builders look for ways to manage land exposure and capital requirements. According to the announcement, the platform will focus on tailored financing solutions that allow builders and developers to navigate changing market conditions while advancing residential projects.

Ryan Brenner, managing director and head of alternative real estate at Wafra, said Strata is also intended to help address the nation’s structural housing shortage by giving builders another source of capital to support new-home development.

For Hunt Cos., the partnership combines flexible capital with an operating team experienced in residential development.

“Strata brings together an experienced operating team and flexible capital to address a critical need in residential development,” said Chris Hunt, CEO of Hunt Cos. “We look forward to supporting the platform as it builds lasting relationships with home builders and developers nationwide.”

#5586. Where Health Care Employment Has the Biggest Footprint

Health care is more than a service for residents. It is also an important piece of the employment landscape. Preliminary August data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows significant differences in both the number of health care and social assistance jobs across states and the industry’s share of total employment.

In absolute terms, the country’s largest states naturally account for some of the biggest health care workforces. Unsurprisingly, California leads with over 3.18 million health care and social assistance jobs, followed by New York at 1.91 million and Texas at 1.76 million.

However, the health care industry’s share of a state’s total employment base may tell a different and potentially more useful story.

West Virginia stands at the top of the list, with health care and social assistance representing approximately 19.6% of total employment. New York follows at 19.1%, with Pennsylvania at 18.9%. Connecticut, Minnesota, and Massachusetts are also among the states where the industry accounts for a comparatively large share of employment, at roughly 18.1%, 17.9%, and 17.8%, respectively.

At the other end of the spectrum, health care represents just 8.8% of employment in Wyoming, 10.6% in the District of Columbia and Nevada, 10.8% in Alabama, and 11% in South Carolina.

That variation matters because a sizable health care sector can serve as an important economic anchor, providing a meaningful source of jobs that support the broader housing market.

Access to health care might become an increasingly relevant consideration in retirement location decisions. Affordability matters, but so do physician availability, provider access, and the distance residents need to travel for care.

Demographic trends reinforce that dynamic. Per the U.S. Census Bureau, the old-age dependency ratio, which measures the number of adults age 65+ relative to the working-age population, rose from 20.8 in 2010 to 29.7 in 2024, pointing to future pressure on health care systems, retirement programs, and elder care resources.

As the population ages, health care will matter to housing markets from both an economic and demographic perspective. The sector supports local employment, while access to care can influence where older households choose to live.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

#5585. Smartsheet AI-powered platform bridges gap between planning and results

Smartsheet Inc. today introduced an artificial intelligence-powered planning and execution platform designed to help enterprises identify when projects are veering off course and take corrective action before delays and cost overruns become serious problems.

Announced at the company’s Engage 2026 conference, the new vsActual platform — pronounced “versus actual” — uses AI agents to continuously monitor work across multiple enterprise systems, compare progress against strategic objectives and recommend adjustments. The company also announced new agentic workflow capabilities, integrations and security controls for its existing work management platform.

The centerpiece of vsActual is what Smartsheet calls Execution Graph, a knowledge graph built from what the company said are two decades of workflow data encompassing millions of projects and nine petabytes of information. The graph maps relationships between tasks, projects, programs and strategic objectives to help AI agents understand how changes in one part of an organization affect others.

The company’s goal is to address a growing disconnect between individual productivity improvements enabled by AI and measurable organizational results, said Pratima Arora, Smartsheet’s chief product and technology officer.

“We were seeing a lot of intelligence and productivity gains getting stuck at an individual level and not translating to a team and organization level,” she said.

VsActual is designed to operate across existing enterprise applications rather than require organizations to consolidate work onto a single platform. It can connect to applications from Oracle Corp., SAP SE, Workday Inc., Atlassian Corp. PLC and ServiceNow Inc. to gather information about budgets, schedules, staffing and project dependencies.

Smartsheet said AI agents can turn strategy documents, spreadsheets and budget proposals into structured plans, model alternative scenarios and monitor execution against those plans. A drift-detection agent (pictured) continuously searches for emerging problems, while other agents generate executive reports and recommend changes as business priorities evolve.

The system can also trace the consequences of disruptions across organizational hierarchies. “If there is a delay in a Jira ticket that has impact five levels up, we can detect it and tell you what is happening,” Arora said.

Smartsheet said its historical workflow data provides an advantage over competing planning and work management products. Execution Graph builds on an existing Amazon Web Services Inc. Neptune knowledge graph containing approximately 100 million nodes and incorporates information about workflow patterns, dependencies and collaboration, Arora said.

The company uses multiple foundation models, selecting them based on workload requirements and cost. AWS and Databricks Inc. are its major underlying technology providers. Arora said Smartsheet isn’t training its own large language models.

The announcements also expand Smartsheet’s existing AI capabilities. New Agentic Workflows allow users to schedule recurring activities such as status reports and risk assessments. Specialized creation and data-quality agents can generate project structures, dashboards and reports or identify problems in underlying data.

New integrations include native connections to ServiceNow, Microsoft Corp. Dynamics 365, HubSpot Inc. customer relationship management, Workday Inc. human resources software and Intuit Inc.’s QuickBooks. Conversational integrations with GitHub, Zendesk Inc., Airtable and Monday.com Ltd. are entering early access, with additional AI-assisted integrations planned for early 2027.

Arora emphasized that agentic workflows combine conventional automation with AI rather than relying exclusively on large language models. “This industry overuses LLMs sometimes where it is just simple deterministic action,” she said.

Although some agents can execute scheduled tasks automatically, Arora said human approval remains the default approach for consequential actions. “Our default stance is human in the loop,” she said.

The compay also announced International Organization for Standardization/International Electrotechnical Commission 42001 certification, security event streaming and data classification capabilities intended to strengthen oversight of AI operations.

Smartsheet developed vsActual with about a dozen enterprise design partners. The company publishes pricing on its website.

#5584. Affordability: Real Solutions for a Real Problem

For buyers, especially first-time buyers, today’s housing affordability crisis (driven by a host of market challenges, from rising mortgage rates to low inventory and lingering inflation) creates many barriers to entry for homeownership. Is there anything agents can actually do at the local level to move the needle and help their clients achieve their homeownership goals?

Four brokerage leaders recently gathered at RISMedia 38th Annual CEO & Leadership Exchange on a panel titled, “Affordability: Real Solutions for a Real Problem,” to say yes and share their tactics and long-term solutions for buyers facing today’s housing affordability problem.

The session, moderated by RISMedia Founder and CEO John Featherston, included panelists Keith Smith, co-owner, Yes Realty Partners, a Keller Williams Alliance Partner; Ennis Antoine, owner and CEO, EA Realty of Georgia; Katey McGrath, vice president, director of operations, Elfant Wissahickon Realtors®; and Ken Baris, CEO, Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Jordan Baris Realty.

Here’s a glimpse into some of the questions and answers that provided attendees with some detailed takeaways to help their clients overcome the affordability challenge.

John Featherston: To set the stage, tell us why brokers should care about the housing affordability issue?

Keith Smith: I’m just going to kind of say the awkward thing to the room. Every single one of us makes a living either directly or indirectly from helping people buy and sell. And if we can’t help people buy and sell, we’re not going to be able to put our key in the door. We’re not going to be able to begin our business. Right now, first-time homebuyers can’t buy, and they’re 40? You have Boomers who will not be able to move on. So if we can’t help people do that, this isn’t just a certain entry point. It’s all the way across the board. I think maybe a little bit later we’ll talk about some possible solutions.

Katey McGrath: Obviously it’s good business. And what’s interesting too is at least in our market, the competition for that business is a lot less intense because it is a little bit more work and it’s not as dollar-productive. It’s absolutely more rewarding and more valuable to your communities, but not everybody gets up and says, “I want to sell lower-priced houses.” And so I love new agents getting into the business and focusing on affordability. We love training them up to pre-qualify renters because most of the time the renters don’t know they can buy a house. So it’s a great way to start your real estate business.

And in our company, we have a lot of things that sort of reinforce that culture of homeownership as the most impactful thing you can do in a community. We also create programs in-house that help leverage gift funds to just get people across the line, which I’ll talk about more, but we thread it through the entire “gestalt” of our organization.

John Featherston: What are some of the ground-level tactics that you’re using in your organization?

Katey McGrath: One of the things we do is we train up. If you get a call for a rental, find out if they are capable of qualifying for homeownership. We lean on our lenders. I rely on them and have a high level of expectation that they’re going to understand the down payment programs and the grant programs and the ability to stack them. We have a program called Building Equity where we crowdfund it. The partners of the company seeded it and now every agent in my company gives $5 to $50 every time they sell a house. We have a nice little fund, and we make a gift to anyone who buys a house for $250,000 or less in the city of Philadelphia. The only question we ask is, are you going to move into it?

We find that we can leverage that. If our lenders want to participate in the program and be on our website, they have to match that gift. We just want to keep the level of homeownership in Philadelphia as high as possible. And we also want people to consider other neighborhoods, other house sizes and conditions that maybe the people saving up for their dream homes are not looking at.

John Featherston: Ennis, how do you educate agents to help them find homes their buyers afford?

Ennis Antoine: When talking to my agents, I have to remind them first, you have to learn to stack resources. And what that means is, get involved in the city, the county and third-party companies like Georgia Dreams and ask them, “What programs do you have available to assist with down payment assistance?” In Atlanta, we have a program where the mayor wants to have 20,000 affordable homes built by 2030, so he has instructed his people to have this agency set aside funds to help buyers with down payment assistance; you have to live in our community for five years and it’s forgivable where you don’t have to pay back those funds. The goal is educating your agents on what funds are available and then once they’re educated, educate the buyers on what to expect and to set realistic expectations.

John Featherston: Are you seeing or anticipating any improvement in affordability issues from the ROAD to Housing Act?

Ennis Antoine: I chaired the FPC advisory committee (Federal Political Coordinators under NAR), and we worked on that bill for two years and got it passed. Now here’s the key, though. It is only an incentive. It’s going to take each one of us to inform our city councilmen and mayors on what’s available, and to pass these bills to say, “Hey, listen, how can we incentivize people to buy a home?” And then second, when it comes to housing supply, that’s going to take a while because we have an inventory shortage. It’s not going to happen overnight, but we have to be patient because it’s only a framework on what could happen if we partner with our city council and Realtor® organizations.

John Featherston: Ken, why is it critical to approach the affordability issue as far as you can see? And is it relevant to the specific markets that you’re now serving?

Ken Baris: Affordability is relative. Somebody who says “I can’t afford” is maybe a kid who grew up in a town, can’t afford to be in the town now, but they may be able to afford in another community. It’s being able to understand the benefits people can get. So for instance, Bank of America’s community reinvestment program with a grant of $17,500. We have a mortgage partnership, and we make sure anyone who will qualify for that is going to get that grant and use Bank of America because it’s good sense for the clients.

And if you are really astute about the business, you have people who are tenants—they don’t know they can afford to purchase. You can train people to purchase. You can help people improve their credit: Higher credit score, lower interest rate. You can train people to do things like say, “I will fall in like with four properties. I will not fall in love with one.” Because if you fall in like with four and we make four lower offers, we actually can turn you into a buyer and something more affordable by being willing to present offers. So we inspire a team to do the work and take the time and good things happen for clients.

We use foyersavings.com. A very interesting website; it has three things. Number one, it gives you an ability to save money at an okay interest rate or a good interest rate so that your money builds. Number two, it gives a modest down payment assistance with $600 credit of the first $10,000 you have, you get 6% additional in interest back. That’s not huge, but it’s something.

And three, it shows programs from all over—banks, lenders, community program—that provide grants. You may not know all the programs in your own market that are available. Foyer goes after these programs and makes them available to people that use the site. So it’s just being aware of these things, using your method of communication to get the information out, inspiring people to understand what they can do. If you don’t buy somewhere, you’re going to make somebody else wealthier.

John Featherston: A follow up to that, because you’re going into a lot of the nuances that help new buyers enter the marketplace. Have you made a concerted effort within your firm to make this type of training and education a competitive differentiator in your organization?

Ken Baris: Hugely. I find units to be sexy, not just high prices. And if you have salespeople that are in more affordable communities and they’re trained for these programs, they do better. Another thing that we’ll do is we’ll send out emails of successful buyers. “John thought he was going to rent. We let him know that we thought he could purchase, and the good news for John is we were right. You might be in the same position. Let’s get together.” And that’s the kind of communication we’re doing. I can’t change somebody’s income, but I could help them learn how to save more, how to improve their credit and how to get down payment assistance. $17,500 can make somebody from not a buyer to a buyer. And it’s a gift. It’s not a loan.

John Featherston: How are you and your agents getting past the current rhetoric that we hear among young people when they say they’re never going to be able to buy a home?

Katey McGrath: One of the biggest myths is that you think you need 20% down. And so it’s education, education, education, myth busting, destigmatizing these programs. It’s super important for young people in your community, but also make sure that your agents feel that way. And it’s great because like I said, the younger agents eat it up and it keeps them busy early in their career.

Ennis Antoine: I put pen to paper. So as far as paying $2,000 a month in rent, I’m saying, let’s talk about this for a second. A landlord just received $24,000 from you for one year. You say I’m staying there for three or four years. Then you have nothing to show for it. Whereas if you bought a home or a condominium, you pay this amount each month, you would have a tax write off and within four or five years, you’ll see a 4% or 5% increase in the value of the property. You can sell that property, walk away with cash, get the tax write off on your tax returns. And so if it was me, I would buy and invest and start to build wealth.

And if you build wealth, you can get a larger home and pay less money. So the key here is you’re a smart person. Let’s make a smart decision. Let’s buy.

Keith Smith: I want to pivot a little bit. We’re talking about how we can make a difference. Just last year through a land trust we put together 40 permanent affordable new construction units. I’m in Charlottesville with the second-highest cost of living in the state of Virginia, the second-highest cost of housing in Virginia. But we were able to do 40 of them. And the way we did this is what I call the four pillars: The local government, the private sector folks—developers, builders, real estate agents, the nonprofits and the people all of us serve. You got to get them into a room. You’ve got to get them all to go into the conversation. We put buyers and sellers together. We negotiate deals together. We put people together that maybe do not want to talk to one another, but they talk to people that get to the end result. And how you put those four pillars together is you show up to the meetings and you do what we all do every day very well, which is negotiate and put people together.

John Featherston: Why isn’t the real estate community playing a more pivotal role than every one of the communities, perhaps the most critical role as far as supporting homeownership?

Katey McGrath: I think everybody in this room is a connector. It’s what we love about what we do. And I think that our credibility and our expertise can help save money in these instances. The earlier we get involved in these conversations, the less mistakes the people with good intentions are going to make to make things more expensive. But also, the credibility that we have as a community member, right? So people are coming to us to buy houses, people are coming to us for education, people are coming to us to build generational wealth for their family. And then we can go to city council, we can go to the state reps, we can go to the zoning meetings and add all of that to just sort of be both sides of the issue.

Housing is bipartisan, so if you can get people together, you have that credibility, everything just becomes more productive and less expensive.

John Featherston: Getting people together over the issue of housing is a common denominator all of us can agree on. When Ennis said, local teachers, first responders, police, essential services, can’t afford to live in the community they’re serving, that is not a unique problem. That’s a problem that permeates around the nation. So the solutions have to be done locally.

Ennis Antoine: That’s correct. So I remind everyone, it doesn’t matter what company you work for, there is a percentage in every company where you deal with first-time homebuyers. It doesn’t have to be your main part of your business, but it should be a part of your business because to whom much is given, much is required. And we must always lead by example because the goal here is homeownership. What can we do? It’s all an education process. In every office, there are agents who are very passionate about their community. Support them, enhance them, show up when they need some help.

They will find a surgeon to have vibrant communities. We need a mixture of people in the community who are willing to work together, live together because we call it a village. And as real estate professionals, we are the fiber of the community. We are the voice of real estate and private property rights do matter.

Ken Baris: Something interesting we did some years ago, we listed 300 brand new two-family homes in Newark, New Jersey. And they were beautiful. The challenge was getting people in. So we had the builder prearrange financing, and we had them buy down the rate. And so it was a much lower interest rate, which lowered the payments. And then we also had the builder give a brand-new computer to every purchaser for one of the units because many of them were going to have kids and they would not have money left over for a new computer. And we thought that was very important. And then when certain buyers were tight, we then created a program where they were giving 5% toward closing costs, and if you get people to pay money toward closing costs, you also make it more affordable.

Keith Smith: “Connected” was the right word. I’ve been in this space for 15 years, and I would hear from elected officials, “Well, I don’t understand what the developer is saying.” The developer’s saying, “I don’t understand what the elected official is saying.” And then the nonprofits don’t understand anybody, and the poor folks that we’re trying to serve are left out there in the dark. Being a connector, that is the perfect word. That’s what we do. We connect and are able to put those four pillars together and put a developer and an elected official who really wants to do the right thing, together. The seller doesn’t trust the buyer; the buyer doesn’t trust the seller. We connect and we put people together and just get that conversation rolling. That’s how you do 40 new construction units in the second-highest cost-of-living area in the state of Virginia and everybody walks away smiling. I didn’t do anything really genius. I just put people in the room and said, start talking.

John Featherston: If you could do one thing to help move this affordability issue forward, what would you do?

Ennis Antoine: The one thing I would do is educate my colleagues and challenge them to get involved. It’s easy to write a check, but it’s amazing what happens when you show up. As a leader, when we show up, our people will follow. So as leaders, show up.

Ken Baris: I think just doing a better job of educating consumers because there’s a lot of buyers that don’t know their buyers. Not everyone will be able to afford. They’ve never always been able to, but there’s many more out there.

Katey McGrath: I’m going to go a little more philosophical. Just remember how important homeownership is to every metric in the community. It reduces crime. It increases education rates. It can lower the temperature in a zip code. It extends life expectancy, but most importantly, it builds generational wealth and creates health outcomes in that community that lift everybody up. And if you internalize that, you’re going to be happier when you go to work. You’re going to have more patience to deal with the hard clients that you’re not going to make a lot of money on and just feel great at the end of the day.

Keith Smith: Invest the one asset you can’t make more of, which is your time. Show up and over time, you’ll make a difference. And of those affordable housing units, every single key I handed to somebody, they were in tears. They never thought they were going to get into the homeownership game. It’s not about the check. It’s about the tears, and it makes a difference.

Beth McGuire is RISMedia’s vice president of online editorial.

#5583. Trend of the Month: 6 Ways Floor Plans Are Changing

Current floor plan trends don’t necessarily bring anything brand new to home design, but rather represent subtle shifts to better support how people want to live in their homes today.

Functionality and flow are driving many of the current trends, including these six:

As a result, floor plans are balancing the benefits of open-plan living with spaces that permit partial or total separation from the main living areas. Ideally, a floor plan lets a homeowner choose.

While the kitchen and adjacent living areas remain open, “what is changing is everything around that center. Homeowners still want visual generosity and togetherness, but they also need places for focused work, calls, study, rest, hobbies, or simply a quiet moment,” says Darian Wagner, managing principal and senior architect, DAHLIN Architecture.

The key, says Justin Julian, senior principal and senior architect, DAHLIN Architecture, is not to treat open and closed spaces as opposites.

The most desirable plans “create layers between fully shared and fully enclosed space, so homeowners can adjust the degree of connection throughout the day,” says Julian.

Meanwhile, “Smaller cozy corners can remain open to the main space while using placement, furniture, partial screens, or an offset opening to create a sense of retreat,” says Wagner.

Away rooms are trending, which are simply secondary living spaces set off the main living area, with a closing door, and often increased soundproofing, devoted to peace and quiet.

Back kitchens and sculleries physically separate food prep, appliances and cleanup from the main kitchen, where much of daily living and entertaining takes place.

Upstairs retreats, homework rooms, and secondary living spaces create further separation, giving household members somewhere to do their own thing without sacrificing the openness of the kitchen and great room.

Wet rooms are not a new feature but are gaining more attention and are influencing bathroom layouts and design, no longer reserved just for higher-end homes.

“One reason is that you can use every inch of that space, which can mean a larger shower and a more spa-like feel,” says Debra Purvis with Design House.

A wet room typically is an open-concept bathroom, where a bathtub and a shower share an enclosure, sometimes separated by a glass partition from the rest of the bathroom.

Wet rooms offer great decorative potential too, with soaker tubs, steam showers, and statement fixtures. They also lend themselves naturally to other trends like tile drenching, which provides a dramatic, upscale look.

They are family friendly too. “Kids splash water out of the tub; it’s not a problem. Between the tile and floor drains, you are covered,” says Purvis.

Flex rooms offer opportunity in a floor plan without adding square footage, one reason they remain among the most sought-after features in new homes. But today’s buyers are looking for flex rooms with purpose, rather than just a blank-slate bonus room.

Practical considerations, such as outlets, storage, layered lighting, and easy access without crossing through other spaces, offer flexible futureproofing. The flex room needs to be appropriately sized and configured for the potential use too.

Location in the home indicates flex room potential too.

While two-story floor plans remain in-demand, one-story floor plans are showing modest growth.

“A one-story plan is going to be more accessible, generally speaking, which opens it up to buyers in many different life phases,” says Aurora Zeledon, director of digital content and marketing for Zonda House Plans, including Houseplans.com.

While land availability and cost might be driving the uptick in one-story floor plans, the versatility of living on one level has design upside and broad-based appeal, including 55+, multigen households, and younger families who appreciate having everyone on the same level.

One-story plans offer easier circulation, without stairs and landings occupying transitional spaces. Typically, one-story homes benefit from a stronger indoor/outdoor connection, often an anchor of the design, an in-demand feature as well.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), two-story plans still accounted for over half of single-family home starts in 2025 nationwide, although that number had dropped slightly, while the number of single-story homes inched up. Notably, there were significant differences across regions.

Meanwhile, Zeledon reports that the majority of floor plans they have sold, dating back to 2019, are for one-story homes, including their current bestseller. However, she notes that year-to-date there has been a modest increase in one-story house plan sales, compared to last year, pointing out that much of the activity is concentrated in the South and Southeast.

As homes generally scale down in size, storage becomes essential for homeowners to retain the functionality of a larger home in a smaller footprint.

“The overarching idea is to utilize every square foot. When storage is thoughtfully integrated into the architecture, we can maximize the home for multiple purposes—and, importantly, multiple storage solutions—without making the spaces feel overly utilitarian,” says Hannah Sloan, creative marketing specialist with Unscripted Interior Design.

She reports that drop zones are gaining attention, as are Costco closets, laundry/mudroom and owner’s entrances.

Sloan says that some rooms are benefiting from space-specific storage that improves functionality, like in the primary bathroom with more thoughtfully designed vanities and built-ins. Meanwhile, fitness closets are appearing in home gyms to free up floor space for exercise.

“Then there are the found spaces—under-stair book nooks, hidden speakeasy-inspired bars, and other whimsical design opportunities. These spaces can become highly functional while also adding personality and surprise to a home,” says Sloan.

This article was originally published on NewHomeSource.com.

Heather Wright is a senior writer for NewHomeSource and Builder with a background in real estate reporting and home design, decor, and architecture. She has written for a number of print and digital publications in the lifestyle space.

#5582. Katy Perry’s Proposed Youth Summer Camp Sparks Wildfire Concern From Santa Barbara Residents

Katy Perry’s Firework Foundation has proposed a youth summer camp just outside of her hometown of Santa Barbara, CA, but nearly 400 residents are opposing the plan, citing a laundry list of concerns from wildfire risk to traffic and noise.

According to the project’s website, Gratitude Canyon “would provide a permanent home for Camp Firework” at a Goleta property that formerly operated as the headquarters of Bragg Live Food Products—the company that popularized apple cider vinegar.

Gratitude Canyon explains that the pop star and her sister, Angela Lerche—the foundation’s president—spent “significant time” at the proposed site of the camp growing up, noting a “close friendship” with Patricia Bragg, the company’s former CEO who died in 2023 at the age of 94.

The foundation estimates that “approximately 97% of the roughly 110-acre property would remain open space, agriculture or landscaping,” and that the camp’s activity would be “concentrated on about 16 acres,” leaving “much” of the existing apple orchard to remain.

The County of Santa Barbara's Major Condition Use Permit Application Project Description supports those claims.

The program has operated for seven years across more than a dozen camp sites, and serves children ages 11 through 13, combining “art, nature, leadership, and relationship-building for young people who may not otherwise have access to immersive camp experiences.”

A petition under the name “Neighbors Against Gratitude Canyon” has garnered 396 signatures from concerned residents in response to the way the project is “currently proposed.”

“The Firework Foundation is seeking County approval to rezone 183 Winchester Canyon with a General Plan Amendment and build a youth camp/event center, bringing 8,000+ visitors a year into a quiet, residential canyon, with amplified noise permitted 9am-9pm, 400-person events, and one way in or out of a high fire-risk, debris-flow zone,” the petition states.

Neighbors Against Gratitude Canyon has organized the neighbors’ “top concerns.” The first on the list is that they believe the camp is a “Trojan Horse” and is a “year-round event center” designed “under the guise of a summer camp for underserved kids.”

However, Gratitude Canyon has stated that the proposal is not intended to serve as “a wedding or concert venue,” and plans to keep limited use outside of summer camp to schools, nonprofits, and “occasional retreats,” as well as “no more than four special events per year.”

Additionally, the petition raises concerns about fire safety, claiming “a formal fire protection plan and independent county-reviewed evacuation analysis still haven’t been completed,” and that evacuation capacity for the camp’s children and staff should be established prior to changing the property’s zoning.

However, Gratitude Canyon’s frequently asked questions page notes “fire prevention has been incorporated into the project form the earliest planning stages” and claim “measures include defensible space, vegetation management, emergency access, onsite water, hardened structures, evacuation planning, emergency communications, and 24-hour staffing while campers are onsite.”

The Gratitude Canyon website also explains that the Firework Foundation is engaging “directly with neighbors” and that the project “remains an evolving proposal.”

The summer camp proposal is not the first time Perry has been involved in a dispute centered around property in Santa Barbara.

The “California Gurls” singer and her former fiance, Orlando Bloom, were involved in a yearslong courtroom battle regarding a $15 million Montecito mansion.

The legal drama began in 2020, when the couple purchased the home from 1-800-Flowers founder, Carl Westcott, who rescinded the deal days later.

Westcott had reportedly purchased the estate for $11 million just two months prior, and sued Perry’s long-time business manager, Bernie Gudvi, who handled the purchase. Westcott claimed he “lacked capacity” to sell his home because he was suffering from a brain disorder and was under the influence of painkillers.

After years of legal back-and-forth, a 2023 ruling concluded that the original sale contract should be upheld. Perry countersued Westcott, seeking nearly $6 million in damages from the veteran, including $3.5 million in lost rental income and more than $2 million in repairs due to his alleged “lack of maintenance” of the property. The damages were later revised to $4.8 million.

Perry was awarded $1.94 million in damages, which was deducted from the $6 million that remained outstanding on the property’s original purchase price, leaving Perry and her representatives responsible for paying just over $4 million.

In October of this year, Westcott alleged he had only received a fraction of the amount owed, leaving Perry and Bloom susceptible to another legal confrontation.

#5581. The Home Depot Foundation Expands Veteran Housing Commitment to $1 Billion

The Home Depot Foundation is increasing its total commitment to veteran causes to $1 billion through 2032, expanding investments in programs designed to address veteran homelessness, housing insecurity, and home accessibility.

Since 2011, the foundation says it has invested more than $650 million in veteran causes and helped improve more than 70,000 veteran homes and facilities. Its latest commitment will combine established housing programs with efforts to test and scale new approaches to veteran housing.

“We believe every veteran deserves a safe place to call home,” said Erin Izen, executive director of The Home Depot Foundation. “Our $1 billion commitment supports the partnerships and solutions needed to help more veterans move from uncertainty to long-term stability.”

Among the initiatives receiving support are programs designed to remove barriers to rental housing. The Landlords, Organizations, and Veterans Engagement (LOVE) Fund, with Open Doors Atlanta, and the U.S. VETS Master Lease Program aim to speed veteran housing placements by addressing costs such as security deposits and application fees or by leasing units directly from property owners.

The foundation is also investing in homelessness prevention and permanent supportive housing through organizations including Operation Homefront and Community Solutions. Additional funding will explore alternative housing approaches, including modular homes from Purple Heart Homes for senior veterans and veterans experiencing housing insecurity.

The announcement coincides with the foundation’s annual Celebration of Service. This fall, Team Depot, The Home Depot’s associate volunteer force, is expected to complete hundreds of projects benefiting veterans across all 50 states and three U.S. territories.

One recent project brought The Home Depot Foundation, Team Depot, and Purple Heart Homes together to construct a fully accessible modular home on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., for James “Jim” Taylor, a U.S. Marine Corps veteran who previously experienced homelessness. The home was subsequently transported to Virginia, where a dedication is planned.

#5580. University AI’s biggest challenge? Scaling research without losing control

The push for sovereign AI is reaching university research labs, where control over data, models and compute now shapes what science gets done.

Universities sit at an unusual crossroads in the current technological shift, as their work spans open education and tightly controlled federal research. Learning sits at the heart of both missions, making AI a core supporting technology for expanding research and education alike, according to Vince Kellen (pictured, center), chief information officer of the Texas A&M University System.

“AI is a platform for thought. It’s a platform for discovery,” Kellen noted. “AI kind of undergirds all of what we’re going to be doing in the future — certainly what we’re doing in the present now.”

Kellen and Casey Bryan (right), chief information officer of the Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station, spoke with Krista Case (left) during theCUBE’s coverage of the AI Cybersecurity & Resilience Summit. They discussed how Texas A&M is building a secure, controlled foundation for AI-driven research. (* Disclosure below.)

The foundation of Texas A&M’s approach is IGNITE, short for Innovative Growth in Next Generation AI Technology Ecosystem. It is a state-funded AI and high-performance computing platform led by TEES, as the experiment station is known. Dell Technologies Inc. is building the system with Advanced Micro Devices Inc. graphics processing units inside an Equinix Inc. data center in Dallas. That investment will give research teams the computing power their existing systems lack, Bryan noted.

“Part of our current challenge is that existing resources, while they are performing some of that work, are severely underpowered,” he said. “Research is getting done but could be helped by capacity and scale, which I think IGNITE’s going to bring to the table.”

But the economics matter as much as the capability. Public attention has centered on neoclouds and cloud providers, yet on-premises data centers are growing significantly because of both security controls and cost, according to Kellen. High retail prices for AI computing resources are now limiting the ability of institutions to conduct scientific research.

“There’s no way we could take the science to your classic neocloud provider today and conduct the same thing,” Kellen said. “It’s 5 to 10x the cost.”

Controlling those assets significantly reduces costs and strengthens security, Kellen said. Sovereignty spans four pillars — data, infrastructure, capability and model, and governance — with Equinix supplying physical protection for the compute itself, Bryan added. As a state agency, TEES follows National Institute of Standards and Technology frameworks 800-53 and 800-171, as well as Texas Administrative Code 202, and it wants IGNITE to be ready for Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification Level 2.

“There’s a lot of controls we have to inherit, but our researchers shouldn’t have to think about all those,” Bryan said. “It should be absolutely seamless when they go to use the capabilities.”

That principle shaped the IGNITE build. When TEES sat down with Dell’s implementation team to schedule workshops, security came first, and the project’s architecture review board has since affirmed that direction, according to Bryan. For institutions starting their own sovereign AI projects, that sequencing is the lesson.

“The idea was to build that security foundation with which all of the other operational components could be built and referenced back to,” Bryan said. “At its core, start with security early — get it embedded in the process earlier on — and it’s much easier to keep it baked in at the beginning than have to worry about adding that at the end.”

#5579. Beyond the Zero Down Payment: The Best States for Homebuyers Using VA Loans in 2026

VA loans can help veterans and active-duty service members turn their dream of homeownership into a reality.

Partly guaranteed by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, they don’t require down payments or charge monthly mortgage insurance, unlike many other loan programs.

If you or a loved one are eligible for a VA loan, you may be wondering where to buy a home. According to Military.com, Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Virginia, and Tennessee are all solid options.

“What makes these states attractive isn't necessarily one standout benefit. It's the combination of things that can make life after the military a little easier, whether that's keeping more of your retirement income, finding a good civilian job, or living somewhere with a strong veteran community,” says Chris Birk, vice president of mortgage insight at Veterans United Home Loans in Columbia, MO.

By becoming familiar with what each state has to offer, you could narrow down your home search and find a property that aligns with your lifestyle budget.

From no property taxes and lower housing costs to veteran-specific tax breaks, these military-friendly states can make homeownership more accessible and affordable.

According to data from the VA, Virginia is one of the leading states for VA-backed loans, likely due to its large military population and steady real estate market growth.

“Northern Virginia’s proximity to government facilities like the Pentagon, Fort Belvoir, and Marine Corps Base Quantico allows many veterans to transition into federal or defense-related employment without uprooting their families,” says Dell Jeanty, real estate agent at Dell Residential in Arlington, VA.

The state offers real estate tax exemption for qualifying veterans with a 100% service-connected, permanent and total disability. Additionally, due to the major military installations and frequent military relocations, Virginia has a high concentration of assumable loans.

“This means you could potentially take over a seller's lower, locked-in historical interest rate and further your savings as a veteran,” Jeanty adds.

Many markets in North Carolina, including Charlotte, offer opportunities for veterans at different stages of life, whether you’re transitioning to a civilian career or retiring.

“There’s an established veteran community and plenty of ways to build new connections through work, recreation, and shared interests. You can choose city living or quieter settings with more land while enjoying professional sports, outdoor activities, and travel access,” says Ashley Horton, global real estate adviser at Premier Sotheby's International Realty in Charlotte.

Also, military installations across the Carolinas like Fort Liberty and Camp Lejeune are within driving distance, and highway connections and a major airport keep you connected to other markets. Plus, North Carolina lets qualifying military retirees deduct military retirement pay from state taxable income.

“Compared with markets in other states, those in North Carolina can give you more home, more space, and more options for the same budget. If you’re relocating from higher-cost cities, the equity from your previous home can stretch further here,” adds Horton.

Florida is one of those states where you’ll never run out of things to do.

You can enjoy country living with land and wide-open spaces, a coastal environment with beautiful beaches and waterways, or a neighborhood close to shopping, restaurants, and entertainment. And of course, you can’t beat being able to enjoy the outdoors almost year-round.

“I live and sell in the Orlando area, which is most well known for the Disney and Universal theme parks. In fact, Universal Studios Orlando just opened the Epic Universe park—fun for the whole family,” says Christina Rordam, a real estate agent at Florida Realty Investments in Orlando.

Also, since there are fewer homebuyers to compete with in Florida, you may have more leverage to negotiate ideal terms.

According to Rordam, there are currently two groups of sellers: the motivated and the unrealistic.

“The motivated home sellers are moving for job transfers, divorcing, having kids, and needing more space. These types of life events really encourage sellers to take a long, hard look at the current market and cut buyers a good deal,” Rordam explains.

In the past, it was almost unthinkable to negotiate price, repairs, and closing costs. Now, it's much more likely.

Rordam has a cash buyer for whom she negotiated $1,600 in repairs and $20,000 off the purchase price on a home that had been on the market less than a week.

In addition, Florida has no state individual income tax and some valuable property tax benefits for qualifying veterans.

“For example, certain veterans with service-connected disabilities may qualify for additional homestead property tax exemptions, and veterans with qualifying total and permanent service–connected disabilities may be eligible for a full exemption from property taxes on their homestead. Those savings can make a real difference in the overall cost of owning a home,” says Sheena Haney, broker and owner at Haney Signature Realty in St. Augustine, FL.

To Haney, Florida is more than just a place to buy a home.

“It’s a place where you can really enjoy the lifestyle, raise a family, retire, and make lasting memories,” adds Haney.

Texas gives veteran buyers something incredibly valuable: options.

In Central Texas, for example, you’ll find everything from established neighborhoods to new construction, where builders may offer incentives to make homeownership more affordable.

“San Antonio is especially attractive because of its relatively low cost of living, allowing many military families to stretch their housing budgets further,” says April Guerra, real estate agent at LPT Realty in Leander, TX.

Put simply, the Lone Star State doesn’t force you to sacrifice space, amenities, or lifestyle to find a home within your budget.

“If you’re a veteran looking to establish roots after military service, that flexibility can make a meaningful difference,” Guerra explains.

Texas also has a long-standing connection to the military.

“I grew up in San Antonio, proudly known as Military City, USA, home to Joint Base San Antonio, including Fort Sam Houston, Lackland, and Randolph. Now, working in the Austin area, I'm also near Camp Mabry and Fort Hood. Military families are an important part of these communities,” says Guerra.

There’s an established VA healthcare system as well.

“For example, in the Dallas-Fort Worth Metroplex, Dallas has a full-service VA hospital.  Fort Worth has a large VA outpatient clinic,” says Elizabeth Lane, real estate agent at HomeSmart Realty in Dallas.

Additionally, Texas offers no state individual income tax, potential property tax exemptions for qualifying disabled veterans, and access to military and veteran support networks.

There's also a strong sense of community and diverse employment opportunities.

“Companies like Lockheed Martin and Bell Textron have a large presence in North Texas and like to recruit veterans,” adds Lane.

Tennessee offers a unique mix of benefits for military homebuyers.

First and foremost, there’s no state income tax.

“On top of that, Tennessee has some of the lowest property taxes in the U.S., ranking roughly eighth to 10th lowest, depending on the specific index,” says Wendy Monday, real estate agent at Broker Onward Real Estate in Nashville, TN.

By contrast, states such as New Jersey and Illinois have significantly higher tax rates, which add considerably to the cost of homeownership.

Also, Nashville is one of the premier healthcare hubs in the country, making top-quality medical care exceptionally accessible locally.

It boasts an incredibly high density of Level 1 Trauma Centers, top-tier children's hospitals, and specialized emergency rooms right in the metro area.

“You won't have to travel to another city or state if you or a family member ever face a complex diagnosis or require a rare medical specialist,” Monday explains.

#5578. LGI Homes Posts Q3 Gains Despite Slower Sales Activity

LGI Homes posted year-over-year gains in closings, revenue, and earnings during the third quarter, even as affordability pressures continued to weigh on buyer demand and slow sales activity.

The Texas-based builder delivered 1,222 homes during the quarter, up 10.4% from a year earlier, including 33 currently and previously leased homes. Its 1,189 new-home closings generated $437.5 million in home building revenue, an increase of 10.3% year over year. Total revenue increased 10.2% to $444.5 million.

“We delivered strong third quarter financial results, generating year-over-year growth in closings, revenue, and earnings while maintaining strong profitability, expanding our community count, and further strengthening our balance sheet,” chairman and CEO Eric Lipar said.

Net income increased to $24.6 million from $19.7 million in the prior-year quarter, while diluted earnings per share increased to $1.05 from $0.85.

Home building gross margin was 20.2% in the third quarter, while adjusted home building gross margin was 23.7%. Both were above the midpoint of LGI Homes’ previous guidance ranges and improved 40 basis points sequentially.

Lipar attributed the margin performance in part to the company’s predominantly self-developed, on-balance-sheet land position and its approach to balancing affordability and profitability.

“Our teams also did an excellent job managing costs. SG&A expenses declined on an absolute-dollar basis, and SG&A as a percentage of total revenues improved 180 basis points year over year,” he said.

The builder also continued expanding its footprint, ending the third quarter with 151 active communities, an increase of 7.1% from the prior-year period.

Despite stronger closings and revenue, LGI Homes said affordability pressure contributed to slower sales activity during the quarter.

Through the first nine months of 2026, net orders totaled 2,869, compared with 4,098 during the same period in 2025. The cancellation rate increased to 48.9% from 28.1%, while ending backlog declined to 685 homes from 1,305 a year earlier.

The trend marks a reversal from the beginning of the year, when LGI Homes ended the first quarter with 1,699 homes in backlog, up 63.4% year over year. At the time, management pointed to improving sales activity and a growing backlog as evidence of steady demand heading into the spring selling season.

By the third quarter, however, affordability had become a more significant headwind.

“We continue to see interest in homeownership and are leaning into our proven sales and marketing strategies to improve sales pace while maintaining our disciplined approach to balancing affordability and profitability,” Lipar said.

Based on its year-to-date results and current market conditions, LGI Homes narrowed its full-year closing guidance and now expects to deliver between 4,600 and 4,800 homes in 2026. The company said the revised outlook reflects slower sales activity as affordability pressures continue to weigh on demand.

The builder maintained the remainder of its full-year guidance, including an expected average sales price between $360,000 and $370,000 and adjusted home building gross margin between 22.5% and 24.5%.

“As we head into the final quarter of the year, our focus is on finishing 2026 strong,” Lipar said. “Affordability remains the key consideration for today’s buyers, and we have intentionally broadened our sales process to work with more prospective customers who may need additional time to qualify.”

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5575. Oracle urges database customers to prepare for quantum security risks

Attackers can copy encrypted traffic today and decrypt it once quantum computers mature, making quantum-resistant cryptography a present-day concern.

Oracle Corp. is applying the philosophy behind its security controls beneath AI agents to encryption across database fleets, according to Vipin Samar (pictured), senior vice president of software engineering, database security, at Oracle.

“Even though we don’t have quantum computers which are sufficiently powerful today, when they come, that can create a risk because people can make a copy of your encrypted data today,” Samar said. “Your TLS 1.2 traffic, 1.3 traffic, I can make a copy of it. And then when quantum becomes available, I can figure out the session key and decrypt … your entire sensitive data.”

Samar spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed security concerns related to quantum-resistant cryptography. (* Disclosure below.)

Oracle’s new Cryptographic Posture Assessment in Oracle Data Safe assesses cryptographic configurations across database fleets, flagging weak spots such as lingering TLS 1.0 and 1.1 support. Agentic AI-driven remediation is in preview, Samar noted.

“It doesn’t help if network encryption is strong, but other parts are actually on the weaker side. And this becomes a challenge, especially when PQC or the quantum computers come along because they can attempt to hack into any of those systems,” Samar said.

Deep Data Security, which enforces row- and column-level access in Oracle AI Database 26ai, uses signed OAuth2 tokens to identify the end user behind an AI agent’s query. Oracle treats AI as one more application accessing the same data.

“We said instead of sprinkling this dust everywhere, why don’t we secure at the source?” Samar said. “When you move something inside the database, you get great security because there are no ways to bypass it.”
