#5574. EXCLUSIVE: ‘The Wolves of Real Estate’ Director Reveals the Unanswered Questions Behind the Alexander Brothers’ Downfall

Before their names became synonymous with a federal sex-trafficking case, Tal and Oren Alexander built careers selling some of the country’s most expensive homes.

Now, a documentary examining the brothers and their crimes is raising questions about the role wealth, professional prestige, and exclusive social circles played in giving them access to women.

Peacock’s three-part series, “The Wolves of Real Estate: The Alexander Brothers,” examines the rise and downfall of Tal, Oren, and their brother Alon, tracing a story that stretched from luxury properties and lavish parties to a Manhattan courtroom.

All three were convicted of federal sex offenses, including conspiracy to commit sex trafficking, on March 9. On Oct. 27, each was sentenced to 30 years in prison, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York.

Speaking exclusively to Realtor.com®, Emma Schwartz, director of “The Wolves of Real Estate: The Alexander Brothers,” says the brothers’ status helped draw women into their orbit, while cautioning against assuming that every allegation involved their professional lives.

“Testimony at trial made clear that the brothers’ wealth and status was one of the reasons they were able to attract so many women,” Schwartz says.

“But many of the allegations we heard about did not involve their jobs or work.”

Tal and Oren rose to prominence at Douglas Elliman before leaving in 2022 to co-found luxury brokerage Official.

Their résumés included the $238 million Manhattan penthouse transaction at 220 Central Park South in 2019, which set a U.S. residential sale record at the time. Alon, Oren’s twin, worked in the family’s private security business.

Prosecutors described a scheme in which the brothers used their money and connections, including Tal and Oren’s standing in ultraluxury real estate, to facilitate sexual assaults.

Women were enticed with trips, accommodations, and exclusive experiences, according to the government’s account of the evidence.

Yet the criminal proceedings were not primarily an examination of the brokerage business, Schwartz explains.

“One of the interesting things about the criminal trial was how little it focused on the brothers’ professional lives,” Schwartz says.

Only one Douglas Elliman agent testified, according to the interview responses, with the government seeking information about a summer lease in the Hamptons.

Nevertheless, some testimony revealed an overlap between the properties associated with the brothers’ business image and the places where women said they were assaulted.

“For instance, the house that two women testified at trial that they were raped and trafficked to, was featured in a business video for the brothers,” Schwartz says.

Another woman testified that the possibility of making a professional connection had interested her in attending a party to which the brothers had invited her friend, according to Schwartz.

Those accounts illustrate how professional opportunity and social access could intersect. They do not, on their own, establish that the brothers systematically used access to clients’ listings to commit crimes.

Questions about what others knew also remain central to the story.

“One of the biggest questions so many have is who knew what about the brothers’ behavior?” Schwartz says.

The interview responses point to an email from an Elliman official, discussed in the documentary and presented at trial, as evidence that at least some people knew about the brothers’ playboy lifestyle.

But Schwartz distinguishes that awareness from knowledge of sexual violence.

“We also know from reporters at The Real Deal that there had been rumors about the brothers’ alleged behavior circulating in the industry for years before the lawsuits came out,” Schwartz says.

Rumors, awareness of partying, and evidence that a particular person knew about a crime are different matters. The responses do not establish criminal wrongdoing by the brokerage or its other employees.

For Schwartz, another striking aspect of the trial was the difficulty women described in acknowledging and reporting their experiences.

“One of the striking things about the trial was how so many of the women said they had been ashamed and too afraid to report what happened to them,” Schwartz says.

Some took months or years to describe what happened as rape or sexual assault, according to the interview responses.

That hesitation is a significant part of the documentary’s larger story: the barriers women faced in coming forward, even as the brothers maintained wealth and social standing.

“This all raises an important issue about sexual assault cases: women often take a long time, sometimes years, before they are ready to speak about what happened,” Schwartz says.

The civil justice system also played a role. New York’s Adult Survivors Act created a temporary window allowing adults to bring certain sexual-assault claims that would otherwise have been barred by expired filing deadlines. That window ran from Nov. 24, 2022 through Nov. 24, 2023.

Schwartz credits that law with allowing the first two women to file their civil claims, helping set in motion the public scrutiny that followed.

“This is a story about why speaking up matters,” Schwartz says.

“It took just two women filing lawsuits, amplified by the media to open the floodgates for dozens of women to come forward.”

Asked whether the case reveals something broader about luxury brokerages, Schwartz resists drawing a sweeping conclusion about the entire industry.

“It’s really hard to know how much anyone can generalize from the brothers to the industry more broadly.”

The hope, instead, is that the women’s accounts will help others feel able to share their own experiences.

“The women and people who spoke for our documentary did so in hopes that sharing their experience would encourage others to speak up and not feel the shame they did.”

She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. #5572. JD Vance Blames Iran War for GOP Rout After Mortgage Rates Soared

Vice President JD Vance is blaming Republicans' election losses on the Iran conflict and rising prices.

"The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," Vance said in a post on X, hours after Democrats shellacked Republicans in the midterm elections, flipping almost three dozen seats in the House and Senate to win control of both chambers.

Vance noted that polling found the war in Iran and cost of living and inflation concerns were the top items on voters' minds heading into Election Day.

Those were among the top reasons that many of the voters who helped propel President Donald Trump to a second term in 2024, with majorities in both chambers of Congress, voted in Democrats on Tuesday, Vance said.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance said in the post. "The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.

"But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there," Vance said.

Indeed, Americans were broadly concerned about affordability in the months leading up to the election. While Trump said he remained focused on it, he spent the run-up to the election detailing projects in Washington, DC, such as a botched effort to renovate the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Both Democrats and Republicans have promised their own affordability agendas for the coming months. But in swing states that turned against Trump, including Iowa, Ohio, Texas, and Maine, housing affordability was at the top of voters' minds. So, too, have many young voters worried that homeownership is rising out of reach.

Most markers of inflation show many costs have risen sharply this year. Gas prices often embody Americans' concerns, and AAA reports the national average price for gas is $4.12 a gallon, compared to $3.05 a year ago.

Trump, for his part, continued defending his economic record on Tuesday, telling media outlets that night that he would accept the election results and might seek common ground with Democrats.

But then he also posted an image of a red hat with the word "veto" on it, before celebrating the rise of the Dow the next morning following the results.

"Stock Market just hit another Record High—91 Days in just a short period of time—Less than two years," he posted to Truth Social on Wednesday. "Your 401(k)s are through the roof. Record Setting All!"

And yet, the war in Iran and its resultant rise in oil prices and other costs hamstrung efforts to improve affordability. The Federal Reserve hiked interest rates earlier this year, and kept them steady in its most recent meeting. Minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee in recent months show that leaders are worried that inflation is stickier than expected and that the conflict with Iran will continue to drive up costs.

Vance said in his post that it was "sound" political advice to call for a diplomatic solution to the Iran conflict. He also indicated that he could be open for change to the controversial immigration enforcement policies that have deeply affected the housing market and home construction.

"I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance," Vance said in the post. "But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you."

Meanwhile, Democratic leaders said in a press conference on Wednesday that they would focus on affordability in the coming term.

New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is likely to become the new Speaker of the House, repeatedly avoided discussing Trump. Instead, he said his focus was on "affordability and accountability."

"We know we have to undertake, with the seriousness of purpose, a relentless effort to make life more affordable for everyday Americans," Jeffries said. Later he added, "We have been focused, relentlessly, on dealing with the affordability crisis and driving down the high cost of living."

Massachusetts Rep. Katherine Clark, who is currently minority whip but stands as a contender to become House majority leader, said that could include efforts to roll back the president's tariffs, which have driven up the cost of many homebuilding materials and household goods.

Jeffries said the House Democratic Caucus will convene next week and lay out a clear plan for what to do next. But neither he nor Sen. Chuck Schumer had heard directly from Trump on Wednesday.

The National Association of Realtors®, in a Wednesday statement, called for more progress on housing.

“Regardless of which party controls Congress, NAR’s priorities remain the same: increasing housing supply, improving affordability, protecting property rights and expanding access to homeownership," NAR said. "Our research shows that 85% of Americans believe homeownership is part of the American Dream, underscoring why housing must remain a priority for lawmakers on both sides of the aisle."

RPAC-supported candidates won in at least 325 races, and a number of ballot initiatives this year involved housing-related issues. NAR also noted the bipartisanship of the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, the housing package aimed at making it easier to build homes. Congress passed it this summer with large majorities from both parties.

"We will continue building on that momentum, working with REALTOR® champions and real estate allies in both parties to advance commonsense solutions that bring more homes to the market and help more Americans achieve the dream of homeownership," NAR said.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5571. Oracle rethinks the lakehouse as AI agents become data consumers

A shared semantic layer is fast becoming the dividing line between lakehouses built for reporting and those built for artificial intelligence.

As AI agents join human analysts in querying corporate data, enterprises need platforms that make sense of information scattered across clouds, formats and rival systems. Oracle Corp. has spent the past year rebuilding its data stack around that shift, part of a broader database modernization push. The company now pitches its Autonomous AI Lakehouse as an open layer that sits across an enterprise’s existing data estate rather than replacing it, according to Nipun Agarwal (pictured), senior vice president of software engineering, Oracle Database, at Oracle.

“Lakehouses were the platform which customers use for running analytics,” Agarwal said. “Now, lakehouses have become the decision backbone for AI.”

Agarwal spoke with theCUBE’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Oracle’s Autonomous AI Lakehouse combines a shared semantic layer with fast, real-time access to data across platforms to support AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)

Oracle’s approach rests on a catalog that can mount other catalogs, such as Databricks Inc.’s Unity Catalog, along with Postgres and MySQL databases, so data is queried in place rather than copied. The company announced a business semantic layer and broader Apache Iceberg support at the October event, with table and column descriptions the system generates applying to non-Oracle sources as well, according to Agarwal. Crucially, Oracle does not see the offering as competing with other lakehouses, he added.

“We really believe that for any enterprise, they’re gonna have a choice,” he said. “They’re gonna be using multiple data sources. They’ll have multiple lakehouses.”

Oracle’s Lake Cache speeds up queries by moving the most-used Iceberg tables into Exadata’s flash cache. Real-time access is also becoming essential as software agents become the main consumers of the data: Scheduled refreshes of copied data can fall short when agents request it on demand, according to Agarwal.

“With AI that’s no longer the case, because for AI, the consumer is not a human necessarily,” Agarwal said. “The need for real-time access is a lot more with AI.”

#5570. The Renovation Cool-Off Is Here, but Delaying Certain Repairs Could Cost You More Than You Save

Spending on home improvements and repairs is only expected to grow by 1.5% by the third quarter of 2027, according to Harvard University Joint Center for Housing Studies. Given the high cost of labor and materials these days, this is no surprise.

But if you’re trying to cut back on home projects to save some cash, it's important to understand which ones are truly optional and which ones actually need immediate attention.

“Not every project needs to happen right away. Your home doesn't have to look brand-new to be safe, comfortable, and in good shape,” says Jeri Goodkin Dausey, president and certified general contractor at SBC in Miami Beach, FL.

By knowing how to prioritze your budget, you can protect your home’s condition and value without draining your savings.

There are quite a few projects you can delay without hurting your home, as long as everything is safe and working properly.

“Sometimes, waiting can save you quite a bit of money in the short term,” Dausey explains.

Here’s what you can put on the back burner until you have more funds at your disposal.

If your cabinets, countertops, and fixtures are still in decent shape and everything works, there's no need to rush into a complete remodel.

“Let's say you were planning to spend $25,000 on a renovation but could take care of the immediate issue with a $500 repair instead. That's $24,500 you can hold onto for now,” says Dausey.

A fresh coat of paint or new trim can make a significant difference in your home’s aestehtics, but these are usually things that can wait if the walls and surfaces are in good shape.

“If you put off a $4,000 paint job and just spend $200 on a few touch-ups, you've kept another $3,800 in your budget,” Dausey explains.

Dmitri Popescu, general manager at Olympic Decks in Seattle, echoes Dausey’s thoughts.

“Repainting a room because you dislike the color or replacing an undamaged backsplash can generally wait. There’s no need to spend your money on a temporary makeover,” Popescu explains.

Not loving the look of your floors doesn't necessarily mean you need to replace them. If they're safe, stable, and free of water damage, you may be able to live with them a little longer.

“Putting off an $8,000 replacement and spending $300 on maintenance leaves you with $7,700. Just be sure to check out loose tiles, soft spots or areas that are lifting,” says Dausey.

An outdoor kitchen, new landscaping, or a bigger patio might be nice to have, but they're not necessities. If everything outside is safe and in good shape, these projects can wait.

“Delaying a $15,000 cosmetic upgrade in your backyard frees up a lot of money for other things. Just don't overlook problems like poor drainage, hazardous trees, or an unsafe deck,” advises Dausey.

These expert tips can help you decide whether a project can wait:

Ask yourself, does this project actually protect my home, or is it simply for aesthetics?

“Cosmetic upgrades can wait, but projects that protect the structural integrity and long-term value of your property can't,” says Roxanne Conrad, chief operating officer at Premium Service Brands in Charlottesville, VA.

Clogged gutters and unstable exterior surfaces like missing shingles and unsealed windows, for example, can be an issue.

“They can lead to much larger problems down the road if neglected for too long,” Conrad says.

If you’ve noticed the issue a while ago and it’s worsening, it likely deserves your time and money.

“Catching problems early is almost always easier and cheaper than repairing them as they fail,” Conrad explains.

Take care of what keeps your home safe, dry, and in good shape, and don't feel pressured to tackle every cosmetic project right away.

Keith Ostendorf, project developer at Next Stage Design + Build in San Jose, CA, recommends phasing.

“Some homeowners move forward in phases, which spreads out the spending and can cut the costs of moving out, since work in one part of the house can happen while the family lives in the rest,” he adds.

#5569. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5568. As AI takes over coding, Oracle rethinks how applications are built

As vibe coding moves from novelty to everyday practice, enterprises face a new problem: Machine-generated software still has to be maintained, governed and understood by people.

Low-code platforms were built to speed up application development, and AI is now rewriting that mission. Oracle Corp. previewed its answer ahead of its annual conference, and the tipping point for software development has already arrived, according to Mike Hichwa (pictured), senior vice president of software engineering at Oracle.

“In 2025, the majority of code was human-authored, and in 2026 and forever afterwards, the majority of code is going to be machine-generated,” Hichwa said. “We’re probably not going back. What we’ve done to address this change is we invented our own language. We call it APEXlang.”

Hichwa spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed vibe coding and the need to maintain and govern AI-generated code. (* Disclosure below.)

APEXlang is a highly abstracted application definition language that captures intent rather than implementation. Oracle introduced it with the APEX AI Application Generator and is publishing its grammar, skills and documentation in the public domain so coding agents such as Anthropic PBC’s Claude and OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex can generate it. Oracle is also working with OpenAI to train models to generate the language more efficiently, Hichwa explained.

“What you’re generating actually matters, because once you generate it, and you generate it 100 times or 1,000 times within your enterprise, then you’re going to need to maintain it. You’re going to need to look after it,” Hichwa said. “What people want with their portfolio of applications, they want consistency, they want governance, they want ease of understanding.”

Governance comes from the runtime, too. Generated APEXlang is interpreted by the APEX engine, which Oracle patches and updates monthly, so customers don’t have to revisit what they built. The same design is meant to curb AI slop, since a compact definition is easier to read than sprawling generated code, according to Hichwa.

“What we’re generating is much, much smaller, much more human understandable, so it is less sloppy because it is more abstracted,” Hichwa said. “It’s like a CliffsNotes. It’s not the full book.”

#5567. Midterm Takeaways: Democratic Subpoenas, State ‘Trifectas’ and Bi-Coastal Ballot Wins

A midterm election that saw both historic turnout and spending ended with big wins for the Democratic party nearly across the board. While voters clearly went to the ballot box seeking change, can real estate expect the landslide result to boost a sluggish housing market, bring down rates or spark more regulatory scrutiny into housing practices?

At this very early stage, the answer to most of these questions is, unsurprisingly, a big maybe.

While the mainstream focus is always on Congressional elections (where Democrats made historic gains), impactful federal legislation for real estate appears unlikely. President Donald Trump promised to leverage his veto powers if Democrats won, previewing even more gridlock in Washington, but also told the Wall Street Journal on election night that he would work with Democrats.

Realtor.com® Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said in a statement that relief for the housing market at large “relies on a calmer geopolitical environment,” saying that it was unclear whether Democratic control of Congress could deliver this.

Real estate professionals understand well, though, housing is a local issue, and the results most likely to be impactful for practitioners are coming in lower-profile state elections. At the same time, though, a strongly Democratic congress in D.C. offers potential new wrinkles to high-profile real estate controversies and investigations.

As the dust settles on ballot initiatives, and new lawmakers set agendas for 2027, here are the biggest takeaways from the midterms:

Florida and California voters back major housing changes

Two of the most populous states in the country—which also have faced some of the most acute issues with housing supply and affordability in the past few years—overwhelmingly approved two unique initiatives that proponents say will offer some immediate benefits to buyers and homeowners.

In California, Proposition 37 was on track to be approved by around two-thirds of voters. The initiative, designed to simultaneously address the state’s long-running housing affordability and supply issues, creates a special “secondary mortgage” loan for down payments, and hopes to incentivize the construction of around 200,000 new homes at (relatively) attainable price points.

Speaking to RISMedia before the election, housing experts were cautiously optimistic the initiative could move the needle in the medium-term, though critics note the extra down payment loan means higher monthly costs for borrowers.

In a statement after the election, one of the initiative’s architects, Bob Hertzberg, thanked the California Association of Realtors®, among other supporters, for “a decisive first step to create generational homeownership opportunities in California.”

Simultaneously in the Sunshine State, voters strongly backed Amendment 3, which creates new tax relief for many property owners. The initiative makes several changes to how taxes are calculated, aiming to lower—or even eliminate—property tax bills for many homeowners.

The change has sparked some controversy, with concerns that it would deprive local governments of significant revenue. Supporters say it provides vital relief for homeowners struggling with rising homeownership costs, and opens up homeownership to more buyers (though notably, only people who establish state residency before December 2026 will be eligible for the exemption).

Both the Florida and California initiatives were supported by state Realtor® associations.

The result of another housing-focused ballot initiative in Massachusetts that would reduce minimum lot sizes for single-family homes was too close to call at press time Wednesday morning (Realtor® associations have supported that initiative as well).

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has demanded investigations into real estate practices—focused on Compass’s acquisitions, and role in building off-MLS “private” inventory.

With Democrats taking control of the Senate, Warren is now the highest-ranking member on the powerful Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee, which wields the power to issue subpoenas and hold high-profile hearings.

Whether Democratic control of Congress results in any new pressure on Compass or its policies remains to be seen. But back in February, Warren signed a letter with 17 other Democratic lawmakers that called the process by which Compass received approval for its acquisition of Anywhere “corruption,” citing media reports that the brokerage had bypassed antitrust concerns with back-channel lobbying.

Another signatory to that letter, Democratic Senator Ron Wyden, simply posted the word “Subpoenas” on social media as election results poured in last night. Wyden is currently the ranking member on the Senate Finance Committee.

Two Democrats (and one Republican) in the house also penned letters to the FTC this year focusing on “lead diversion” practices used by portals like Zillow, which they called deceptive. Lawmakers largely framed these practices as harming consumers amid larger affordability struggles.

With a significant focus on housing, it appears possible that Democratic oversight could very well shift more scrutiny onto real estate, even though enforcement power largely still rests with the executive branch.

State houses flip amid focus on ‘private’ listings, affordability

At least six state governments (Nevada, Wisconsin, Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Minnesota) appear on track to flip to a Democrat “trifecta” this year—meaning the party controls both the lower and upper legislative chambers, and the governor’s office. Other states saw significant Democratic gains, rebalancing legislative power that (often) has more of an impact on real estate issues.

Notably, a handful of (mostly) Democratic states passed laws over the last year or so restricting “private” marketing, though at least some of those bills had bipartisan support.

A trifecta, at least on paper, allows more legislation overall to move through state governments, and can result in previous shelved legislation getting another shot at becoming law. Governors also have significant executive power to regulate issues that impact housing in those states.

Among the many regulatory and legislative issues previously or currently being considered in these now-Democrat controlled states are rent control (Nevada), denser housing in suburbs (Arizona), state-wide accessory dwelling units (Pennsylvania), zoning reform for starter homes (Minnesota) and property tax cuts or refunds (Michigan and Wisconsin).

None of these issues are guaranteed to remain in the spotlight once lawmakers are seated and legislative sessions ramp up, but real estate advocates have pointed out that housing issues remain top-of-mind for many voters, who will likely expect substantive action and reforms in places where Democrats are newly empowered.

Jesse Williams is content director for RISMedia Premier.

#5566. Meghan Trainor Lists $18 Million Encino Mansion Formerly Owned by Joe Jonas and Sophie Turner

Meghan Trainor is saying goodbye to her sprawling Encino, CA, mansion, and has listed it for $17,995,000.

Although the manse is only 6 years old, it's already been home to a number of celebrity residents.

The “All About That Bass” singer and her husband, “Spy Kids” actor Daryl Sabara, purchased the abode in 2024 for $17,125,000. Previously, the dwelling belonged to music producer Zedd, who had listed the home for just under $19 million in January of that year.

The “Clarity” producer snapped up the six-bedroom, 12-bathroom property for $15.2 million in September 2021 from Joe Jonas and Sophie Turner.

The Jonas Brothers rocker and “Game of Thrones” star were the original owners, having bought the home for $14.1 million when it was built in 2019.

Spanning about 14,779 square feet, the home was designed by "distinguished” architect Jae Omar and sits on a near-acre of land in the exclusive Royal Oaks enclave.

A lavish two-story entrance creates an “incredible indoor/outdoor feel,” according to the listing, which notes that the compound is “for the most discerning buyer.”

With an impressive scale and an open-concept flow, the home is well-suited for hosting large gatherings as well as intimate dinners.

A generously sized great room with wall-to-wall sliding doors opens the home to an idyllic courtyard, while a built-in bar and a soothing fireplace keep things cozy.

The chef's kitchen has a sleek aesthetic, with modern cabinetry and countertops and a picture-frame window located above one of the two sinks. It’s also equipped with Miele appliances and a discreet refrigerator.

An oversized island seats seven, creating a perfect spot for families to spend quality time together.

There’s even a separate catering kitchen for more involved occasions.

Young children—like Trainor and Sabara’s three little ones, Riley Thomas, Barry Bruce, and Mikey Moon—could never be bored here. A one-of-a-kind playroom boasts a foam pit, slide, art station, and hidden reading nook. In fact, the entire home caters to readers, with floor-to-ceiling bookcases found throughout.

The property also includes an office space, a professional music studio with a vocal booth, and a fitness center with a steam shower.

The second floor includes yet another family room and five en suite bedrooms.

In its own wing, the primary suite has a sitting area, wet bar, and multiple patios. The spalike bathroom is impossibly luxurious, with an oversized walk-in shower and a soaking tub.

According to the listing, the primary suite’s two walk-in closets are “reminiscent of a luxury boutique.”

The backyard is yet another destination for a young family to enjoy, with “park-like” grounds that can be used for lounging, entertaining, and play.

Outdoor amenities include a kitchen and barbecue, a putting green, a fire pit, and a projection screen. “Enchanting” lighting and a robust sound system add to the magic.

The sparkling pool has a spa and runs alongside a separate guest structure that has a pub with a billiard room and fish tank. On the second floor is a fully decked-out screening room.

The property comes with a four-car garage, a security room with high-tech cameras throughout, and a Control4 smart home system.

This is the second Encino property Trainor has had on the market this year.

In April, she sold a $6.8 million property in the affluent neighborhood, hours before announcing she had canceled “The Get In Girl Tour” to prioritize time at home with her family.

The seven-bedroom, 7.5-bathroom dwelling was listed for $11.99 million in June 2024, with the price steadily decreasing over the following 21 months before falling to $6.99 million in March 2026.

Trainor and Sabara purchased the home in 2020 for $6.5 million and completed a full renovation, including a recording studio.

#5565. The Holiday Season Is the Best Time For Homebuyers to Score a Deal in These 7 U.S. Metros

Early November is the best time for homebuyers to score a bargain in three U.S. metro areas: Milwaukee, Riverside, CA and Tampa, FL.

In Detroit and three Florida metros–Fort Lauderdale, Miami and West Palm Beach–house hunters may benefit from holding out a little longer. Mid-December is typically the best time of year to get a deal in those places.

This is according to a Home Economics and Redfin analysis of housing market data; the analysis was originally completed in April. The analysis identifies the time of year when discounts off a home’s original asking price–through price drops and/or negotiations between buyer and seller–typically approach their seasonal peak.

Nationwide, discounts tend to peak in early fall before plateauing or shrinking as winter approaches. But housing is local, and in these seven metros, peak discounts typically arrive later. Homebuying slows as the holidays approach, leaving sellers with fewer potential buyers–giving the buyers who remain more room to negotiate. And some late-year listings have been sitting for months, making sellers more motivated to strike a deal before the end of the year.

“There’s a tradeoff to shopping for a home late in the year: Buyers may have fewer fresh listings to choose from, but they also face less competition, and many sellers are ready to make a deal,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “A seller who has been waiting months for an offer may be more willing to negotiate on price or other costs than they were in the spring. Buyers shouldn’t purchase a home just because the calendar says it’s a good time for deals, but those who find the right home may have room to negotiate.”

In Florida, the best deals for buyers typically arrive in November or December, partly due to weather. South Florida’s biggest wave of buyers–retirees and seasonal residents–often show up after the new year, when the weather is sunny and comfortable in Florida but cold in the Northeast.

“Local buyers have a good shot at getting a deal in November, mainly because it’s just before the snowbirds arrive,” said Todd Edwards, a Redfin Premier agent in Tampa. “House hunters have a window of opportunity to negotiate on listings that have been lingering on the market since summer: Sellers want to close a deal before the new year, and there’s often not much competition from out-of-towners yet.”

Hurricane season, which runs through early fall, also keeps some house hunters away and leaves lingering listings ripe for discounts once it passes. Additionally, Florida’s high concentration of luxury homes tend to sell below asking price, especially late in the year when sellers are eager to get those properties off their books.

The story is a bit different in Milwaukee and Detroit. Those northern metros have a fairly short selling season: Cold-weather markets compress the window for touring and closing on homes; sellers keep at it later into fall, trying to close a deal before the depth of winter hits and buyers hibernate.

That delays the usual seasonal slowdown until November in Milwaukee and December in Detroit, later than in most of the country.

The November and December discount windows in Milwaukee, Riverside, Detroit and much of Florida aren’t a one-time event; they show up as a recurring pattern each year, regardless of whether the broader market favors buyers or sellers.

But the seasonal advantage could be particularly useful to buyers this year. The U.S. housing market is already firmly tilted toward buyers, with 63% more sellers than buyers—the biggest imbalance in Redfin records dating back to 2013. A jump in listings coupled with sluggish homebuying demand has given house hunters in many parts of the country more options and more negotiating power. Miami is one of the strongest buyer’s markets in the nation, with more than twice as many sellers as buyers. Tampa, West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale, Riverside and Detroit are also buyer’s markets.

Milwaukee is one of just five seller’s markets in the country. With more buyers than sellers in Milwaukee, deals aren’t commonplace–so buyers there may want to pay extra attention to seasonal patterns.

The best time to buy a home is more complex than the week when buyers are most likely to score a discount.

There’s typically a tradeoff between selection and savings. New listings generally peak months before the best deals arrive. For instance, Milwaukee typically has the most new listings in mid-May and the most fresh inventory in mid-July,then its best deals arrive in early November. Detroit’s new listings typically peak in early August and fresh inventory in early September, months before its mid-December dealmaking sweet spot.

That means buyers who wait until November or December may have fewer homes to choose from. But those who prioritize price—and are flexible about their timing—may find sellers more receptive to negotiations. Ultimately, buyers should balance price, selection and their own circumstances.

Please note that this table includes 3 key moments for buyers; it’s important for buyers to balance what’s most important for them–choice or price

To identify the best time to buy, this Home Economics and Redfin analysis focuses on the seasonal indexes for three metrics: new listings, fresh inventory, and the average discount.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends. Redfin is a full-service real estate brokerage that uses modern technology to make clients smarter and faster. For more information about working with a Redfin real estate agent to buy or sell a home, visit our Why Redfin page.

Asad Khan studies housing market trends and the forces behind them as a senior economist at Redfin. Previously, he was an economic consultant at Analysis Group where he worked on antitrust and valuation matters. Asad taught urban economics as a Research Fellow at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and earned a PhD in economics from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. His research has focused on the economics of city structure and zoning policy.

#5564. Home prices rise in 78% of metros while weekly demand sinks to a low

Prices climbed in 78 percent of metros in the third quarter, according to NAR, as Redfin data shows pending sales at the lowest level in its records.

Home prices rose in 78 percent of U.S. metro areas during the third quarter, while pending sales in the four weeks ending Oct. 25 fell to the lowest level in Redfin’s records.

The national median single-family existing-home price rose 1.7 percent year over year to $432,900, matching the second quarter’s revised annual growth rate, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday. Prices rose in 78 percent of the some 235 metros NAR tracks, down from 80 percent in the second quarter, and fell in 21 percent, up from 20 percent. Four percent of metros posted double-digit gains, down from 5 percent.

“Even with affordability challenges causing the housing market to stagnate, home prices continue to set record highs in most parts of the country,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “Homeowners are the beneficiaries of the price gains. Over the past seven years, the average house has appreciated by $146,000.”

Redfin’s data for the four weeks ending Oct. 25 shows prices dipping. The median U.S. home-sale price fell 0.1 percent year over year to $389,601, according to Redfin, following a 0.2 percent decline the prior week. The two drops are the first in more than three years.

NAR and Redfin measure different things. NAR tracks quarterly sales of existing single-family homes, while Redfin’s figures cover homes listed or sold across more than 900 metros on a rolling four-week basis.

The Northeast posted the largest annual gain, and the West was the only region where prices fell, according to NAR.

Prices declined in many Florida markets over the past year, Yun said.

“This quarter, however, homes in nearly all Florida markets are showing price gains,” he said. “In a similar vein, price declines in other markets may also be brief if the local job market and economy are solid.”

Gulfport-Biloxi-Pascagoula, Mississippi, led large markets with an 11 percent price increase, followed by Rochester, New York (10.9 percent) and Jackson, Mississippi (10.1 percent). Grand Rapids-Wyoming, Michigan; Cleveland-Elyria, Ohio; and Fort Wayne, Indiana, were among the Midwest markets in the top 10.

“Many markets in the Midwest offer exceptional value with more affordable homes, making homeownership more attainable,” Yun said. “Meanwhile, the artificial intelligence technology boom continues to push Bay Area home prices higher, keeping the region the most expensive in the country.”

San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, California, remained the most expensive market at a median of $1.92 million, up 0.3 percent. Anaheim-Santa Ana-Irvine, California ($1.47 million) and San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, California ($1.35 million) followed. Nine of the 10 most expensive markets are in California or Hawaii.

The monthly mortgage payment on a typical existing single-family home with a 20 percent down payment was $2,251 in the third quarter, up $48 from the second quarter and $69 from a year earlier, according to NAR. Typical families spent an average of 24.1 percent of income on mortgage payments, up from 23.9 percent last quarter and down from 24.5 percent a year ago.

First-time buyers faced a monthly payment of $2,208 on a typical $368,000 starter home with 10 percent down. That payment took up 36.3 percent of income, up from 36 percent last quarter and down from 37 percent a year earlier.

Pending sales fell 1.8 percent from a week earlier and 15.9 percent year over year, declining in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metros for the third straight week, according to Redfin. Seattle (down 31.6 percent) and Atlanta (down 25.9 percent) posted the steepest annual drops.

Redfin’s median monthly mortgage payment, calculated at a 7.32 percent rate, reached $2,786, up 10.7 percent year over year and the second-highest level in its records. The weekly average rate is down from 7.4 percent a week earlier and near a three-year high.

New listings fell 0.6 percent from a week earlier to their lowest level since January. Total inventory rose 0.3 percent because pending sales fell faster than new listings, Redfin reported. The share of listings with price drops rose to 21.5 percent from 20.9 percent a year earlier.

Redfin reported hundreds of thousands more sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they have had in more than a decade.

A First American analysis found that since 1991, rising mortgage rates have coincided with falling national home prices in some cases. In eight periods of sustained mortgage-rate increases since 1993, national home prices generally continued to appreciate, though the pace varied, First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming found.

During the rate run-up from December 2021 through October 2023, national prices rose an estimated 14 percent, according to the analysis. Affordability worsened at a steeper rate than prices, Fleming found. First American’s Real House Price Index, which adjusts prices for changes in income and mortgage rates, rose more than 70 percent over the same period.

Limited inventory can offset weaker demand when rates rise, Fleming wrote. Homeowners with mortgages below current rates may hold off on selling, and some sellers pull homes from the market rather than accept lower prices.

“Higher mortgage rates can put pressure on home prices, but the economy, household incomes and the number of homes for sale all play a role in what happens next,” Fleming wrote.

#5563. Democrats Eye Tougher Data Center Regulations as They Regain Control of Congress

Democrats who rode data center discontent to victory in the midterms are expected to pursue strict new regulations on data centers when they take control of Congress in January.

The Democratic sweep flipped dozens of House and Senate seats, and a number of those races hinged on broadsides against Republicans for their purported support of the industry. Meanwhile, voters considered more than 40 local measures to constrain data center development, and almost all of them passed.

The results are likely to bring new life into Democrats' efforts to add guardrails to the artificial intelligence buildout. But their majority does not go far enough to override a veto from President Donald Trump, who has sought to aggressively promote data centers in the United States, in the pursuit of what he dubs "super intelligence."

Polls show broad concerns that the pace of data center construction could drive up power costs, raise land prices, and create environmental problems. Recent Realtor.com® research on data centers found they're increasingly moving into rural areas.

"If the Democrats take control of Congress, it could be a major problem for data center developers," Balaji Tammabattula, CEO of BaRupOn LLC, which develops energy infrastructure for data center companies, recently told Realtor.com.

Data center companies, he said, are already reconsidering future investments. In Texas, Senate winner James Talarico released a blueprint for data center regulation with more enforcement. The state has a temporary moratorium on data centers in place, which Democratic Gov.-Elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged to extend.

Just a few hours before polls closed, The Hill reported that Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Google, and other tech companies were considering a more formal framework for data center development.

"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Elon Musk posted on X shortly after the results came in.

Congress' one effort to rein in the impacts of data centers fell short just before the midterms. Several weeks ago, the House passed a bill to encourage utilities to shield ratepayers from the costs associated with data center buildouts, the Ratepayer Protection Act.

That followed widespread backlash against data center buildouts. But Senate Democrats tanked the bill because it didn't go far enough. They've coalesced around a few competing ideas for how to regulate data centers at the federal level.

In the meantime, Democrats put forth their own bill, the Guaranteeing Rate Insulation from Data Centers (GRID) Act, with more enforcement power and penalties. Among its powers, it would require data center developers to provide their own energy, so they don't pull from the local power grid. It would also require more disclosure about data center developments and give the government the power to issue fines.

Also, 20 Democrats signed on to a bill that would create a total moratorium on data center development. But the president has veto power, and he has opposed such a harsh move.

Trump has advocated for data center development in the United States to prevent the technology being developed abroad. In the face of public backlash, he convened technology leaders in Washington in September and asked them to self-police the build-out of super intelligence.

The White House also released an accord signed by those major companies committing to developing the technology safely. Trump called it "morally binding."

While data centers affect property taxes, the exact impact on homeowners' tax burden is complicated. And the study found no impact on property values from large facilities in the two years after they open.

Democrats may find an opening to create more rules around data center construction. Although Democrats also took control of governor's offices in many major states with data center developments, Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel says that doesn't necessarily mean they will lead to sharp constraints on data centers.

"Utilities costs, rather than home values, are probably the biggest immediate change voters are feeling or fearing," Krimmel says. "Our analysis of data center impacts on the housing market found essentially no effect on inventory or sales behavior so far."

The Urban Institute suggested a few levers to help data centers support housing affordability. It suggested tax relief or energy cost offsets for communities that host many data centers. Otherwise, they risk straining local housing markets due to rising electricity costs, especially in high-growth regions.

Meanwhile, Brookings suggested an electricity tax on data centers or some kind of offset to local governments. But it warned that regulation of the sector could encourage developers to build more centers overseas.

It's unlikely the currently divided Congress will use the remainder of its term to pass rules around data centers. But when the new one comes in, it can reintroduce the GRID Act or other bills. The GRID Act’s 20-megawatt threshold would cover essentially the entire pipeline, more than 99% of planned capacity, Krimmel says.

"That would give homeowners the most direct protection on rates," Krimmel explains. "Requiring new projects to bring their own power could also slow data center development, and the jury is also still out on the local economic and labor market impacts of data centers on localities."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5562. Oracle connects AI-driven testing with a new approach to database security

Frontier AI models that uncover software flaws by the hundreds are forcing database providers into larger, faster patch cycles, and real application testing is becoming the safeguard that keeps those fixes from breaking production systems. The same AI wave is also undermining security rules written into applications.

Oracle Corp. has responded on two fronts, hardening its code against outside attackers while moving agent controls down to the data layer. The first effort began when the company turned an early-access frontier model on its own software, according to Juan Loaiza (pictured), executive vice president of Oracle Database Technologies at Oracle.

“Back in March, we got early access to the Mythos model and we ran it against our code and it started finding all these security vulnerabilities,” Loaiza said. “It’s turning up some very serious security issues. And so we said, ‘Hey, this is a code red moment. The house is on fire.'”

Loaiza spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why AI-discovered vulnerabilities, AI-generated code and AI agents require enterprises to treat security as a data problem. (* Disclosure below.)

Most of Oracle’s response to AI-discovered vulnerabilities is landing in its regular quarterly patches, which have grown much larger as a result, Loaiza explained. A quarterly security update earlier this year addressed more than 1,400 vulnerabilities across the company’s portfolio. Customers must automate patching and stay current, but every large patch raises fears of regression in systems that cannot fail.

“We have something called Real Application Testing where we can capture real workload and run it to make sure that your workload is not affected by these patches,” Loaiza said. “It’s not quite as simple as just apply because the applications that people run are extraordinarily complex. They run entire countries, entire industries.”

Patching handles outside attackers. Internal AI use is a separate threat, because applications have traditionally enforced end-user security, and AI now writes much of that code or goes straight to the data. Oracle’s answer is Deep Data Security, which began shipping in April and passes an authenticated user’s identity as an encrypted token through to the database. The company has since extended those authorization controls across remote databases, lakehouse data and related tables.

“The new world as I see it is all these end-user security rules have to be enforced where AI can’t bypass them, which means all the way down in the data,” Loaiza said. “The AI agent has to get your identity. It’s acting on behalf of you. It can’t leak the data if it can’t see the data.”

Business rules follow the same logic. Application code has always blocked a credit card charge above the customer’s limit, but an AI agent told to enforce that rule may not comply, Loaiza noted. Oracle is providing declarative ways to define such rules, along with SQL Assertions that check whether changes made through SQL are valid.

“There’s credit limits, there’s all sorts of things that are business rules that can’t be violated. And again, if we move those all the way down into the data, then no matter how you access the data, what mechanism you use, how AI is used, it cannot violate those rules,” Loaiza said.

Takeaway: The Fed skipped hiking rates at today’s meeting, as expected. But they set up a hike at the December 9th meeting.

Chairman Warsh also announced a big change for Fed meetings starting next year, setting aside one meeting for big picture deliberation.

#5560. Carolyn Fugere Named President and CEO for William Pitt – Julia B. Fee Sotheby’s International Realty

Paul Breunich, executive chairman of William Pitt – Julia B. Fee Sotheby’s International Realty, announced that Carolyn Fugere has been appointed president and Chief Executive Officer.

According to a release, Fugere will lead the real estate company serving Connecticut, Westchester County and the Hudson Valley in New York, and the Berkshires in Massachusetts.

During her service as co-president and chief sales officer—where she was responsible for overseeing 31 offices and 1,100 sales advisors—the company posted the highest total closed dollar volume for any five-year period in the company’s history, the release states.

Fugere will become the fourth CEO in the company’s 77-year history, and the first-ever woman to hold the position. The release notes that in 2026, William Pitt – Julia B. Fee Sotheby’s International Realty rose to the rank of the top-producing, independently-owned Sotheby’s International Realty affiliate by sales volume and closed units worldwide for the global brand, which encompasses nearly 1,075 offices throughout 81 countries and territories on six continents.

Fugere commented that this No. 1 ranking serves as an opportunity and a responsibility to continue raising the standard of professional real estate advisory services.

“I’ve always believed that the measure of our success is the positive impact we have on the people around us,” Fugere said. “Whether we’re helping our advisors grow, supporting our colleagues, guiding our clients through important moments in their lives, or contributing to the communities we serve, we have an opportunity every day to make a difference. We have an extraordinary organization, and I believe we have both the opportunity and the responsibility to continue raising the standard of our profession.”

Fugere’s tenure in residential real estate spans 25 years in total and 16 with William Pitt – Julia B. Fee Sotheby’s International Realty, where she has grown in her career through multiple roles.

She embarked in the industry as a sales advisor, marketing and selling in suburban, urban and rural markets, and then advanced into brokerage management, leading eight sales offices across Connecticut, Massachusetts and New York.

Fugere was honored twice as a Manager of the Year, and she oversaw the firm’s expansion in a brand-new territory in the Berkshires. She also restructured and headed the company’s training department, leading training initiatives for agents and staff before stepping into the co-president role.

From his initial recruitment meeting with Fugere in her days as a brokerage manager with her prior firm, Breunich recalled recognizing her talent.

“I told her she could stay at her old company and be a soldier, or she could come to our company and become a generaI. I got the general,” he said.

As executive chairman and owner, Breunich will continue to be actively involved. His own tenure with the firm spans 38 years including 30 years as CEO, the release states.

“Rather than a change in direction, this appointment is an exciting evolution in the leadership of our firm, and a natural progression of Carolyn’s work and commitment to the organization,” Breunich added. “She has been deeply involved in shaping the company’s culture, vision and strategy for many years.”

“Real estate is more than a profession to me. It is a lifelong passion centered entirely on the success of our agents,” Fugere said. “I am honored to step into this role and lead an organization I care so deeply about. Backed by an extraordinary team, my focus remains on supporting our advisors, strengthening the relationships that drive our business and continuing to build on what makes our organization so special.”

#5559. How Kyle Whissel built eXp’s top real estate team

The San Diego-based CEO recruits up to 15 agents a month, has a dress code and gives his trainer authority to cut newcomers.

Kyle Whissel has a standing instruction for his “60-day” bootcamp trainers: they should be willing to cut people.

His team brings in 10 to 15 new agents a month, puts them through approximately 60 hours of training over two weeks, and gives the trainer a goal of removing two people from each class.

It’s a striking approach from the leader of eXp Realty’s highest-volume U.S. team in San Diego, California. Whissel is CEO of the Whissel Beer Group, formed in 2025 when his Whissel Realty Group merged with Daniel Beer’s Beer Home Team.

According to Whissel, the team made $875 million in sales volume across 1,042 transaction sides last year (it was the first team in San Diego to break 1,000). The median price in San Diego — which is where he likes to focus his attention  (“we love that median price,” he said) — is around $1 million, he told Inman.

They’ve done that by hiring — and retaining — the right people. “We’ll give people an opportunity to prove themselves … but we’ve grown far more by cutting people than simply by hiring more people,” Whissel told Inman‘s Taylor Anderson during an interview at eXpcon in Salt Lake City earlier this month.

The company’s saying: “Expectations without enforcement are simply suggestions.”

Whissel’s recruiting process starts with a conventional, short interview, but he views the company’s two-week training period as a far better measure of whether someone belongs on the team.

Spending 60 hours in training gives leadership a chance to observe how that person behaves, learns and responds to expectations. Role-playing and scripting exercises also reveal whether new agents have the communication skills needed to work with clients.

The process continues after training, too. New agents are assigned mentors, and Whissel said those mentors are empowered to recommend removing someone who fails to meet team standards.

“If you’re going to be disrespectful to our team, I’ll be damned if I’m going to give you a client because you’re probably going to be disrespectful to them too,” he said.

Whissel also has activity and production expectations for agents already on the team. They include participating in role-playing sessions and attending meetings, along with meeting production targets.

Whissel’s hiring philosophy reaches back to his own first job, scooping popcorn at a movie theater, where he would compete with others to see who could serve the most customers. He looks for that same competitiveness in prospective agents, even if their previous accomplishments have little to do with real estate.

An applicant who participated in a college sorority, for example, might be asked whether they held a leadership position. Whissel said he wants to understand whether someone has a history of taking initiative.

In August 2025, Inman reported the merger of Whissel Realty Group and Beer Home Team, two of eXp’s highest-producing organizations. The combined company launched with approximately 160 agents and more than 60 staff members across five offices.

He said the first six months involved understanding the two organizations’ systems and getting them aligned. Whissel now believes it could take 18 months to fully integrate the companies.

“We’re going to be almost flat year-over-year,” he said, referring to the team’s expected 2026 performance, “but we’re setting up for a really, really big 2027,” he said. “You’ve gotta take a step back to take two steps forward.”

He remains optimistic about 2027, when he expects the operational investments to begin contributing to stronger growth.

Agents need to understand assumable mortgages, he said. “If you are working with a seller … and you’re not asking questions to figure out ‘does this seller have an assumable mortgage?’ (If it’s FHA, VA or USDA, those are assumable), I’m gonna beat you, because I am asking those questions.”

To find out whether a mortgage is assumable, agents simply need to get the closing disclosure from the seller. “It’s simple,” he said.

#5558. Kylie Kelce Reveals the One Thing That Makes Someone the Perfect Houseguest

Kylie Kelce has revealed what a visitor needs to do to be the perfect guest in their home—and it has to do with impressing her and her NFL-star husband Jason Kelce's daughters.

On a recent episode of her podcast, "Not Gonna Lie," the mom of four revealed that their daughters— Finnley, 18 months, Bennett, 3, Elliotte, 5, and Wyatt, 7—love having guests read to them.

“I know one way to my girls’ hearts, and really kids, I always tell people you don’t need to bring gifts when you come to our house. If you come in, you sit down, you offer to read our girls a book, they will be like forever," she revealed.

Kelce added, “Like genuinely, we have obviously family [that] will come and they’ll bring this and they’ll bring that, but if when you come and you sit down, you read a book, I think it’s one of the best ways to connect with kids.”

The glimpse of her houseguest request came just days after she defended her and her spouse's decision to snap up multiple Philadelphia properties right next to each other.

In an episode of her podcast, which featured guest Nikki Glaser, Kelce, 34, and the comedian chatted about hate comments.

"Do you ever get in the comments? Do you ever get feisty?” Glaser asked.

In her reply, Kelce detailed an Instagram account that frequently posts information about their real estate.

“One of the ones that I did it—which was not to a person so it doesn’t really feel as aggressive—was like ‘Celeb Homes.’ They put a bird’s-eye view of where we live with our children, and they were trying to give details of our property," she said.

The account then revealed that the Kelce family had also purchased the home "next door."

She then told the comedian, "I think I typed ‘get f---ed.’ And then when I tried to post it, it wouldn’t let me. Why? I want to tell people to get f---ed."

Her admission came after she offered a glimpse of the family's childcare arrangements during an appearance on an episode of "IMO with Michelle Obama and Craig Robinson." She explained that she and the former Philadelphia Eagles star prefer to keep their relatives closely involved in raising their children.

The couple have built a support system that allows them to balance their professional commitments with family life.

A major part of that arrangement involves Kelce's parents, Lisa and Ed McDevitt, who live just 15 minutes from the family's Philadelphia-area home.

Kelce explained that her parents regularly help care for the girls, making it possible for her and Jason to navigate their busy schedules without relying on round-the-clock childcare.

Although the couple do employ a nanny, Kelce revealed that the arrangement is limited to traditional working hours rather than having someone live in their home.

“My husband and I have very busy schedules. We don’t necessarily want a live-in nanny or someone who’s going to be raising our kids void of us. That feels weird. So we do a lot with my parents every chance we get. We do things with Jason’s parents. We find that those are the values that we were raised with that we want our kids to have, not just because we tell them that, but because we live it," she explained.

The decision, she explained, reflects their desire to remain actively involved in their daughters' everyday lives.

Rather than bringing in someone to provide full-time care, the Kelces turn to their extended family for additional support.

Kelce said maintaining those close family relationships is particularly important because she wants her daughters to grow up with the same values that shaped her and Jason's childhoods.

She also emphasized how grateful she is for the nanny who helps the family during the workday, acknowledging that the additional support is essential to managing their responsibilities.

However, the couple's approach to childcare goes beyond convenience.

For Kelce, living close to her parents has been a priority, and she admitted that the thought of settling somewhere far from her family has never appealed to her.

“We couldn’t do it without my parents. My parents live 15 minutes from us, and they have helped us in every way imaginable," she said.

The Pennsylvania native explained that remaining in the area where she grew up has allowed her to preserve those relationships while raising her own family.

That connection to her hometown has also influenced the kind of upbringing she hopes to provide her daughters.

Kelce wants the girls to become familiar with the places that shaped her childhood, from local businesses to the community organizations that continue to play a role in her life.

She believes that growing up with those personal connections can help children develop a stronger sense of responsibility toward the communities around them.

Her own involvement with the Eagles Autism Foundation is one example of how she has maintained those local ties.

For Kelce, the opportunity to contribute to the community where she was raised is another benefit of remaining close to home.

“Now, granted, we do have a nanny. I always give a shoutout because we couldn’t do it without her, but we have her during regular work hours and really nothing outside of that," she added.
