#5539. AI agents meet billable hours as Certinia rethinks services delivery

Certinia Inc. is bringing AI into the software firms use to sell projects, assign staff, deliver work and bill clients.

AI’s ability to instantaneously draw from a deep well of information and provide guidance in practically any field of expertise has changed the paradigm for professional services. For Certinia Inc., whose business facilitates 7.1 billion professional services operations per month, AI represents a significant opportunity for its clients.

“I think the only industry that’s probably been more disrupted by AI than the technology industry has probably been the services industry,” Robert Cesafsky, chief operating officer of Certinia, told theCUBE. “Whether you are a software company, a hardware company, a tax and accounting firm [or] management consulting … all of these industries are being directly targeted or impacted by AI. Whatever your strategy is, you need to be able to have the right tools. You need to be able to have control of that services business, and that’s what Certinia provides.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s coverage of the Certinia at Dreamforce event. (* Disclosure below.)

Certinia launched in 2009 as FinancialForce.com Inc., a cloud-based accounting and enterprise resource planning provider built natively on the Salesforce Inc. platform. It rebranded in 2023 as it broadened from accounting and ERP to managing services businesses.

Certinia’s Salesforce-native platform connects a wide range of processes spanning sales, project delivery, financial management and customer success. The company’s approach helps clients transform cost centers into profit centers by improving visibility into customer activities, optimizing resource deployment and maintaining connectivity throughout the customer lifecycle.

“We can take away all the administrative tasks and outsource that to AI in order to help them deliver faster time outcomes, but it also helps them deliver a lower cost to serve that project,” said Mimi Spier, chief marketing officer of Certinia, in an interview with theCUBE. “We can identify expansion opportunities, [and] at-risk customers where we need to optimize renewals. Everything we’re doing is ultimately affecting the bottom line.”

Certinia’s long-time relationship with Salesforce is a key element in the company’s overall strategy. Certinia is featured under the AI agents and tools category for Salesforce’s AgentExchange and has provided AI-powered sales and delivery for Salesforce’s consulting partner network.

“We have a deep partnership with Salesforce,” said Raju Malhotra, chief product and technology officer of Certinia. “I spend personally a lot of time with the Salesforce executives on business and engineering, and we collaborate. We bring our customer use cases, they tell us about what’s coming up from a capability perspective and we work very well together. They’re led by a founder [chief executive officer] who’s very much in tune with the market, and they want to stay ahead.”

Certinia has sought to stay ahead in its own right by introducing Veda, an enterprise-grade intelligent operations engine that functions as the company’s suite of AI specialist agents and intelligent actions. The solution delivers rules-bound, trusted and ROI-focused autonomous workflows, combining Certinia’s years of institutional memory with advanced AI reasoning. Certinia’s goal with Veda is to provide customers with enough flexibility so that agents integrated into existing business workflows can drive immediate and measurable value.

“We’ve infused Veda throughout the experience for users to be more productive,” Malhotra said. “We have package agents, which are Veda agents. We launched Veda with 10 packages. Now we have 24, and we will finish the year with more than 40 package agents. Those agents are very much persona based, and they help our customers.”

Veda is not simply a layer of generic automation; it represents a key shift in how AI is being used in the enterprise. Certinia’s focus on serving the professional services market motivated the company to ground its AI offering in operational reality, where context, coordination and control matter as much as speed, according to Scott Hebner, principal AI analyst at theCUBE Research.

“Certinia’s recent announcement of Veda is more profound than it may appear on the surface,” he said. “Veda is notable not simply because it introduces a new suite of AI agents and intelligent workflow-based actions, but because it offers a glimpse into what the future of enterprise AI is likely to look like: AI that works alongside humans in consequential workflows, helps people make better decisions and earns trust by being grounded in business context, governance and real operational outcomes.”

Since the launch of Veda in April, Certinia has taken several actions to enhance its AI capabilities. In July, the firm acquired Moonnox, an AI-native services delivery platform purpose-built for the professional services sector.

This acquisition added a contextual layer to Veda through knowledge graphs, persistent project memory and services-specific agents. The combined platform can now connect a new client request with approved scope, staffing requirements and financial impact, then recommend governed actions for professional review, according to Hebner.

“Certinia provides the deep, structured foundation of professional services, customer success and financial management; Moonnox brings the missing half: capturing the unstructured reality — the emails, chats, and calls — where delivery actually happens,” he explained. “Together, they fuse everything a services business knows with everything their teams do, moving Veda beyond orchestration toward context-aware, AI-native services delivery.”

The context graph can also draw on structured records such as timecard entries and utilization figures. Moonnox helps bring that information into the graph for client-facing teams managing projects, according to Cesafsky.

“That’s been where Moonnox has really showed up for us over the last couple of months,” he said. “It’s those capabilities to help the client-facing services [and] delivery teams run and operate their projects. [Moonnox] is effectively an intake machine for a lot of that structured data to bring that into the context graph as well.”

In September, Certinia unveiled its System of Action for services businesses. The offering significantly expanded the Veda AI suite with new agents and more than doubled the Veda Intelligent Actions library from 64 to 135.

Certinia’s System of Action uses a three-tier architecture to bring AI agents into services workflows. The first tier brings together structured records and unstructured project data. The second draws on more than 17 years of Certinia’s experience in services to inform decisions. The third lets agents act within existing workflows.

“We want to accelerate the delivery for our customers,” Malhotra said. “Our customers are solving some specific problems in the professional services world. We don’t want to just give you a project plan. If you choose to execute that project plan with some agents, we’ll give you that. If you want to really think about agentic capabilities to help you in making money, in expanding your time [and] in terms of delivery, we will help you with that.”

For professional services firms, adopting AI agents means deciding which parts of project delivery to delegate to them.

“We view professional services as a leading indicator of where enterprise AI is heading because it combines knowledge-intensive work, dynamic context, collaborative decisions, measurable economics and human accountability,” Hebner said. “If Certinia executes well, Veda could become an important blueprint for translating digital labor into economic outcomes.”

#5538. Homebuilder Stocks Surge as Democratic Sweep Raises Hopes for Affordability Gains

Homebuilders and housing suppliers saw significant jumps in their share prices following Tuesday’s midterm elections.

At the closing bell on Wednesday, shares of major builders Lennar and PulteGroup were up more than 7% on the day, and D.R. Horton rose more than 8%.

Suppliers showed similar increases. Home Depot finished the day up 6.5%, after spiking as much as 17% during midday trading, according to Yahoo Finance. Lowe’s Companies ended the day up 7.5%, but also had a midday spike to 15% before leveling out.

For comparison, the broad S&P 500 index ended the day up 1.6%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 3%, or over 1,500 points, marking its best single-day performance since April 2025.

The stock movement comes in the wake of Tuesday’s midterm election, where Democrats gained control of Congress in a dramatic sweep.

The homebuilding sector has faced massive cost increases in recent years. Several factors have played into the building sector’s hardships, which have led to a shortfall of roughly 4 million homes throughout the U.S., according to a March report from Realtor.com®.

Tariffs, supply chain issues, and inflation have caused substantial increases in material costs, according to Ronald Gestiehr, director of wealth management at Luttner Financial Group.

“Labor continues to be a major issue, with a shortage of skilled workers driving wages higher,” Gestiehr tells Realtor.com. “Add in land prices, permitting, insurance, and financing costs, and it becomes increasingly difficult to build homes at prices the average buyer can afford.”

Builders have experienced a squeeze from both sides, Gestiehr explains, because at the same time that the cost to build a home has increased, skyrocketing mortgage rates have put limits on what buyers can afford.

Just days ago, major builders including D.R. Horton and the PulteGroup reported net income declines, with PulteGroup CEO Ryan Marshall stating that the company’s year-over-year net income dropped by 17% in the third quarter.

Suddenly, there’s a renewed sense of optimism surrounding the industry after Tuesday’s election results.

While the underlying challenges remain, Gestiehr says that investors are likely expecting more federal attention to turn to policies surrounding affordability.

“Housing affordability has become a major concern, and investors may be anticipating more attention on policies that encourage new construction and make homeownership more affordable,” says Gestiehr. “Investors may be anticipating additional housing incentives, policies that encourage new construction, and potentially lower mortgage rates.”

Affordability, particularly when it comes to housing, was a key part of many Democratic candidate platforms.

To address affordability overall, there should be focus on building up the supply of homes before offering incentives for buyers and spurring more demand, says Gestiehr.

"If you increase demand without increasing supply, you may end up pushing home prices even higher,” adds Gestiehr. “Reducing regulatory costs, streamlining permitting, encouraging additional development, and potentially lowering tariffs on building materials could all help builders.”

Rolling back tariffs was a major talking point for several incoming Democrat senators, including Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Texas’ James Talarico, as well as Alaska’s Mary Peltola, whose race results were pending.

Gestiehr maintains that many other factors, including inflation, interest rates, employment, and corporate earnings, as well as actual policy changes, will still have a much greater impact on homebuilder results than the election results alone. It’s not uncommon for markets to perform well following midterm elections, in part because the uncertainty surrounding the election is removed.

“The election may have given homebuilders a reason to be optimistic, but optimism doesn't necessarily translate into stronger earnings,” says Gestiehr. “At some point, these companies need to see improvement in demand, affordability, and profit margins to justify higher stock prices.”

Congress already passed one major bipartisan housing bill this year, the 21st Century Road to Housing Act. The bill lays out 45 provisions aimed at cutting red tape and constructing more homes, as well as banning institutional investor homebuyers.

Adding new members to Congress, many of whom have been elected on the promise of ushering in affordability, could mean more meaningful change is on the way.

“With a divided government, I wouldn’t expect major changes overnight, but housing affordability is an area where both parties have an incentive to find common ground,” says Gestiehr.

Meta Platforms Inc. has acquired artificial intelligence coding startup Conductor in a deal first reported today by Axios.

Conductor confirmed it’s joining Meta in a post on its website. Terms were not disclosed.

The company’s software lets a developer run several coding agents at once, each in an isolated copy of the codebase, and then review and merge what they produce. Supported agents include Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code, OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex and Space Exploration Technologies Corp.’s Cursor, and users pay for them through their own subscriptions and keys.

The desktop app runs on Macs. A hosted version, Conductor Cloud, puts agents in sandboxed virtual machines where they can keep working for hours, and users can check on them from an iPhone app.

Engineers at Meta were using Conductor well before the deal. When the startup announced its Series A in March, it named Meta, Google LLC and Spotify Technology SA among the companies with dozens of engineers on the product. Conductor now says on its website that more than 100,000 people use it.

People familiar with the deal told Axios that Meta expects the Conductor team’s speed at shipping products to help it build its next generation of AI coding tools. The acquisition follows two Meta model releases last month that both pitched coding as a strength.

On Oct. 15, Meta released Muse Spark Open, an open-weights version of its Muse Spark model aimed at coding and long-running agent work. Meta’s more capable Muse Wonder models stay closed inside its own Muse Code terminal and application programming interface.

The Conductor deal landed the same day OpenAI said it plans to acquire developer tools startup Pierre Computer. OpenAI had already announced plans in June to buy Ona, which runs coding agents in cloud sandboxes.

Local copies of the Mac app keep working until early 2027, when the team expects to release a new interface it has not yet described. New models and critical bug fixes stop arriving at that point, and Conductor will delete the app’s user data. The company said it has never sold Conductor user data or trained models on it, and does not plan to.

Chief Executive Charlie Holtz and Chief Technology Officer Jackson de Campos founded the company, formally Melty Inc., in 2024. Conductor raised a $22 million Series A in March from Spark Capital and Matrix. Y Combinator and the founders of Notion and Linear are also backers.

#5533. A Halloween tale: Spooky events and a haunted house sale

Author and trainer Bernice Ross shares a spooky tale of unusual home happenings and a sale process plagued by tragedy.

When you’re in the real estate business, sooner or later there will be a house that someone says is haunted. The story below is true. Were these events just coincidence, or were they something else?

When I was working on my doctorate, my closest friend and study partner was living in a new house in Orange County. She was in the antique business. Her home was like a showcase, every last inch of it beautifully decorated. When I met her, she was in the process of getting a divorce.

Although her house was a little over a year old, it already had the makings of a strange history. While the house was being built, a little girl was sexually assaulted in it. A few months after she and her husband moved in, he became manic-depressive.

Over the next few months, he had numerous confrontations with the police. He refused to take his meds. Unbeknownst to his wife, he placed a warranty deed on the property to access part of the equity. He then took off to Hawaii, where he was reportedly living in the bush outside the Honolulu airport.

We would normally study together at her house about twice per month. The lights would flicker periodically. If we went out for dinner, it was common for pieces of the furniture to be moved away from the wall.

Since my friend had changed the locks and placed a security system on the house, there was no one who had access to move the furniture. There was also a window in the family room overlooking the canyon that would vibrate for no apparent reason. You could put your hand on the window and tell it to stop vibrating, and it did.

After spending the afternoon preparing for our upcoming qualifying exams, we decided to go out to dinner to take a break. When we returned, the lights were flickering, and a number of pieces of furniture were moved again.

As we sat back down to hit the books again, there was a loud rustling in the garage where she refinished her antiques. Her German shepherd, a very mellow dog who never barked, started barking and scratching crazily at the door to the garage.

Although this didn’t disturb my friend, I made sure the dog was between me and whatever was in the garage. As soon as she opened the door, the dog broke away from me and raced into the garage. The dog raced to the other side of the garage, sat down and acted as if nothing had happened.

After consuming a carton of chocolate ice cream to soothe our jangled nerves, we decided to watch a movie — The Ghost of Flight 401. This probably wasn’t the smartest movie choice, but that was the best of the evening’s shows back in the days of seven TV channels and no cable.

As I was getting ready to leave, we were standing by the front door adjacent to the stairway. Her stairs had beautiful wrought iron work topped with a heavy oak banister.

As we were standing there talking, the banister and the wrought iron started to vibrate. Everything else in the house was still. I turned and asked her, “Do you see what I see?” She did.

We were both mesmerized because nothing else was moving. This went on for about five minutes, and then it stopped. At that point, I was out of there, and there was no way I was going back.

My friend wanted out of the house. Needless to say, there were numerous challenges that had to be addressed before she could legally sell the property. California law allowed her to list the property, but both she and her husband had to sign the grant deed to close the transaction.

The lender who held the warranty deed was demanding payment as per the terms of the note. Normally, their option would have been to foreclose. The challenge was that the police reports documented the fact that the husband was probably not legally competent at the time he signed the deed.

Since he was nowhere to be found, my friend and the lender petitioned the court to order the sale as part of the divorce proceedings. The court granted her request.

The house was listed and finally went under contract. The buyer was a deputy sheriff. Two days after opening escrow on the property, the escrow officer had a heart attack and died. The title officer handling the file also had a heart attack but recovered.

About four weeks into the transaction, the deputy sheriff’s right arm became mysteriously paralyzed. He saw several specialists, but no one could find a cause for the problem. He was forced to take disability leave from his job. This meant he didn’t have sufficient income to qualify for the loan. The transaction was canceled. Within a few days after he canceled, the paralysis disappeared.

After almost a year, the house finally sold. The buyer was a psychiatrist.

Fortunately, this transaction took place prior to California passing its disclosure laws. I have to wonder how you would make those disclosures today. Much of what happened could be coincidence. I still don’t have an explanation for the moved furniture, the strange window and, most of all, the vibrating staircase. Perhaps it’s just as well that I don’t.

Bernice Ross is president and CEO of BrokerageUP and RealEstateCoach.com, the founder of Profit.RealEstate and a national speaker, author and trainer with over 1,500 published articles.

#5529. ‘Haunted as a matter of law’: How real estate agents handle stigmatized listings in 2026

Stigmatized homes have long sold at a steep discount. Agents and attorneys say an unaffordable, low-inventory 2026 market may be shrinking it.

Many may assume that the rule of thumb on stigmatized homes is simple: A murder, suicide or infamous ghost story knocks a big chunk off the price. Real estate agents who’ve sold these homes say it’s more complicated, and today’s unaffordable, short-on-inventory market may be shrinking the discount.

A “stigmatized” property can mean many things. It can be a home tied to a violent crime, a suicide, a notorious former owner or an alleged haunting.

Would you live in the Amityville Horror house, where Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed six members of his family in 1974?

Or what about the Menendez mansion in Beverly Hills, where Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents, José and Kitty, in 1989, a case that has stayed in the headlines for more than three decades?

These gruesome crimes may not always change the bedroom count or the square footage. But they can change who’s willing to buy, and for how much.

Ahead of Halloween, Inman asked real estate agents and attorneys how they handle stigmatized listings in 2026.

Their answers suggest the discount is real but uneven. It often depends less on the stigma itself than on how many buyers it drives away. And in a market with increasingly few affordable options, fewer buyers may be walking away.

The best-known estimate for stigmatized listings comes from real estate economist Randall Bell, who has put the typical “murder-house” discount at 10 to 25 percent. Bell has also said he’s seen some stigmatized homes sell at full value — usually smaller, more affordable homes — while others sit unsold for a long time.

Bell is an expert on real estate damage, earning the nickname “Master of Disaster,” and he runs the advisory firm Landmark Research. He has consulted on some of the most notorious crime-linked properties in history, from the Rancho Santa Fe mansions where the bodies of 39 Heaven’s Gate cult members were found to the home of Sandy Hook shooter Adam Lanza.

While Bell’s estimates are frequently cited, academic research suggests the price discount effect on stigmatized properties may fade over time.

A 2020 study of Tokyo apartment buildings by economist Taisuke Sadayuki found that a homicide in one unit initially cut rents on other units in the same building by about 10 percent, with the effect disappearing after roughly seven to eight years.

Survey data suggests buyers may also be less squeamish than agents assume. In a 2023 Zillow survey, 67 percent of prospective buyers said they could be persuaded to buy a “haunted” house with the right features, location or price.

When Inman covered stigmatized homes more than a decade ago, we framed them as bargains. The market has changed a lot since then.

Rebecca Chambliss, an agent with Carmody Real Estate in the Santa Monica, California, area, recently sold a home in a gated community where the previous owner had died by suicide only a few months before it was listed. All of the neighbors knew.

Chambliss disclosed the death to serious buyers who were discussing an offer. In her experience, buyers don’t spread out along a spectrum of tolerance. They split into two groups.

“Some people will never buy a home where a suicide or other non-natural death occurred no matter what, and then there are people who it doesn’t bother,” Chambliss told Inman. “There aren’t people in between.”

One interested buyer made an unexpected offer. When Chambliss disclosed the death, he demanded to know exactly where in the house it happened and how. Chambliss had chosen not to learn those details herself and told him as much. He wouldn’t move forward without them and withdrew the offer.

The home did eventually sell at a discount because of the suicide, Chambliss said. The buyer understood that he’d have to disclose the death if he ever sold. He relisted it about a year later, asking $1 million more than he paid, and the home still hasn’t sold.

Chambliss also brought in an energy clearer before marketing the home. It’s a reminder that for some agents, handling a stigmatized listing takes more than paperwork.

The discount doesn’t always stay with the property. Sometimes a savvy investor who knows about it collects it.

Jonathan Carcone, principal of 4 Brothers Buy Houses and a licensed agent in Washington state, bought a home in Poulsbo, Washington, with local ghost stories attached.

He said the home was listed at $640,000, while comparable homes were selling for about $650,000. Carcone said the listing didn’t mention ghost stories, but neighbors told him about them.

Carcone used the ghost stories in negotiations and bought the house for $585,000, about 9 percent below list and roughly 10 percent below comps.

Carcone’s company buys, renovates and sells dozens of houses every year, including “challenging properties.” After renovating the house in Poulsbo, he sold it for $660,000 about two months later.

“The ghost stories had no influence on the sale, and we made a good profit,” Carcone told Inman.

He said Washington law doesn’t require agents to disclose a home’s reputation, including ghost stories, so he didn’t. No buyer asked about it during showings, either. So, in this case, Carcone used the stigma to his advantage.

Because the resale price reflects a renovation, it isn’t a clean before-and-after comparison. Still, the pattern is worth noting. The seller absorbed a 10 percent discount for the stigma, and the next buyer paid none.

What agents must disclose for stigmatized properties varies widely by state.

California sets a three-year line. Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, sellers and agents aren’t required to disclose a death that occurred on the property more than three years before a buyer’s offer. They also can’t be sued for staying silent. Whether it must be disclosed depends on whether it’s material, and the common practice is to disclose to be safe.

Answering a direct question is a separate matter. The law doesn’t protect anyone who lies when asked.

“The main point of contention between sellers and buyers is whether answering questions truthfully violates the seller’s wishes,” Nick Heimlich, founder and attorney of San Jose, California-based Nick Heimlich Law, told Inman. “Under California Civil Code, a seller’s agent cannot refuse to answer questions about the property’s history.”

Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) says a seller or seller’s agent has no duty to disclose a death on the property from natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property’s condition. But not homicide, which may still be a material fact that must be disclosed.

Tennessee goes further. Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-5-207 lists a homicide, felony or suicide on the property among the things sellers don’t have to disclose. It also covers any act or occurrence that didn’t affect the property’s physical structure.

Ghost stories bring their own risk. In the famous case of Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991), a New York appellate court let a buyer back out of buying an allegedly haunted home in Nyack, New York.

The seller had publicized the ghost stories herself in Reader’s Digest and the local press, then didn’t tell the out-of-town buyer. In effect, the court held that because she’d told everyone else the house was haunted, it was haunted as a matter of law.

Donald Leeth, managing partner at Leeth & Gaglione, has spent 27 years as a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, and the Poconos. During that time, he’s encountered many homes where crimes took place. He advises disclosing rather than gambling on the legal minimum.

“It’s always best to be honest up front so you’re not dealing with misrepresentation claims once your transaction has closed,” Leeth said.

The more interesting question for 2026 is whether affordability is eroding the discount stigmatized listings usually have.

Median prices for new and existing homes now both top $400,000, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Existing-home prices have climbed 54 percent nationwide since 2020 and sit at nearly five times median income, well above the 3-to-1 ratio that held in the 1990s.

Leeth thinks the affordability crisis is negating the discount effect on stigmatized listings.

“Many buyers won’t care if there’s an infamous story behind a house because they simply don’t have other options,” he said. “Stigma isn’t as much of a factor as it once was because the price will determine what someone buys.”

That fits with Chambliss’s two-camp theory. If the buyers who’ll never consider a stigmatized home stay out no matter what, the discount depends on how many buyers are left in the other camp. In a tight, low-inventory market, more buyers are in that camp, and they may have fewer alternatives.

Heimlich said the type of event still matters. Buyers might shrug at a home that sat empty for a long time, he said, but something like a murder “can severely influence the property value.”

Still, he added, it likely depends on the market. And if stigma leads to a bargain, that helps, too.

“Some buyers may be willing to invest in stigmatized real estate if it falls within an affordable price range,” Heimlich said.

For agents, the practical takeaway is that a stigmatized listing’s real challenge is finding the buyers who don’t care, not pricing in a fixed discount, and disclosing in a way that doesn’t create legal exposure after closing.

Sometimes the stigma bothers the buyer’s friends and family more than the buyer themselves.

Years ago, Chambliss, the California-based agent, sold a home where a murder had taken place in the front yard. The buyer was a young single father whose Italian immigrant parents were involved in the buying process and may have been helping with the purchase. Chambliss took him outside and told him what had happened there.

He became very concerned, then immediately asked, “Do you have to tell my parents?”

His whole body relaxed, and he laughed. Then he said, “OK, I have no issue with it. But my parents would never let me buy this house if they knew.”

He bought the house, and Chambliss assumed he never told them.

#5528. Cyber ups and downs: Datadog falls 14% on outlook tied to one customer as Rapid7 jumps and Fastly slides

Datadog Inc., Rapid7 Inc. and Fastly Inc. all beat Wall Street’s third-quarter forecasts today, but Rapid7 was the only one of the three to see its shares rise.

A cautious outlook tied to one large customer knocked about 14% off Datadog’s stock in regular trading. Rapid7 jumped 18% after hours on results that came despite a decline in revenue.

For its third quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, Datadog reported adjusted earnings of 81 cents per share, up from 55 cents a year earlier, on revenue of $1.20 billion, up 35% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting 64 cents per share on revenue of $1.14 billion.

Unadjusted net income climbed to $118.3 million from $33.9 million, and the adjusted operating margin widened five points to 28%. Billings in the quarter rose 30% to $1.16 billion, Chief Financial Officer David Obstler said on the earnings call, with remaining performance obligations up 38% at $3.85 billion. Free cash flow came to $251 million.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Olivier Pomel told analysts that more than 850 artificial intelligence companies now use Datadog, roughly 100 more than at the end of June. Adoption is strong across the platform as customers scale “their digital operations and use of AI,” he said in the earnings release. Customers worth $100,000 or more a year in recurring revenue rose 20% to about 4,860.

Full-year guidance went up. Datadog now expects 2026 revenue of $4.515 billion to $4.525 billion, against the $4.45 billion to $4.47 billion it projected in August, and adjusted earnings of $2.73 to $2.75 per share. Fourth-quarter adjusted earnings are forecast at 69 to 71 cents per share.

Revenue for the fourth quarter is guided at $1.19 billion to $1.20 billion, roughly what analysts had expected, with the top of the range only about $3 million above third-quarter revenue. The forecast assumes Datadog’s largest customer, an AI provider the company has not named, spends no more than its contractual minimum, according to Obstler.

Usage on that account dropped in the third quarter while staying above the floor. Excluding it, implied fourth-quarter growth is in the low- to mid-30% range. Early renewals with some large AI customers, signed at higher commitments in return for better pricing, are also holding back near-term revenue.

The roughly 14% drop today made it two straight quarters in which a beat failed to hold up the stock. Datadog shares closed 19% lower in August, the day the company disclosed the customer’s planned cutback.

In Rapid7’s third quarter, also ended Sept. 30, the cybersecurity company posted adjusted earnings of 60 cents per share, up from 57 cents a year earlier, on revenue of $212.4 million, down 2.5% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting 46 cents per share on revenue of $209 million.

Annualized recurring revenue slipped 2.2%, to $819.7 million, ahead of the roughly $812 million the company had guided to in August. Adjusted operating income rose to $46.2 million from $36.9 million. Unadjusted net income fell to $3.5 million from $9.8 million after $10 million in restructuring costs from the 12% workforce cut announced in August and a $5.5 million write-down on a strategic equity investment.

Rapid7 demonstrated its Agentic SOC at Black Hat USA in August, using AI agents to speed up investigations while leaving high-impact decisions to analysts. Wael Mohamed, who took over as CEO in June, said the core business “is becoming more stable” and that “one quarter of stability is just a start.” Rapid7 is “not declaring victory,” he added.

The company’s full-year adjusted earnings forecast moved to $1.94 to $1.96 per share, well above the $1.78 to $1.83 it gave three months ago. Revenue guidance edged up to $841 million to $843 million. For the fourth quarter, Rapid7 sees revenue of $208 million to $210 million, down 3% to 4% from a year earlier, and adjusted earnings of 53 to 55 cents per share.

The stock climbed about 18% in extended trading.

Edge cloud platform provider Fastly reported adjusted earnings of 17 cents per share for its third quarter, up from 7 cents a year earlier, on record revenue of $190.2 million, up 20% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting 12 cents per share on revenue of $187.9 million.

Most of Fastly’s revenue still comes from network services, which grew 16%, to $138 million. Security sales rose twice as fast, to $44.7 million, in a quarter when the company also launched AI Firewall to block prompt injection and other attacks before they reach a model. Trailing-12-month net retention was its highest since 2022, at 119%. The top 10 customers now account for 39% of revenue, up from 32% a year ago.

Fourth-quarter revenue is forecast at $198 million to $202 million, ahead of the $197 million analysts had modeled. Full-year revenue guidance moved up to $744 million to $748 million from $732 million to $746 million in August. Adjusted earnings for 2026 are now expected at 61 to 63 cents per share. None of that stopped Fastly shares from falling about 14% after the bell.

#5527. Inside ‘My Big Fat Fabulous Life’ Star Whitney Way Thore’s ‘Dopamine Apartment’

When “My Big Fat Fabulous Life” star Whitney Way Thore moved back to her home state of North Carolina, she fell in love with Jake Beaudoin—and the whimsical Charlotte apartment they now share.

The 42-year-old reality TV personality began renting the “tiny, but enough” one-bedroom, one-bathroom, 830-square-foot unit in December 2025 following her unintentionally brief residency at a New England-style cottage in Salem, MA.

“I love Salem so much, but I had some issues that we didn't really cover in the season, some extended family things. My dad needed a little bit more help at home, so I decided to come on back,” Thore reveals in the latest installment of Celebrity Sanctuary.

Rather than returning to her old stomping ground at the Greensboro, NC, home she still holds or her family’s nearby property, Thore settled into a place inside a “new and modern” building where she could focus on a fresh start with her dog Goosie, cat Wandaleezza Rice, and shortly after her arrival, Beaudoin, now her fiancé.

In an exclusive clip shared with Realtor.com® from the Season 14 premiere of Thore’s TLC series, due to premiere on Nov. 10, Thore unveils her personal pad and its rainbow color palette for the first time while giving her friend and co-star Ashley Baynes a tour.

“I wanted it to be my dopamine apartment. You see how it’s colors, you see how it’s tchotchkes, you see how it’s fun?” asks Thore, as she points out the colorful mod decor she curated for the Queen City dwelling.

While Thore reports Beaudoin was immediately welcoming of the apartment’s playful style, she admits it’s been a challenge to accept his additions since moving in together.

“I don't love his stuff—that's the only issue—but luckily, he's cool with the aesthetic. It fits his vibe,” states Thore.

“It’s been very difficult to have a man in the apartment. ... I made him rent one of the storage units in the apartment for a lot of his stuff. I was basically like, ‘I don't want to see any evidence that you live here,’” she teases. She adds that they have made plans to "move out to a bigger place."

In this edition of Celebrity Sanctuary, Thore debuts the cheerfully decorated Charlotte dwelling where she’s found happiness, including the special living room nook she calls the most mood-boosting spot in her home.

When you walk in the door to this apartment, the view of uptown Charlotte through the windows is the most beautiful thing you've ever seen. It is exactly why I picked this apartment.

I feel instantly happy every time I walk in here. This is my favorite place I've ever lived, by miles. I really love what I've done in here.

When I moved to Charlotte, I wanted to feel creative. I was really moving here as a single girly—I didn't think that I was going to be dating anyone—and I wanted to make the space really conducive to feeling stimulated and creative.

I took a lot of liberties in this apartment that I would not do in my family home or in my Greensboro home where I felt like it has to be more grown-up or something like that. I [felt] the freedom to be like, “That's the cutest thing I've ever seen. I'm gonna get that, whether it fits or not.”

It's eclectic. It’s very funky. I have locker cabinets. There's a lot of texture and color, and it feels like motion to me. I have a lot of roundness and waviness: my coffee table, another table, my lamp, my candlesticks—I have a lot of shapes that I wouldn't normally have.

I have a lot of fun, whimsical things in this apartment, and I have a lot of color and a lot of art.

I am obsessed with [Henri] Matisse. I have, like, nine Matisse prints in here, and I even started doing art, which I hadn't done in almost 20 years. That was really exciting for me. I just wanted this space to feel bright and stimulating and exciting.

I have a lot of my own creations in here, things that I've drawn or done. Honestly, the thing I'm most proud of in this apartment is my little basketball gold net chain that I constructed. I got really into basketball when I moved to Charlotte. I started watching the Hornets and I got so into the season.  I don’t consider myself to be very crafty, [but] I ended up making a basketball net with chains and charms and I have that up.

I have a really cool digital picture of my mom that someone on the crew did for me. I have some little things of hers throughout the apartment that make me feel like she's here. I even have some of her handwritten notes on the refrigerator.

Just yesterday I found these glasses [for] $8. They’re like wrought iron. I reorganized ... to make room for the glasses. I'm still constantly picking and refining and moving things, and I'm just such a person that needs to feel so good in my physical space.

My physical space is such a representation of my mental space, so I can't have things super messy. I can't have things out of place.

In terms of the art and the shelving, I put a lot of work into making it fit me and my needs perfectly. I'm so particular and I like things done perfectly, measured perfectly, spaced perfectly.

I have ADHD, so I need little systems exactly how I need them to help me. If there's an extra step, then it's not going to happen.

I have a Russian handyman named Pavel. He is my lifesaver. Pavel and I have spent many, many hours together figuring out just how to make everything exactly how I wanted it, conducive to how I needed things. So no real renovations, but a lot of modifications.

Where I'm sitting right now is what I would consider [my sanctuary]. It's my armchair in the living room. It’s Ikea, so it's probably not real leather, but it's cognac. My rug is a beautiful bright blue; it’s not a pastel. The paint color is a light gray.

I like to read here. I can see straight out the window at night. The skyline and the view is so beautiful and soothing. I see the moon. I see Venus right outside my window. It gives me a peace that I usually experience in nature. I love this little corner where I look out the window, or I can watch TV, or do whatever. I spend a lot of my time out here just sitting.

I actually spend a lot of time in the apartment because I don't have a 9-to-5 job that brings me out of the apartment. That is one of the biggest reasons I've put so much into it and wanted to feel so comfortable in it, because I'm here all the time.

I don't often feel the need to even be out because where I live, you can see the skyline, there's life happening outside everywhere. There's always music, people. There's a train that goes by right outside my window. I feel like I can be in the safety and comfort of my home and still feel like I'm in the world, which is something that I would never have in Greensboro. That's something that I really missed. I felt very isolated and that I had to be out of the house to feel connected to the world. In Charlotte, I feel I'm part of it.

Charlotte really feels good to me. It really feels like home. I don't see myself leaving Charlotte in the next few years at least. I love the neighborhood that I live in. It's the same neighborhood that I lived in pre-COVID and during the beginning of COVID. It's a really wonderful mix of city life, and also, it’s still calm. It’s a really good fit for me and I love it here.

I really do feel like this specific apartment is such a big part of my experience in Charlotte. I'm very attached to it.

Karli Mullane is a celebrity and entertainment journalist at Realtor.com. She previously worked at Celeb Map, POPSUGAR, and NBC, covering pop culture, lifestyle, travel, and news of all kinds. Karli earned a BA in History from UCLA and an MA in Broadcast Journalism from San Francisco State University. She is equally grateful to have reported from both Hollywood red carpets and the comfort of her Bay Area home.

#5526. Zillow Says Lawsuits in the Past, ‘Not Obvious’ How Market Recovers

Real estate’s biggest name is struggling, just like everyone else, but company leadership is promising that it—and the industry—have ways to hang on amid a tech revolution, a sluggish market and legal woes the company claims are in the past now.

Speaking to investors after reporting earnings for Q3 2026, Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman said lawsuits are “not impacting our business,” with CFO and COO Jeremy Hofmann adding that legal costs are “normalized” going forward as the company hunkers down for what is expected to be a tough environment for real estate.

“It’s not obvious to us how things are necessarily going to improve,” Hofmann said.

Zillow’s report comes as mortgage rates remain elevated from earlier this year and existing home sales are on track to come in around 4 million—down more than 20% from pre-pandemic norms. The company’s stock fell sharply, down around 17% in after-hours trading.

The company still faces a proposed class-action lawsuit from a real estate agent who claims Zillow’s “monopoly power” inflates fees and commissions. A judge ruled in September that the lawsuit could move forward.

Democratic lawmakers previously offered pointed criticism of some of Zillow’s business practices, which are also used by at least some other portals, as the party made big gains in the midterms yesterday.

On the tech side, Zillow said it has not seen major impacts from increased use of AI by consumers, or Google’s ongoing push into residential real estate.

“(Google’s program) is very different than a ‘Preferred’ connection and an integrated transaction and helping agents grow their business that way. So we haven’t seen any impact from it today, even though it’s supposedly live nationwide,” Wacksman said.

As the company previously announced, agent partners are all being transitioned from other programs to the company’s Zillow Preferred service, which executives said is integrated with Zillow Home Loans.

The transition is expected to be fully implemented by the first half of 2027, and 75% complete by the end of this year.

Zillow’s residential for-sale revenue was down 4% year-over-year, $419 million in Q3 2026 compared to $435 million in Q3 2025. On the other hand, mortgage revenue grew 32%, and the company touted durable rental income, up 26% from the same period last year.

Overall revenue came in up 7% from last year at $724 million, with the lawsuit payment—$165 million after insurance covered part of the settlement—dinging the top—line. Outlook for Q4—historically the slowest for real estate—was $635 to $665 million, roughly the same as last year’s reported $654 million.

Late last year, Zillow was targeted by a high-profile class-action firm with claims from recent homebuyers focused on those “lead diversion” and loan referral practices. A judge initially threw that lawsuit out (though plaintiffs are seeking to revive it).

The company also agreed last week to pay $212.5 million to settle a lawsuit over its long-shuttered iBuying business, something the company said it was happy to put behind it.

“I think we’ve been pretty consistent and transparent to the degree we could be, that we didn’t expect these cases to impact business. And I think as you’re seeing them resolve, get settled, move on, you’re seeing that come to light. They’re not impacting our business,” Wacksman said.

As far as the macro picture, Hofmann said that without any sign of a market rebound, “its our job (to) just keep driving on the underlying structural growth drivers we have,” including software and rentals that are not rate dependent.

“We’re also fortunate in that the business has diversified pretty rapidly over the last four or five years,” he said.

Addressing the use of agentic AI and potential changes in how consumers search for homes, Wacksman and Hofmann both promised that Zillow’s model was built to thrive in this new environment.

“We see the human experiences remaining human,” Wacksman said. “The dreaming and shopping part is the part you want to do and the transaction part is the part you need to do, and Zillow is the best place to do both those things…and then our ability to make the professional’s job easier so they can serve the customer better is where we’re focused, and why we are so confident in the strategy.”

Jesse Williams is content director for RISMedia Premier.

#5525. Cigna beat profit expectations and raised its annual earnings forecast

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Adjusted earnings were $7.98 a share, up from $7.83 in the third quarter of 2025, and Cigna lifted its 2026 outlook by 15 cents

The Cigna $CI Group raised its 2026 profit forecast on Thursday after reporting third-quarter adjusted income from operations of $7.98 per share, compared with $7.83 in the third quarter of 2025.

The company expects full-year adjusted income from operations of at least $30.60 per share, up 15 cents from its prior projection. The third-quarter adjusted figure exceeded the average analyst estimate, according to Bloomberg. Revenue and profit at both Evernorth Health Services and Cigna Healthcare also exceeded analyst estimates.

Total revenues rose 6% to $73.7 billion. Shareholders' net income was $1.4 billion, or $5.47 per share, compared with $1.9 billion, or $6.98 per share, in the third quarter of 2025. The company said the decline mainly reflected the absence of an after-tax gain on a sale recognized in the 2025 quarter.

Adjusted pre-tax income at Evernorth Health Services fell 4%, while adjusted revenues rose 6%. Pharmacy Benefit Services adjusted pre-tax income dropped 22%, which the company attributed to large client contract renewals and strategic investments. Specialty and Care Services adjusted pre-tax income rose 15%, driven by organic growth in specialty businesses, including higher adoption of biosimilars and specialty generics.

Cigna Healthcare adjusted pre-tax income rose 15%, which the company attributed to higher net investment income and improved operating efficiency. The segment's medical care ratio, which measures medical costs as a percentage of premiums, was 85.0%, compared with 84.8% a year ago.

For 2026, Cigna Healthcare adjusted pre-tax income is projected at no less than $4.6 billion, up $50 million from the prior projection. The company narrowed its medical care ratio outlook to 84.2%, plus or minus 25 basis points. Evernorth adjusted pre-tax income is projected at no less than $6.9 billion.

Cigna raised its full-year forecast in July to at least $30.45 per share after second-quarter adjusted earnings of $7.78 per share.

Chief Executive Officer Brian Evanko said in a statement that the company is advancing its Accelerate to One initiative to drive productivity and reduce costs. The company hosted an Investor Day, where it set targets of 10% to 14% compound annual growth in adjusted earnings per share and about $50 billion in cumulative operating cash flow through 2030. It also announced a multiyear, $3 billion modernization and productivity initiative.

Management will host a conference call on the results at 8:30 a.m. ET on Thursday.

#5524. Bombardier is raising its free cash flow outlook after record services revenue

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Quarterly services revenue rose 19% to $701 million, while net income slipped to $81 million from $85 million

Bombardier raised its 2026 free cash flow guidance, lifting the target above $1.3 billion from the earlier level of more than $1.0 billion, according to third-quarter results released Thursday. It is the second increase to that target this year.

Services revenue reached a record $701 million, up 19% from a year earlier, and topped $700 million in a quarter for the first time. Total revenue rose 3% to $2.4 billion on 33 aircraft deliveries.

Net income from continuing operations declined to $81 million, down from $85 million in the same quarter last year. Diluted earnings per share were $0.73, compared with $0.77. Adjusted net income rose 41% to $182 million, and adjusted earnings per share were $1.72, up from $1.21. The adjustments include a net loss of $94 million tied to certain financial instruments.

Adjusted EBITDA increased 7% to $382 million, with a margin of 16.1% compared with 15.4% a year earlier. Reported EBIT was $266 million, up 17%.

Free cash flow for the quarter was $183 million, up 20%. Cash flows from operating activities totaled $259 million, up 36%, while net additions to property, plant and equipment and intangible assets were $76 million. Free cash flow for the first nine months was $771 million.

Bombardier left its other 2026 targets unchanged: more than 157 aircraft deliveries, revenue above $10.0 billion and adjusted EBITDA above $1.625 billion. Net additions to property, plant and equipment and intangible assets are expected to be near $300 million.

Backlog stood at $22.2 billion on Sept. 30, up $4.7 billion from the end of 2025. The unit book-to-bill ratio was 1.7 for the quarter.

The company ended the quarter with $2.4 billion in available liquidity, including $1.6 billion in cash and cash equivalents. It has cut debt by $1.1 billion this year and reached its target adjusted net debt to adjusted EBITDA ratio of 1.5.

"We are entering the final stretch of 2026 with a healthy backlog, strong demand and solid visibility on all remaining deliveries," President and CEO Éric Martel said in a statement.

Bombardier plans to hold an in-person Investor Day on Feb. 18, 2027, to update its strategic priorities and outlook. The company said details on timing and location will follow in the coming weeks.

#5523. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

#5522. Wendy's rejected Trian's $1.4 billion bid to take the burger chain private

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Wendy's board also adopted a one-year shareholder rights plan as its independent committee called the $7.35-a-share offer too low

Wendy's $WEN rejected a $7.35-a-share cash proposal from an investor group led by Trian Fund Management on Thursday, concluding the offer undervalues the burger chain.

A committee of independent directors, unaffiliated with Trian, reviewed the unsolicited, non-binding bid with outside financial and legal advisers, the company said. The committee's vote was unanimous. It found the proposal "substantially undervalues" Wendy's, does not reflect the value expected from the company's Dave's Way strategic plan, and is not in the best interests of Wendy's and its shareholders.

The investor group also includes Flynn Group LP, BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners. The proposal covers all Wendy's stock the group does not own.

"The Independent Committee thoroughly evaluated this Proposal and unanimously concluded that it substantially undervalues Wendy's standalone prospects and long-term earnings potential," Chairman Art Winkleblack said in a statement. He expressed confidence in the ability of CEO Bob Wright and his executive team to carry out the plan.

Wendy's board adopted a limited-duration shareholder rights plan on Nov. 4, the company said. Rights become exercisable if a person or group acquires beneficial ownership of 15% or more of Wendy's stock, or if a holder of 15% or more buys additional shares, without approval from the board or the independent committee. The plan expires Nov. 3, 2027, and the board may consider ending it sooner.

The board said it weighed the investor group's rejection of a company offer to enter a standstill agreement when it adopted the plan.

Wendy's announced Dave's Way on Thursday alongside its third-quarter results. The multi-year strategy focuses on growing customer traffic and market share while strengthening restaurant profitability. Wendy's stock slipped by under 1% ahead of the opening bell. Trian declined to comment, according to CNBC.

Trian submitted the proposal on Oct. 28, valuing the deal at about $1.4 billion and offering a premium of about 20% to the prior day's closing price. Trian and affiliated parties own about 16.3% of Wendy's stock. Flynn Group operates more than 340 Wendy's restaurants in the U.S. The proposal had no financing condition, and Trian reserved the right to withdraw or change the terms.

Wendy’s board set up the independent committee in February, prompted by a securities filing Trian had made, according to CNBC. Trian had been assembling investors for a take-private bid since August 2025, around the time Wendy’s cut its quarterly dividend in half and withdrew its full-year outlook. Wright became permanent president and CEO in May.

#5521. Amazon, Microsoft and other tech giants close higher after Democrats’ midterm sweep

Shares of Amazon.com Inc., Microsoft Corp., Alphabet Inc. and Meta Platforms Inc. closed higher today following Democrats’ resounding midterm victory.

Amazon jumped 8.3% at one point and ended the trading session 6.1% higher than Tuesday. Microsoft gained nearly 6.7% while Alphabet and Google rose by about 3.1% and 1.4%, respectively. Multiple industry analysts tied the stock gains to the companies’ artificial intelligence buildout.

Democrats won both chambers of Congress on a campaign that emphasized data center restrictions. Furthermore, voters approved 40 ballot measures focused on blocking or limiting AI infrastructure projects. Bloomberg cited Robert Pavlik, a senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth Management, as saying that tech giants’ shares jumped because investors believe a data center slowdown could improve their finances.

Amazon, Meta and Google have become cash-flow-negative in recent months because of their steep infrastructure investments. Last Wednesday, the search giant reported a negative cash flow that exceeded the consensus estimate by about $6.4 billion. Google’s stock price plummeted 10% in after-hours trading even though its cloud revenue more than doubled.

Needham & Co., B. ‌Riley ⁠Wealth and prominent tech industry analyst Ben Thompson highlighted another possible contributor to the stock rally. New restrictions on AI projects would make computing infrastructure more scarce, which would boost the value of existing data centers. That would benefit the tech giants that logged share price gains today.

Thompson noted that neoclouds, or emerging AI-focused cloud providers, may also benefit in certain respects. Developments for which they have already secured regulatory permission could become more valuable. At the same time, they may find it more difficult to finance new sites.

That dynamic weighed on chip stocks today. Nvidia Corp. and Intel Corp. both shed more than 3% of their value, while Broadcom Inc. declined 2%. SK hynix Inc., the world’s largest supplier of HBM memory for graphics cards, dropped by more than 5%. One notable exception was Advanced Micro Devices Inc., which ended the trading day about 1% higher.

Thompson noted that the midterms could also affect the AI industry in other ways. He pointed out that a stricter regulatory environment may give space-based data centers a boost. Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC, in turn, could see their hardware costs decline if new restrictions are placed on frontier model training. Such a development may ease their path to profitability.

Last month, Meta announced plans to sell up to $95 billion in shares to finance new data centers. On Monday, Oracle Corp. filed to issue $20 billion worth of bonds and shares in connection with its own AI buildout. It’s currently unclear how the midterm results will affect those initiatives and other large-scale data center projects currently underway.

#5520. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.

#5518. From Bhutan to Zurich: Risk Map 2027 Reveals Where Travelers Are Safest

LUND, Sweden, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Which countries and cities are among the safest for travelers in 2027, and where are the risks highest? Which countries have become safer over the past year, and which have become riskier? These questions are addressed by the Risk Map 2027, released today by Safeture, a leading provider of People Risk Management technology, and by travel risk intelligence company Riskline.

The map rates countries worldwide on Riskline's five-level scale: Low, Moderate, Medium, High, and Extreme. Risk levels are based on factors such as security, crime, health and environmental risks, and access to medical care. Over the past twelve months, six countries have improved their risk level, and 15 have moved to a higher level.

Ten of the safest and ten of the least safe

For this year's map, Riskline's analysts have selected ten countries and ten cities that stand out as among the safest for travelers, along with ten of each that are among the least safe. The selection spans all global regions and is not a ranking. The destinations are listed alphabetically:

Safe destinations can be found across Europe, Asia, Oceania, and the Americas, from Bhutan and Singapore to Chile, Costa Rica, and Canada. Ottawa is the only city to appear among the safest for the second consecutive year. At the other end of the scale, Kabul, Quetta, Port Moresby, Goma, and Port-au-Prince are again among the least safe cities, joined this year by Bamako, Guayaquil, Sana'a, San Pedro Sula, and Tehran.

Sharpest rise in the Gulf and the wider Middle East

The most striking shift over the past year has occurred in the Middle East. Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates have each moved up two levels, from Moderate to High. Saudi Arabia and Jordan have risen from Medium to High, and Oman from Moderate to Medium. Iran has moved from High to Extreme, the highest level on the scale. For many organizations, these changes matter: the Gulf states are major hubs for business travel, aviation, and regional operations.

Germany and Finland leave the lowest risk level

In Europe, Germany, Finland, and Cyprus have moved from Low to Moderate, as has Greenland. Moderate remains the second-lowest level on the scale, and Europe remains home to several of the map's safest destinations, including Switzerland, Iceland, Slovenia, and Denmark, as well as Oslo, Vienna, Zagreb, and Zurich.

There are also positive developments. Bangladesh, Cameroon, Mozambique, and Nepal have all moved from High to Medium, while El Salvador and the Maldives have improved from Medium to Moderate. Elsewhere, South Sudan has risen from High to Extreme, Guinea-Bissau from Medium to High, and Cuba from Moderate to Medium.

A risk map cannot replace an organization's own risk assessment. Threats describe the situation in a country, while the actual risk depends on the individual traveler: where they are, what they are doing, and how well their organization can support them. As a neutral reference point, the map helps organizations understand the broader landscape, identify emerging patterns, and prepare travelers before they depart.

"This year's map shows how quickly the risk picture can change. Several Gulf states that many companies regard as stable business hubs have moved up two levels in a single year, and even Germany and Finland are no longer at the lowest level. For organizations, the lesson is that duty of care cannot rely on last year's assumptions. It requires up-to-date intelligence and the ability to reach your people quickly," said Jonas Brorson, Chief Marketing Officer at Safeture.

As in previous years, the Risk Map 2027 is free to download at: www.safeture.com/riskmaps

For additional information, visit safeture.com or contact:

Safeture CMO Jonas Brorson: jonas.brorson@safeture.com

By combining real-time risk intelligence, location awareness, and instant mass communication, Safeture enables faster response, stronger duty of care, and better decision-making for global operations. Trusted by medical assistance providers, security companies, insurers, and multinational organizations, Safeture supports travel, facility, and workforce safety through a scalable, partner-centric platform. Safeture AB is listed on Nasdaq First North Growth Market Stockholm (ticker: SFTR). Redeye Nordic Growth AB is the company's Certified Adviser.
