#5502. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5501. Bright turns on Ocusell integration so agents enter listings once

Bright MLS launched a live integration with Ocusell’s network, letting agents enter and edit listings once and syndicate to Bright and other MLSs. Ocusell says it can cut listing creation time up to 75% and prevent over 85% of compliance errors.  AI Summary

Bright MLS has turned on its live integration with Ocusell’s listing network, allowing brokers and agents who work across multiple MLSs in the Mid-Atlantic to enter and edit listings once and syndicate them into Bright and other participating MLSs without double data entry, the companies announced Tuesday.

The operational launch marks the first major product milestone from the joint venture Bright and Ocusell formed in 2025 and introduces OneList, a co-developed listing input platform built on the Ocusell Network that is designed to give brokerages and MLSs a single, connected listing interface nationwide.

“We entered into this joint venture to remove friction from the daily work of our brokers and agents,” said Bright MLS President and CEO Brian Donnellan, who is also a HousingWire Vanguard award winner. “Our role as an MLS is to adapt to how real estate pros operate and to help them succeed. This partnership with Ocusell is a clear example of that.”

The launch comes as the Open Real Estate (ORE) initiative is running a national request for proposal search for a vendor that can deliver “input once, distribute everywhere” listing entry across markets. Ocusell says it is already live across 30 MLSs, and with OneList now operating at Bright, one of the nation’s largest MLSs, the company is positioning its network as a scalable solution for multi-MLS entry.

For brokers, the integration is aimed at reducing staff time and compliance risk tied to re-keying listing data into separate MLS systems. Agents can enter listing specifics, photos and disclosures once; the platform then auto-validates those fields against each local MLS’s rules while maintaining existing access and display policies. According to Ocusell, its infrastructure can cut listing creation time by up to 75% and prevent more than 85% of compliance errors.

On top of cross-market sync, according to the announcement, the forthcoming OneList interface layers in real-time AI-driven compliance and Fair Housing screening, intelligent media management with automated photo tagging and organization, and integrated listing promotion that lets agents launch targeted marketing campaigns from the listing input workflow.

“This is a total game changer for agents, brokers, and home buyers and sellers,” said Steve Mapes, executive in charge of growth strategy at Bright MLS. “When agents aren’t stuck doing double data entry because they belong to multiple MLSs, they have more time to serve their clients and do what they do best. Technology should make things better, faster and more efficient, and we’re excited to get this up and running.”

“Now is the time for MLSs to help shape what comes next for their brokers,” Hayden Rieveschl, the CEO of Ocusell and a 2026 HousingWire Insider, said in a statement. “Bright and Ocusell are demonstrating what’s possible when you listen to brokers and turn their needs into action. As more brokerages operate across markets, MLSs have an opportunity to remove barriers and make doing business easier.”

The move reflects a broader shift in organized real estate as large regional brokerages, teams and franchises increasingly span multiple MLS territories while regulators and plaintiffs’ attorneys scrutinize how listing data is shared and displayed.

For brokers and agents, multi-MLS input has historically meant duplicate work, inconsistent data, higher error rates and delays getting listings in front of buyers across markets. A centralized entry layer like OneList, if widely adopted, could streamline operations for multi-market firms, tighten compliance controls and create more standardized listing data for downstream tools, portals and valuation models.

For MLS organizations, the Bright-Ocusell rollout is a signal that listing input may increasingly be handled through connected, vendor-operated platforms rather than bespoke MLS-only interfaces, potentially reshaping how MLSs think about technology procurement, interoperability and data licensing.

Ocusell said the integration is live now for active Bright MLS brokerages that manage listings across multiple markets, according to the announcement. Bright said rollout timelines and early-access details for the broader OneList platform will be shared in future communications.

#5500. Supermicro Launches KV Cache Solution with IBM and NVIDIA Demonstrating Significant Inference Performance Benefits

SAN JOSE, Calif., Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Supermicro, Inc. (NASDAQ: SMCI), an AI, Enterprise, Storage, and 5G/Edge Total IT Solution Provider featuring Data Center Building Block SolutionsÂ® (DCBBS), today announced a new KV cache storage solution with IBM and NVIDIA. The joint solution integrates Supermicro Petascale all-flash storage servers using AMD EPYC 9005 Series processors ("Turin"), IBM Storage Scale software, along with NVIDIA Dynamo inference framework software and Spectrum-X Ethernet networking.

Together, these technologies can dramatically reduce the time it takes AI models to begin generating a response, a critical advantage as enterprises adopt agentic and long-context AI workflows. Extending KV cache capacity beyond local GPU memory can improve GPU utilization and inference throughput, while enabling high availability of KV cache content and non-disruptive scaling of KV cache capacity. The result is a more scalable, resilient inference architecture that delivers faster, more responsive AI experiences.

"As AI workloads expand from training to inference, enterprises and neoclouds deploying high-throughput inference workloads characteristic of agentic AI and long-context, multi-turn generative AI need to remove bottlenecks to improve GPU efficiency," said Charles Liang, president and CEO of Supermicro. "Our solution with IBM and NVIDIA clearly demonstrates these performance benefits."

For a video recap of this release, click here.

Inference workloads consist of two phases: prefill and decode. During prefill, input text is converted into tokens and processed by the LLM to generate the intermediate key-value (KV) states needed for inference. By storing these previously computed KV states in a persistent KV cache, the system can reuse them instead of recomputing the same context for subsequent requests. Agentic workflows, coding assistants, long-context RAG, multimodal AI, and multi-turn applications can generate substantial KV state as they process large codebases, documents, conversations, images, and other context, quickly exceeding GPU and CPU memory and driving the need to offload KV cache to high-capacity, shared network storage.

The KV cache solution from Supermicro, IBM, and NVIDIA provides this persistent storage layer, helping improve inference efficiency, throughput, and scalability while reducing redundant computation.

Key customer benefits of the KV cache solution include:

"Enterprises need a fundamentally better way to scale AI inference. Together, IBM, Supermicro, and NVIDIA are delivering a high-performance, resilient KV cache solution that helps customers maximize their GPU investments, scale independently of compute, and significantly improve infrastructure efficiency," said Sam Werner, GM, IBM Storage. "This collaboration represents an important step toward making enterprise AI inference more scalable, reliable, and cost-effective."

"Agentic AI and long-context applications depend on reusing context efficiently across many steps, and NVIDIA Dynamo helps orchestrate distributed inference so enterprises can get more usable throughput from every GPU," said Shruti Koparkar, NVIDIA AI Inference Product Lead. "By pairing NVIDIA Dynamo and Spectrum-X Ethernet with Supermicro Petascale storage servers and IBM Storage Scale, this KV cache solution creates a high-performance shared storage tier that can reduce redundant computation, improve time-to-first-token and help customers scale resilient AI inference services."

For more information on Supermicro and IBM solutions click here, and to read the IBM Redbook, Context without Limits: A High-Performance KV Cache Platform for Large-Scale AI Inference, click here.

About Super Micro Computer, Inc.Supermicro (NASDAQ: SMCI) is a global leader in Application-Optimized Total IT Solutions. Founded and operating in San Jose, California, Supermicro is committed to delivering first-to-market innovation for Enterprise, Cloud, AI, and 5G Telco/Edge IT Infrastructure. We are a Total IT Solutions provider with server, AI, storage, IoT, switch systems, software, and support services. #5499. Zillow pushes Preferred agent program toward 100% of buyer connections

Zillow reported Q3 2026 traffic down 3% to 215 million monthly users and a $158 million net loss. It highlighted AI mode expansion, Preferred growth and gains in mortgage and rentals revenue.  AI Summary

Zillow may be facing calls for investigations into some of its practices by consumer advocacy organizations and federal lawmakers, but the real estate listing portal giant is doubling down on its belief that it is “building the faster, easier and more affordable moving experience.”

“As more consumers and professionals use Zillow to move from dreaming to transacting, the old real estate experience will feel slow, difficult and expensive by comparison,”  Zillow CEO Jeremy Wacksman and Zillow COO and CFO Jeremy Hofmann wrote in a letter to shareholders published on Wednesday.

Despite this confidence, Zillow may be facing some headwinds. The company said that in the third quarter of 2026, visitor traffic to its apps and sites was down 3% during the quarter to 215 million average monthly unique users, while overall visits were down 5% annually to 2.3 billion according to Comscore data. Despite the declines, Comscore data shows that Zillow attracted 77% of average monthly unique visitors in the real estate category in Q3. In addition to this, the company said it has found that its AI search mode is deepening engagement, with visitors who use this option spending nearly three times as long as those who don’t on the site.

Zillow said that AI mode is now available to 100% of its signed-in users. The company said it was also exploring ways to use AI to make real estate professionals more productive and to help its internal engineers, who are using AI to ship 60% more changes to production than they did in 2024, according to Zillow.

“Buyers spend an average of two to three hours a week with us over about five months — and then for most, Zillow software and services power their transaction: the majority of residential real estate transactions in the U.S. run through our professional software,” the executives wrote. “Because of Zillow’s transaction infrastructure, our agentic AI does more than guide the shopping experience people love; it assists consumers and professionals throughout the transaction itself.

In addition to the decline in traffic, Zillow also reported a net loss of $158 million for the quarter, down from a $10 million net income generated in Q3 2025. This decline came even as revenue rose 7% annually to $724 million.

Zillow’s Preferred lead referral program is one of cornerstones of its revenue generation engine. The company reported that in Q3, two-thirds of buyer connections came to a Preferred agent partner in the integrated experience, roughly double what it was a year ago. Zillow said it was on track for Preferred to represent over three-quarters of connections by the end of the year, with it anticipating reaching 100% of connections in the first half of 2027. Zillow also noted that Preferred connections generate 35% more revenue per connection that its previous lead generation model.

Even with the growth of the Preferred program, Zillow’s for-sale revenue was flat year-over-year at $489 million. In addition to this, its residential segment recorded a 4% annual decline in revenue to $419 million, which the company attributed to higher-than-expected mortgage rates putting downward pressure on housing transaction volume.

Bright spots in Zillow’s Q3 earnings report occurred in its mortgage and rentals segments. Zillow’s mortgage rose 32% annually to $70 million, due to a 55% increase in purchase loan origination volume to $2.0 billion.

In markets where Zillow has integrated its mortgage product with its Preferred program the longest, Zillow said adoption rates of Zillow Home Loans is around 20%.

“We are also making Zillow Home Loans a trusted lender for Preferred agent partners’ entire book of business, not just for clients they connect with through Zillow,” Wacksman and Hofmann wrote.

Rentals revenue was up 26% year-over-year to $220 million, which the company attributed to multifamily revenue growing 35% year over year. Zillow said its rentals segment now accounts for roughly 30% of its total revenue, up from 21% two years ago. Additionally, the company noted that 81,000 multifamily properties were advertised on Zillow at the end of the third quarter, a 17% annual increase.

“Diversifying into this space has brought us a large growth opportunity and made our business more robust,” the executives wrote. “Our rentals strategy is to offer the broadest, most comprehensive inventory from single-family homes to large apartment buildings, and to streamline the transaction experience for consumers and housing providers.”

Executives added that they believe Zillow is still just scratching the surface of the opportunity presented by the rentals sector.

“We see a clear path to more than $1 billion in annual rentals revenue and a substantial opportunity to keep growing across both multifamily and longtail rentals well beyond that milestone,” Wacksman and Hofmann wrote.

The company also highlighted the performance of some of its other offerings, noting that its CRM product, Follow Up Boss, recorded roughly 141,000 monthly active users in Q3, up 16% annually. In addition to this, Zillow said over 800 brokerages had signed up for its pre-marketing product Zillow Preview and its listing enhancement product, Zillow Showcase, was on 5.4% of all new U.S. listings.

“Even as housing conditions deteriorated sharply, Zillow kept growing and outperforming, powered by our brand, audience, value to partners, disciplined cost management and strong growth levers across our well-diversified business,” Hofmann and Wacksman wrote. “These advantages are driving our performance through an exceptionally difficult macro environment today and position us to accelerate when conditions improve.”

#5498. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5497. Phaze raises $8.75M to give AI agents remote access to powerful workstations

If autonomous artificial intelligence agents are really going to become the future of the enterprise then they’re going to need to have a computer of their own so they can get on with their work without disturbing anyone else.

The founders of the remote desktop firm Parsec Technologies Inc. have come up with a new offering that’s designed to give those agents the computer access they need. Their new startup is called Phaze Inc., and it has just launched its offering after raising $8.75 million in seed funding from Andreessen Horowitz. Today’s round also saw participation from Index, NextView, Makers and Lerer Hippeau.

Phaze has developed a high-performance remote desktop platform that’s designed to accommodate both humans and AI agent workers, giving them access to powerful computers, including high-end workstations. With its platform, those users can control a distant workstation with the same low-latency responsiveness and visual fidelity they’d get if they were accessing hardware locally.

The startup says it’s trying to solve a couple of glaring efficiency problems at many enterprises. One issue is the emergence of computer-use agents that like to hijack worker’s screens while automating mundane business tasks, reducing human productivity.

Another challenge is that many enterprises invest in powerful workstations capable of rendering complex 3D graphics and compiling massive codebases that can cost upwards of $10,000. Those machines are needed, but many information technology departments tend to have a policy of assigning one machine to each employee, which means that expensive hardware is often left sitting idle if that person goes out for lunch, sits in a meeting or takes a few days off.

Phaze’s solution is to transform those workstations into a shared pool of elastic compute, allowing anyone at an organization to access it via its proprietary low-latency streaming technology when they need it. This streaming tech is backed by a specially developed Model Context Protocol server that allows computer use agents to log into and operate expensive workstations the same way a human employee would.

The result: Instead of working exclusively through expensive and brittle application programming interfaces, agents can access a computer directly and navigate its operating system, launch applications and get work done.

Phaze co-founder and Chief Executive Benjy Boxer said the platform also supports human-to-agent collaboration, so they can work together to get more complex tasks done. For instance, an automated IT support bot might work to diagnose problems when new tickets are created, and then pass the session to a human engineer if the solution is more nuanced than what it’s authorized to do by itself.

“The computer sitting on your desk shouldn’t determine what compute you can access,” Boxer said. “People need powerful workstations to do their jobs, and now AI agents need computers they can actually operate. We’re building the access layer that lets either one connect to the machine they need, wherever it happens to be.”

By transforming expensive workstations into shared infrastructure, administrators can assign their computing resources dynamically to whoever needs access as people’s and agent’s workflows fluctuate. The workstations themselves can be sat on a desk, installed in a data center, or locked away in a cupboard. Wherever they’re located, organizations will be able to get maximum efficiency out of them.

Phaze’s job now is to convince enterprises of the benefits of its platform, and Boxer said the money from today’s round will be used to accelerate its go-to-market plans and onboard new customers. The startup will also look to expand its engineering team and develop more features.

Andreessen Horowitz General Partner Martin Casado think Phaze is likely to see a lot of interest in its remote access platform, because workstations are too expensive to be left sitting idle for hours at a time. “Phaze is turning those machines into shared infrastructure for people and AI agents,” he said. “Benjy and the team have been building in this space for more than a decade and they bring that experience to a new era of remote access and machine management.”

Inferentieworkloads bestaan uit twee fasen: prefill en decode. Door deze eerder berekende KV-toestanden op te slaan in een permanente KV-cache, kan het systeem ze opnieuw gebruiken in plaats van dezelfde context bij volgende verzoeken opnieuw te berekenen. Agentische workflows, programmeerassistenten, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) met lange contexten, multimodale AI en toepassingen met meerdere interactierondes kunnen aanzienlijke hoeveelheden KV-toestandsgegevens genereren wanneer ze grote codebases, documenten, gesprekken, afbeeldingen en andere context verwerken. Daardoor kan de capaciteit van het GPU- en CPU-geheugen snel worden overschreden, waardoor het noodzakelijk wordt de KV-cache onder te brengen in gedeelde netwerkopslag met een hoge capaciteit.

"Agentische AI en toepassingen met lange contexten zijn afhankelijk van het efficiÃ«nt hergebruiken van context over meerdere stappen. NVIDIA Dynamo helpt gedistribueerde inferentie te coÃ¶rdineren, zodat ondernemingen meer bruikbare doorvoercapaciteit uit elke GPU kunnen halen", aldus Shruti Koparkar, AI Inference Product Lead bij NVIDIA. #5495. HECM broker rankings for August stay steady as shift to proprietary products rolls on

August HECM endorsements kept Atlantic Avenue Mortgage, loanDepot and Caliver Beach atop 12-month broker rankings. RMI data later showed September endorsements fell 6.7% to 1,790, the lowest since April 2020.  AI Summary

Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM) endorsements for August show that Atlantic Avenue Mortgage, loanDepot and Caliver Beach Mortgage remain the top brokers on a 12-month rolling basis, according to a report published Wednesday by HECMWorld.com based on data compiled by Reverse Market Insight (RMI).

The three leading brokers have remained intact for much of 2026, with Atlantic Avenue now at a rolling total of 1,002 endorsements, down slightly from 1,009 in July. loanDepot endorsed 43 loans in August, upping its rolling total to 476, while Caliver Beach produced 19 loans, dropping its rolling total slightly to 352.

The rest of the top 10 on a rolling basis includes West Capital Lending (194), C2 Financial Corp. (191), Barrett Financial Group (155), NEXA Lending (140), Carrington Mortgage Services (122), Senior Lending Corp. (115) and Integrity 1st Mortgage (107).

West Capital Lending had a strong month and jumped ahead of C2 Financial for #4, 194 to 191, after adding 15 loans in August. Caliver Beach Mortgage stays at #3 with 352.

HECMWorld.com noted in an email that it’s still waiting for data from the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to compile its HECM direct lender rankings for October. The data for the prior month is typically released in the first few days of each month.

September data published by RMI showed that HECM endorsements were down 6.7% from August, with the 1,790 loans in September representing the lowest total for any month since April 2020.

Last month, New View Advisors released the newest edition of its Proprietary Reverse Mortgage Production Index, which shows that private-label products are driving overall growth for reverse mortgage originations even as HECM production wanes. The company said that prop loans represented more than 60% of reverse mortgage volume in September — a share that is likely to rise further.

“Rising interest rates may challenge the reverse mortgage industry in the fourth quarter, but proprietary loans could still propel reverse mortgage industry totals to over $8 billion in 2026, versus $7.3 billion in total new originations of reverse mortgages in 2025,” New View explained.

In his weekly “Ribler on Rates” video series, Dan Ribler of Longbridge Financial said Wednesday that the 10-year Treasury yield, which closely connects with long-term mortgage rates, has offered some relief to capital markets and borrowers in recent weeks.

“In the last 30 days, the 10-year Treasury yield is down about 35 basis points at the same time as the S&P 500 is down about 2.5% to 3%. This is not a structural, massive repricing of anything,” Ribler said.

“This is just a 30-day cycle of risk-off — currencies, dollars moving out of riskier assets, whether it’s stocks, whether it’s AI infrastructure, into safer assets and Treasurys. As more dollars move into Treasurys, the price goes up and the yield comes down, and we get a little bit of rate love on our rate sheets.”

HousingWire‘s Mortgage Rates Center on Wednesday showed that 30-year fixed rates averaged 7.34%, although rates for reverse mortgage products typically run higher than that figure. Higher rates impact reverse mortgages differently than traditional forward mortgages as they eat into available proceeds for borrowers.

As lenders look to keep business flowing through the end of the year and beyond, they’re looking to technology as a potential spark plug.

On Wednesday, Nationwide Equities Corp. announced the launch of ReverseReach, which aims to help traditional mortgage brokers with lead generation efforts through their databases of past clients.

“We created ReverseReach to make uncovering those highly lucrative opportunities simple, efficient and accessible — even for brokers who have never closed a reverse mortgage before — so they can confidently and comfortably begin originating them,” CEO Paul Lamparillo said.

#5494. Tannenbaum Helpern Appoints Legal Marketing Veteran Damien E. Cohen as Chief Marketing and Business Development Officer

NEW YORK, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Tannenbaum Helpern is pleased to announce that Damien E. Cohen has joined the Firm as Chief Marketing and Business Development Officer. Damien has spent more than 35 years helping law firms grow, and he brings that experience to the Firm's strategic marketing, branding, communications, and client initiatives.

His arrival is an important investment in the Firm and in our ability to continue delivering value to our clients."

Damien has built and led marketing and business development teams at prominent law firms, most recently serving as Chief Marketing Officer of a global Am Law 100 firm. Throughout his career, he has advised law firm leaders on business development strategy, competitive intelligence, market positioning, and initiatives designed to support revenue growth. His work has focused on aligning marketing and business development efforts with firmwide priorities while enabling attorneys and teams to cultivate client relationships.

"I was drawn to Tannenbaum Helpern's culture, its commitment to client service, and the opportunity to help shape the future of a premier New York law firm," said Cohen. "I look forward to working with the Firm's leadership, attorneys, and business professionals to build on that foundation."

Since 1978, Tannenbaum Helpern has combined a powerful mix of insight, creativity, industry knowledge, legal talent, and experience to successfully guide clients through periods of challenge and opportunity. Our mission is to deliver the highest quality legal services in a practical and efficient manner and to provide the judgment, common sense, and legal acumen of well-trained, business-minded lawyers, all within a culture that fosters an inclusive and respectful workplace. Through our commitment to exceptional service and driven by a focus on results, Tannenbaum Helpern continues to earn the loyalty of our clients and a reputation for excellence.

#5493. Mortgage policy faces tight runway in split Washington

Democrats now control both chambers of Congress while President Trump retains the White House and agency leadership. Trade groups including the MBA and ALTA are pushing for cost relief, FHA premium cuts and stronger consumer protections, while analysts warn that geopolitical tensions, looming debt ceiling fights and tougher confirmations at agencies like the CFPB will keep rates and regulatory timelines uncertain.  AI Summary

Housing and mortgage industry leaders say there is room for housing policy to move in Congress even as Washington, D.C., divides power between a Democratic-controlled House and Senate and a Republican-led White House.

Democrats captured both chambers on Tuesday night, but any housing bills under the new leadership will need support from President Donald Trump and enough Republican votes to clear the Senate. “Voters made it clear that affordability is a central concern, and housing is the biggest line item in most family budgets,” said Isaac Boltansky, head of public policy at Pennymac. “The ROAD to Housing Act laid a solid foundation, and we believe lawmakers on both sides of the aisle should work on a ROAD to Housing 2.0 package that builds on it and helps more families buy and keep a home.”

Asked what should be included in a 2.0 package, Boltansky cited the lock-in effect created by capital gains taxes, which can discourage homeowners from selling, and the Neighborhood Homes Investment Act as a “good starting point.”

The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) said in a statement that housing remains a bipartisan issue and it will “work with new and returning lawmakers as well as the Trump administration to advance common sense proposals to lower costs.”

The trade group in October released a policy road map to reduce closing costs, expand credit access and lower rental housing financing costs. Its proposals include easing tri-merge credit report use, aligning loan-level price adjustments (LLPAs) and lowering the annual mortgage insurance premium for Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans.

Scott Norman, CEO of the Texas Mortgage Bankers Association, told HousingWire that the election shifts power but also creates opportunity for policy changes.

“It was a surprising night, but every election brings opportunity,” Norman said. “In Austin and in Washington, a gavel is something you borrow, and last night voters took a few back. That’s the system working as designed. No chairmanship belongs to the person holding it, and no majority is permanent. In much of the world, a change in power signals a crisis. Here, it simply means new leadership and a fresh look at policy.”

The American Land Title Association (ALTA) said that as policymakers continue addressing housing affordability challenges, consumer protection must remain part of the conversation.

“Fraud is unaffordable, and increasingly sophisticated schemes are putting American homeowners and their property rights at risk,” ALTA said.

Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com, said many Democratic campaigns emphasized economic issues, but the impact of the elections on the broader economy and mortgage rates is still unclear.

“Democrats have a clear mandate to focus on pocketbook issues, but whether they can translate that into a legislative agenda that delivers on that mandate remains to be seen,” Krimmel said.

Krimmel pointed to the conflict in the Middle East as a key variable. He said uncertainty remains around how the election outcome will affect the Iran war, which has been a source of inflation pressure. Democrats have been vocal critics of the conflict, and a resolution that improves oil supply would likely ease inflation and “potentially provide relief for mortgage rates.”

“Wanting the conflict to end, and finding terms that work for all involved are two different things,” Krimmel said.

On fiscal policy, Boltansky said another debt ceiling confrontation is likely in 2027: “Any focus on addressing the country’s harrowing fiscal trajectory would be welcome for the bond market, which obviously has a direct impact on rates,” he said.

While Congress can set agendas and control oversight, executive branch leadership will still drive most regulatory implementation for housing and mortgage markets.

Tim Rood, founder and CEO of Washington, D.C.-based advisory and technology firm Impact Capitol, said in his newsletter that Democratic majorities can control the agendas for the House financial services and Senate banking committees, investigate agencies, shape spending negotiations and withhold Senate confirmation of nominees when the new Congress convenes in January.

But he pointed out that Trump retains executive authority and leadership at agencies “does not change automatically with Congress.”

Rood said that for mortgage executives, the new alignment means more hearings, tougher confirmations and a more contested implementation calendar, “not an overnight rewrite of the rules.”

“The real fight will be over which existing policies can still be executed, funded and defended,” he said.

One closely watched appointment is Brian Johnson’s nomination to lead the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB). An attorney told HousingWire the confirmation is now at risk as Democrats may demand additional representation across financial agencies as part of broader negotiations.

The same attorney said one of the industry’s top regulatory priorities — changes to the loan originator compensation rule — remains unresolved.

“There are things that both sides of the aisle could help, like increase the availability of credit to borrowers by allowing lenders to claw back compensation in certain situations or compete. Maybe something will happen that is coordinated, but I think it’s kind of open in the air at the moment,” the attorney said.

Editor’s note: Sarah Wheeler contributed reporting to this story.

#5492. Marelli confirms its appointment of Laurent Favre as Chief Executive Officer to lead its next phase of transformation

Bram Schot expected to become Chair of Marelli on emergence from Chapter 11

SOUTHFIELD, Mich., Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Marelli, a global technology partner to the automotive industry, today confirmed the appointment of Laurent Favre as Chief Executive Officer (CEO), with immediate effect, succeeding Frederick "Fritz" Henderson as he concludes his tenure as Interim CEO.

Mr. Favre will lead Marelli through its emergence from Chapter 11 and the next phase of its transformation. His appointment follows the announcement in April this year from the Ad Hoc Group of Lenders to Marelli that he would succeed Mr. Henderson (https://marelli.com/en/news/marelli-announces-leadership-appointments.html).

Separately, the Ad Hoc Group of lenders to Marelli today announced that upon emergence from Chapter 11 and once all conditions precedent to the restructuring have been satisfied, they plan to appoint Bram Schot as Chair of the Board of Marelli. As Chair, Mr. Schot will support the CEO and leadership team on delivering the company's strategic priorities. Mr. Schot has held senior roles across Mercedes-Benz then the Volkswagen Group for over three decades and was most recently the CEO of Audi. Mr. Schot brings extensive board experience, including roles at Shell, Richemont, Cognizant, Signify, two of which as deputy chairman. He is also a Senior Advisor at the Carlyle Group.

The Marelli Board thanks Mr. Henderson for his leadership during a critical period for Marelli. He has brought stability and focus to the business, supported its people and customers, and made significant progress in discussions with Marelli's OEM partners.

Dinesh Paliwal, Executive Chairman, said:

"Fritz stepped into the role at a demanding moment and has led Marelli with judgement, clarity and commitment. On behalf of the Board, we thank him for everything he has done for the company, its customers and its people.

"Laurent brings deep knowledge of the global automotive industry and a strong record of leading complex international businesses. He understands the operational discipline needed to deliver for customers and the opportunities ahead for Marelli's products and technologies".

Mr. Favre has spent more than two decades in senior roles with leading automotive suppliers, including ThyssenKrupp, ZF and Benteler, where he served as Chief Executive Officer of the Automotive Division. From 2020 to 2025, he was Chief Executive Officer of Plastic Omnium, later renamed OPmobility. During his tenure, he led the company through significant transformation, expanding its international footprint, diversifying its customer base and broadening its technology and product portfolio.

"I am honoured to lead Marelli at this pivotal point in its history. I want to thank Fritz for his leadership and for the progress he and the Marelli team have made during a challenging period.

"Our immediate priority is to complete the work required for a successful emergence from Chapter 11. Emergence is a critical milestone, but the turnaround must continue beyond it. We will focus on restoring Marelli's financial strength, improving performance across the business and strengthening customer confidence through consistent delivery.

"Beyond emergence, our ambition is to build a financially stronger, more competitive Marelli, combining operational excellence with focused innovation and profitable growth. We have talented people, strong technologies and longstanding customer relationships. I look forward to working with colleagues across Marelli to turn those strengths into lasting results and build a business our people are proud to be part of."

"It has been a privilege to lead Marelli during this important period. I am proud of the progress our colleagues have made and grateful for their commitment to the business and its customers.

"Laurent brings extensive automotive experience and a clear understanding of what it takes to succeed in this industry. I wish him and the entire Marelli team every success as they take the company forward."

"Marelli has the talent, technology and customer relationships to succeed. I look forward to supporting Laurent and the team when I will take up the role as Chair following emergence from Chapter 11. Our long-term focus is clear: deliver on our commitments, strengthen customer partnerships and build a stronger, more competitive and sustainable Marelli."

Marelli will continue to work closely with its customers, employees, suppliers and other stakeholders as it progresses towards emergence and builds the foundations for long-term success.

Marelli is a global mobility technology supplier to the automotive industry. With a strong and established track record in innovation and manufacturing excellence, our mission is to transform the future of mobility through working with customers and partners to create a safer, greener, and better-connected world. With around 40,000 employees worldwide, the Marelli footprint includes over 150 sites globally. For more information, visit the Marelli website at www.marelli.com.

#5491. Ocient raises $100 million as agentic AI drives growth in large-scale analytics

Ocient Inc., the maker of a speedy data analytics platform, today said it has raised $100 million in a Series C funding to expand its agentic artificial intelligence analytics business.

That business is fueled by growing demand from national security organizations and telecommunications providers seeking to analyze massive datasets without sampling. The new round brings the Chicago-based company’s total funding to $260 million.

Ocient said it expects revenue to more than triple in its current fiscal year, which ends in January, after doubling revenue the previous year. The company said the new financing will accelerate delivery of its OcientAIQ Solutions, which enable AI agents and human analysts to query petabyte-scale datasets.

Chief Executive John Morris said much of the growth is coming from new customers in national security and telecommunications, particularly organizations using the platform to consolidate cybersecurity information.

“They’ve been accustomed to having to sample data coming off the network,” Morris said. “They don’t have anything that can handle the ingest rates, nor that can store at an affordable price tens of petabytes of data.”

Ocient’s original business focused on high-performance analytics, but the emergence of AI agents has expanded its potential market. Increasingly, software agents rather than human analysts are querying its systems, driving higher utilization and creating demand for more comprehensive datasets.

The OcientAIQ Unified Data Platform combines ingestion, analytics, governance and agent orchestration. Its architecture minimizes data movement and uses forward error correction instead of conventional replication to provide data protection with reduced storage overhead.

“The architecture is designed not to move data around constantly as most architectures do, and to have nothing replicated,” Morris said.

The company competes with Snowflake Inc., Databricks Inc. and open-source analytics implementations, although its technology frequently complements existing platforms rather than replacing them, the CEO said.

Cybersecurity has emerged as a particularly promising market. Ocient provides the underlying data infrastructure that enables security tools and AI agents to analyze network activity across complete historical datasets, potentially identifying threats that conventional sampling would miss.

However, Morris said the company isn’t positioned as a cybersecurity tool. “We don’t do the detection algorithms and the sort of things that the companies in that space do,” Morris said.

Government and defense customers account for a substantial portion of Ocient’s business. The company recently established a dedicated national security subsidiary to serve those markets.

Morris said the new funding should be sufficient to help Ocient reach breakeven, although he declined to provide a timetable. Ocient plans to direct much of the investment toward hiring sales and customer delivery personnel while continuing engineering development.

The company is also seeing increasing demand for on-premises deployments as customers seek greater control over costs and sensitive information. “Most of our opportunities now are on-prem because they’re either repatriating for cost reasons or for data sovereignty and data protection issues,” Morris said.

The company is also looking to expand geographically, particularly in Europe, Asia-Pacific and Latin America, while pursuing additional cybersecurity customers.

The round was co-led by Boka Capital Ltd. and OCA Ventures LLC, with participation from previous investors Greycroft Partners LLC, In-Q-Tel Inc., Blue Bear Capital LLC, Buoyant Ventures Management LLC, PSP Partners LLC’s PSP Growth fund and Pritzker Group Venture Capital LLC.
